# CivilKit Calcs: the guide in one file

Source: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/ . Each chapter below starts with its address.

---

Chapter: Introduction
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/

# Introduction

CivilKit Calcs is an engineering calculation sheet that runs in your browser. You write a
calculation as readable text, with quantities, units, formulas and notes, and the page works it
out and shows a formatted report. You can plot the results, export the report to Word, Excel or
PDF, and keep working with no network connection.

Everything is calculated on your own computer. The engine is compiled to WebAssembly and runs
inside the page, so a calculation is never sent to a server.

> **Try it.** [Open CivilKit Calcs](https://civilkit.io/calcs/) in a new tab and start typing, or
> begin from a worked example in [Calculators and guides](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/): a beam,
> a retaining wall, a pad footing, a pipe or a pump, each of which opens as a form. The
> [product page](https://civilkit.io/calc/) gives the short overview.

## What you get

* **Real units.** `6 m`, `12 kN/m`, `300 MPa`. The engine multiplies, divides and converts
  them, and it refuses to add a length to a time. A moment comes out in kilonewton metres
  because the units said so, not because you typed a label.
* **Two ways to write.** The *sheet* format is Markdown prose with `name: value` lines. The
  *Calcpad worksheet language* (`.cpd`) is the full language of CalcpadCE, with macros, input
  forms and every directive. Both run on the same engine, and a sheet can show you the Calcpad
  it becomes.
* **Vectors, matrices and a large function library.** Linear solves, eigenvalues, interpolation,
  numerical integration, root finding and more.
* **Plots.** A one-line `plot` command, the Calcpad `$Plot` and `$Map` commands, and a Python
  block that draws with a matplotlib-style or Plotly-style interface, including 3D charts.
* **Python blocks.** Small Python programs inside a sheet, run in the page, with results handed
  back to the sheet as ordinary quantities.
* **Templates with inputs.** Put a `?` in front of a value (`L: ? 6 m`) and it becomes a box, a
  drop-down, radio buttons or a checkbox in a fill-in form. A template is one file.
* **Symbolic maths.** Rearrange a formula, differentiate, integrate or solve exactly.
* **A worksheet importer.** Bring in worksheets from another calculation tool.
* **Export.** Word with real equations, Excel with native charts, and PDF through the print
  dialog.
* **Free and open source.** The source is on GitHub under the MIT licence.

## Where to start

If you have never used it, open [Your first sheet](getting-started/first-sheet.md) and follow it
through once. It takes about five minutes. After that, read [The sheet format](sheet/index.md),
which describes everything you can write on a sheet line. The later chapters are independent: read
the ones you need.

Each chapter that matches a short how-to video carries a line starting with "Video:". The
videos are recorded from the scripts in the `book/videos` folder of the source.

## The videos

| --- | --- | --- |

The lengths are the planned ones in the storyboards.

## Credit

CivilKit Calcs is built on [CalcpadCE](https://github.com/imartincei/CalcpadCE), the continuation
of Calcpad by Nedelcho Ganchovski (Proektsoft) and contributors. The worksheet language, the
editor support and the sample worksheets all come from that work. See
[Credits and licences](appendix/credits.md).

## A note on the examples

Every `sheet` and `cpd` example in this guide was run through the real engine when the guide was
built (`book/check-examples.sh`). The results shown beside them are what the engine printed, with
the default setting of two decimals. The seven template sheets quoted in [Templates with
inputs](templates.md) are checked to be identical to the samples the app ships. The Python examples
and the input forms need the browser: they are run in the built app (`book/check-python.mjs`),
which also counts the controls each form draws.

Chapter: Your first sheet in five minutes
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/getting-started/first-sheet

# Your first sheet in five minutes

<!-- description: Build a bending check for a simply supported beam in five minutes: type inputs with units, add a pass or fail message, change a number and save. -->

<p><strong>Video:</strong> Your first calculation in 5 minutes</p>
<video controls preload="none" poster="../videos/01-first-calculation.jpg" style="width:100%;max-width:960px" src="../videos/01-first-calculation.mp4"></video>

This walk-through builds a bending check for a simply supported beam. You will type a few lines,
see units work, add a pass or fail message and change a number.

## 1. Open a new sheet

Open https://civilkit.io/calcs/ . The first tab is a short welcome sheet. To start your own, use
**File > New sheet**, or the **New** button at the top left. A sheet opens with a few lines of
example text. Select all of it and delete it. The editor is on the left and the result is on the
right.

> A sheet is a plain text file. Its first line is `<!--sheet-->`, which the editor adds for you.

## 2. Type the inputs

Type these lines. Each one is a *quantity line*: a name, a colon, a value with a unit, and after
a bar `|` a note.

```sheet
# Beam check

A simply supported beam under a uniform load.

L: 6 m | span
w: 12 kN/m | design load
```

The result pane shows the heading, the sentence, and two lines like these:

```text
L = 6 m    span
w = 12 kN/m    design load
```

The result updates as you type. If it does not, press **Calculate** on the Calculation tab, or Ctrl+Alt+X.

## 3. Calculate with units

Add a line below the inputs:

```sheet
L: 6 m | span
w: 12 kN/m | design load
Mstar: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum bending moment
```

The result shows the formula, the numbers put in, and the answer:

```text
M⋆ = w·L²/8 = 12 kN/m · (6 m)² / 8 = 54 kN·m    maximum bending moment
```

Three things happened:

* `Mstar` was written as M with a subscript "star". A name that ends in `star` after a capital
  letter becomes a subscript. Greek names work the same way: `phi` is φ, `sigma_c` is σ with a
  subscript c.
* `^` is a power. `L^2` is L squared.
* `-> kN*m` asked for the answer in kilonewton metres. Without it the engine picks a unit
  itself, which here is also kN·m. Write `->` when you want to be sure which unit you get, or a
  different one (`-> N*mm`).

## 4. Add a capacity and a check

Now add the section capacity and a utilisation ratio. This is the complete sheet:

```sheet
# Beam check

A simply supported beam under a uniform load. The moment **comes out in kN·m** because the
engine tracks the units.

L: 6 m | span
w: 12 kN/m | design load
Mstar: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum bending moment
fy: 300 MPa | yield stress
Ze: 1230000 mm³ | section modulus
Ms: fy * Ze -> kN*m | moment capacity
utilisation: Mstar / (0.9 * Ms)
if utilisation <= 1: "OK" else: "Fails"
```

The result ends with:

```text
Ms = fy·Ze = 300 MPa · 1230000 mm³ = 369 kN·m    moment capacity
utilisation = M⋆ / (0.9·Ms) = 54 kN·m / (0.9 · 369 kN·m) = 0.163
OK
```

Look at the `Ms` line. A stress in megapascals times a volume in cubic millimetres came out as a
moment in kilonewton metres. You did not convert anything. The `utilisation` line divides a
moment by a moment, so the units cancel and it is a plain number.

The last line is a one-line condition. It prints the text `OK` when the ratio is at most 1 and
`Fails` otherwise.

## 5. Change a number

Change `w: 12 kN/m` to `w: 80 kN/m`. The moment becomes 360 kN·m, the ratio 1.08, and the last
line reads `Fails`. Everything after the changed line recalculates as you type.

## 6. See what the sheet compiles to

A sheet is turned into the Calcpad worksheet language, and the engine runs that. To see the
translation, open the **Resources** tab and choose **Show compiled**. For the sheet above it is:

```text
'<h1>Beam check</h1>

#markdown
A simply supported beam under a uniform load. The moment **comes out in kN·m** because the
engine tracks the units.
#end markdown

L = 6 m
w = 12 kN/m
M_star = w * L^2 / 8|kN*m
fy = 300 MPa
Ze = 1230000 mm^3
Ms = fy * Ze|kN*m
utilisation = M_star / (0.9 * Ms)
#if utilisation ≤ 1
'OK
#else
'Fails
#end if
```

(In the compiled view each note is kept as a comment at the end of its line.) You can read it as
a short lesson in the Calcpad language: `|kN*m` is the conversion, `#if` ... `#end if` is the
condition. The language is covered in [The Calcpad language](../calcpad/index.md). **Convert to
Calcpad**, next to Show compiled, replaces the sheet with that text, for when you want to leave
the sheet format for good.

## 7. Save it

Press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac). In browsers that can write files, you choose a place and the sheet
is saved as a `.sheet` file. In other browsers the file downloads. See
[Saving, opening and working offline](saving.md).

## Where next

* All the line kinds: [The sheet format](../sheet/index.md).
* Why the units came out right: [Units](../units.md).
* Draw the moment along the beam: [Plots](../plots.md).
* Turn the sheet into a form you fill in: [Templates with inputs](../templates.md).

**Related calculators:** [Simply supported beam](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/simply-supported-beam-calculator/), [Cantilever beam](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/cantilever-beam-calculator/). More pages are in [Calculators and guides](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/).

Chapter: The screen

# The screen

<!-- description: A tour of the CivilKit Calcs window: the ribbon, the editor, the results, the sidebar, and how the layout changes on a phone. -->

The window has five parts.

```text
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| (suite bar, wide browser windows only)                      |
| File  New Open Save Undo Redo                               |
| Math | Input/Output | Functions | ... | Resources           |   ribbon
|  [groups of buttons for the selected tab]                   |
+----------------------------+-----------------------+--------+
| tab: Beam check            |  Results              |Sidebar |
|                            |  Preview Unwrapped    | Insert |
|  editor                    |  Input Report         |  ...   |
|                            |                       |        |
+----------------------------+-----------------------+--------+
```

## The ribbon

A quick-access strip at the top holds **New**, **Open**, **Save**, **Undo** and **Redo**. Under it
are ten tabs. In a sheet the buttons insert the sheet form of each item, and a button that has no
sheet form inserts Calcpad text as `>>` lines and carries a small `>>` mark.

| Tab | What is on it |
| --- | --- |
| Math | Regions (math line, text, heading, image, plot, table), operators, Greek letters and symbols, programming (conditions, loops, macros), constants, numerical methods, units, clipboard. |
| Input/Output | Input fields: entry, slider, dropdown, radio, checkbox (the `?` form in a sheet, `#UI` in a worksheet), data grid; reading and writing files; breakpoints; the **Input form** view. |
| Functions | Trigonometric, hyperbolic, logarithmic, rounding, statistical, logical, complex and other functions; define a function; the **Symbolic** dialog. |
| Matrices/Tables | Vector and matrix literals, vector and matrix functions, determinant, inverse and transpose, tables. |
| Calculation | Calculate, auto-calculate, the four result views, settings, and the Variables and Errors lists. |
| Plots & Diagrams | Function, parametric, multiple and colour-map plots; plot settings; the **Figures** group: the **Diagrams** menu of starter diagrams (see [Diagrams](../sheet/diagrams.md)) and **Image**. |
| Math Formatting | Rounding, number format, angle units, output control (`#hide`, `#val`, `#nosub` and so on). |
| Text Formatting | Headings, bold, italic, colours, links, lists, rules, page break. In a sheet these write Markdown. |
| Document | Import worksheet, the tidy tools, header and footer, page break, the report, contents, metadata, and Save as, Print PDF, Word, Excel and Export. |
| Resources | Samples, library, New sheet, New Calcpad, Show compiled, Convert to Calcpad, themes, zoom, the sidebar and Settings, help. |

The tabs follow the work: write (Math to Matrices/Tables), calculate, plot, format, then the
document. Hover over a button for what it inserts or does; where it teaches syntax the tooltip shows
the typed form.

## The editor

The editor is on the left, one tab per open file. It colours the text, completes names, Greek
spellings and function names, and underlines mistakes. Hover over a name to see where it is
defined; F12 jumps to the definition. Format Document (Shift+Alt+F) tidies a sheet. See
[Editing](../editing.md).

## The results

The right-hand pane shows the calculated worksheet. The Calculation tab chooses between four
views:

* **Preview**: the document as written, with every `#pre` and `#post` part. This is the usual
  view while you work.
* **Unwrapped**: the source listing with macros and includes resolved. Useful for finding errors
  in macros.
* **Input**: the fill-in form of a sheet or worksheet that has inputs (`L: ? 6 m` in a sheet, `#UI`
  in a worksheet). See [Templates with inputs](../templates.md).
* **Report**: the print layout, as it will come out in a PDF or Word file.

Results update as you type; **Auto-calculate** can be turned off on the Calculation tab, and
then **Calculate** (Ctrl+Alt+X, and F5 in the desktop app) runs the sheet on demand.

Under a plot there is a row of small buttons (log axes, 1:1, copy data, save as PNG or SVG).
These are in the preview only and are not part of a printout or export.

## The sidebar

The sidebar holds the **Insert** tab, a searchable library of every symbol, function, unit and
snippet (a click inserts it at the cursor), and tabs for the table of **Contents** and the
**Variables** of the worksheet. **Settings**, **Export**, **Errors** and **Prettify** open as
dialogs over the page. Hide the sidebar with the button at its top right, or Resources > Sidebar
(Ctrl+Shift+B in the desktop app).

## Settings

The gear at the right end of the top strip opens **Settings** (so do Calculation > Calculation settings and
Resources > Settings). It has five tabs:

| Tab | What is on it |
| --- | --- |
| General | Language, number format, and the appearance (colour theme, preview theme). |
| Calculation | Decimals, angle units, complex numbers and the other math settings, plot defaults, US or UK units. |
| Editor | Quick typing, comment format, formatting keys, auto-run, cursor sync, the linter. |
| Export | The PDF page: paper size, orientation, margins, header and footer. |
| Advanced | Script libraries, logging and limits, the server address, saved configurations. |

The search box above the tabs looks through all of them and lists each match under its tab's name; clear it to
get the tabs back. Settings opens on the tab you last used, until the browser tab is closed. Calculation settings
opens it on Calculation, and Document > Header and footer on Export. On the tab strip, the arrow keys, Home and End
move between the tabs.

## On a phone

At 760 pixels wide or less, one pane shows at a time, switched from a bar along the bottom:
**Edit**, **Results** and **Insert**. The ribbon starts folded; tap an open tab to fold it. See
[Editing](../editing.md) for touch editing.

---

Chapter: Saving, opening and working offline
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/getting-started/saving

# Saving, opening and working offline

<!-- description: Save and open worksheets from the File menu, use the recent list and the browser library, install the app and keep working offline. -->

## The File menu

The File button at the top left of the ribbon opens a menu:

| Item | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| New sheet | A new sheet in a new tab. |
| New Calcpad worksheet | A new `.cpd` worksheet, the advanced syntax. |
| Open... | Opens a `.sheet`, `.cpd` or `.txt` file. Data files and pictures you pick join the library. |
| Import worksheet... | Converts a worksheet from another tool. See [Importing worksheets](../importing.md). |
| Samples... | The sample browser. See [Samples tour](../samples.md). |
| Save, Save as... | Saves the active tab. |
| Print PDF..., Export..., Export Excel... | See [Exporting](../exporting.md). |

Below the commands are the **Recent** worksheets and the **Library**. The library holds the files
that `#include` and `#read` use: data files, pictures, shared definitions. Everything you open
or drop on the page goes into it. It is stored in your browser.

You can also drag a file onto the page. A `.cpd` or `.sheet` file opens in a tab, and any other
file joins the library.

## Saving

Press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac), or use Save in the quick-access strip. Ctrl+Shift+S is Save as.

* In a browser that can write files in place (Chrome and Edge on a computer), you choose a file
  once and later saves write to it.
* In other browsers the file downloads each time you save.

A sheet is saved with the extension `.sheet` and a Calcpad worksheet as `.cpd`. Both are plain
text. You can open them in any text editor and keep them in version control.

> Saving is manual. Nothing you type is uploaded anywhere, and the browser keeps no copy of
> unsaved text, so save before you leave.

### Knowing what is unsaved

A document has unsaved changes when its text differs from what Save or Save As last wrote.

* Its tab shows a dot (●) after the name, and the browser tab's title starts with ● while that
  document is the active one.
* Undoing back to the saved text clears the dot again.
* Closing a tab with unsaved changes asks **Save**, **Don't Save** or cancel (click outside the
  box).
* Closing or reloading the browser tab while any document has unsaved changes makes the browser
  ask whether to leave. The wording of that box is the browser's own.

Print PDF, Word and Excel exports are copies of the report. They do not save the document, so the
dot stays until you save it.

## Working offline

CivilKit Calcs is a progressive web app. After one visit the whole app (about 22 MB) is cached by
the browser, and it opens and calculates with no connection. To make it behave like an installed
program, use your browser's **Install** or **Add to home screen** command.

The page's own files include the calculation engine, the Word and Excel writers, the importer,
the Python runtime and the Symbolic dialog, so all of them work offline after the first visit.
The one exception is the Plotly chart script: **interactive Plotly charts** from Python blocks load
the Plotly script from its CDN the first time a chart is shown, and cache it after that. Without
it the chart's place shows a note instead of a blank. See [Python blocks](../python.md). The
first visit itself needs a connection, and so does installing the app.

When a new build is available the app tells you with a small box (Reload and Later). It never
reloads by itself, so unsaved work is safe.

## Themes

The Resources tab has Light and Dark. Adding `?theme=dark` or `?theme=light` to the address forces
the theme for that visit.

---

Chapter: The sheet format
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/sheet/

# The sheet format

<!-- description: A sheet is a calculation written the way you would explain it: Markdown prose, plain name: value lines with real units, and LaTeX formulas. -->

A **sheet** is a calculation written the way you would explain it to a colleague: Markdown
prose, plain `name: value` lines, and LaTeX where you want a typeset formula. The sheet compiler
turns it into the Calcpad worksheet language and the engine runs that. There is no second engine:
units, vectors, matrices, plots, and the Word and Excel exports all work because the engine sees
an ordinary Calcpad worksheet.

A file is a sheet when its first non-blank line is `<!--sheet-->`, or when its name ends in
`.sheet`. The editor adds the marker line for you.

## A whole sheet

```sheet
# Beam bending check

A simply supported beam. The moment **comes out in kN·m**.

L: 6 m | span
w: 12 kN/m | design load
Mstar: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum bending moment
Ms: 300 MPa * 1230000 mm³ -> kN*m
utilisation: Mstar / (0.9 * Ms)
if utilisation <= 1: "OK" else: "Fails"
```

The result:

```text
Beam bending check
A simply supported beam. The moment comes out in kN·m.

L = 6 m    span
w = 12 kN/m    design load
M_star = w·L²/8 = 12 kN/m · (6 m)² / 8 = 54 kN·m    maximum bending moment
Ms = 300 MPa · 1230000 mm³ = 369 kN·m
utilisation = M_star / (0.9·Ms) = 54 kN·m / (0.9 · 369 kN·m) = 0.163
OK
```

## The line kinds

Every line of a sheet is one of these.

| Line | Looks like | Chapter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prose | `A simply supported beam.` or `## Heading` | [Prose, LaTeX and tables](prose.md) |
| Quantity | `L: 6 m \| span` | [Quantities and notes](quantities.md) |
| Input | `L: ? 6 m \| span` | [Templates with inputs](../templates.md) |
| Section marker | `## Workings {collapse}`, `M: ... {key}`, `{key results}` | [Folding sections and key results](sections.md) |
| Function | `f(x): x^2 + 1` | [Functions](functions.md) |
| Condition | `if u <= 1: "OK" else: "Fails"` | [Conditions and loops](flow.md) |
| Block | `for i in 1..5:` with an indented body | [Conditions and loops](flow.md) |
| Plot | `plot M(x) for x in 0..L` | [Plots](../plots.md) |
| Python | a fenced `python` block | [Python blocks](../python.md) |
| Diagram | a fenced `mermaid` block | [Diagrams](diagrams.md) |
| Calcpad | a line starting with `>>`, or a `calcpad` fence | [Mixing in Calcpad](passthrough.md) |

A line that looks like a quantity but is really prose (`Note: see the drawing`) is prose, because
its right-hand side is not an expression. To force prose, start the line with a backslash.

## What a sheet cannot do

* There is no symbolic algebra in the sheet itself. The engine is numeric. Use the
  [Symbolic dialog](../symbolic.md) to derive a formula and paste it in.
* A vector or matrix literal cannot carry a unit after the bracket (`[1, 2] kN`). Put the unit on
  the elements.
* A formula is typeset in the page, but in Word and Excel it appears as its TeX source in
  italics.
* **Convert to Calcpad** works one way. Calcpad text is not turned back into a sheet.

Everything else in the Calcpad language is reachable by passing lines through. See
[Mixing in Calcpad](passthrough.md).

---

Chapter: Quantities, units and notes
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/sheet/quantities

# Quantities, units and notes

<!-- description: Quantity lines in a sheet: names, units, converting the answer with ->, notes, several quantities on one line, operators and input lines. -->

A quantity line defines a name:

```text
name: expression [-> unit] [| note]
name = expression
a: 1; b: 2 | note for b
```

The colon and the equals sign both work. The result shows what an equation line shows in
Calcpad: the name, the formula, the numbers put in, and the answer with its unit.

## Names

A name is made of letters, digits, `_` and primes. Greek spellings become Greek letters:

```sheet
phi: 0.9
sigma_c: 25 MPa
Delta_T: 40 K
phiMs: phi * 369 kN*m
Mstar: 54 kN*m
```

```text
φ = 0.9
σ_c = 25 MPa
Δ_T = 40 K
φMs = φ · 369 kN·m = 0.9 · 369 kN·m = 332.1 kN·m
M_star = 54 kN·m
```

* `phi` is φ, `sigma_c` is σ with a subscript c, `Delta_T` is Δ with a subscript T.
* A Greek spelling followed by a capital or a digit (`phiMs`, `sigma2`) is the letter and the
  rest.
* Capital Greek letters are written only where they differ from a Latin capital: `Gamma`,
  `Delta`, `Theta`, `Lambda`, `Xi`, `Pi`, `Sigma`, `Upsilon`, `Phi`, `Psi`, `Omega`.
* A name that ends in `star` after a capital or a digit (`Mstar`) is that name with the subscript
  `star`.
* The first `_` in a name starts the subscript: `my_long_name_2` is shown as `my` with the subscript
  `long_name_2`, as Calcpad writes it. Names with digits and several underscores calculate normally;
  only the way they are typeset changes.

The same rule renames every use of a name, so you spell it one way throughout the sheet. Inside
`>>` lines and `calcpad` fences the sheet's spelling is used too: `phi` in a raw line is φ.

## Units

Write a unit after a number. The engine checks and combines them:

```sheet
a: 2 m; b: 350 mm
A: a * b -> m^2
v: 90 km/h -> m/s
t: 2 h + 30 min -> min
F: 10 N * 3 m -> J
```

```text
a = 2 m
b = 350 mm
A = a·b = 2 m · 350 mm = 0.7 m²
v = 90 km/h = 25 m/s
t = 2 h + 30 min = 150 min
F = 10 N · 3 m = 30 J
```

* `²` and `³` after a name or unit are `^2` and `^3`. `mm³` and `mm^3` are the same.
* A unit written after a number is never renamed, so `3 psi` is a pressure and `psi` alone would
  be the Greek letter ψ.
* Adding a length to a time is an error. Multiplying and dividing them is fine.
* Several units in a sum convert to the first: `5 m + 30 cm` is `5.3 m`.

The whole subject, with the unit list and custom units, is in [Units](../units.md).

## Converting the answer: `->`

`-> unit` converts the result. It must come last, before the note:

```sheet
Mstar: 12 kN/m * (6 m)^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum bending moment
Mnmm: Mstar -> N*mm
```

```text
M_star = 12 kN/m · (6 m)² / 8 = 54 kN·m    maximum bending moment
Mnmm = M_star = 54 kN·m = 54000000 N·mm
```

Without `->` the engine chooses the unit itself, from the units in the formula. Use `->` when you
want a particular unit in the result, and always when the result goes into a report.

## Notes

The first `|` outside brackets starts a note, a short comment shown beside the result in a muted
style. `||` is the logical *or*, not a note. A note can contain LaTeX (`| load at stage $i$`).

## Several per line

Separate quantities with `;`. A note belongs to the last one:

```sheet
a: 3; b: 4 | note for b
c: sqrt(a^2 + b^2)
```

```text
a = 3
b = 4    note for b
c = √(a² + b²) = √(3² + 4²) = 5
```

## Numbers and operators

* You can write `1.23e6` or `2.5e-3`. The engine has no exponent notation, so the compiler writes
  the plain number (`1230000`, `0.0025`) and that is what the result shows.
* Operators are `+ - * / ^ %` and the comparisons `< > <= >= == !=`, with `and` and `or`. The
  Unicode forms `≤ ≥ ≠ ≡ ∧ ∨ × · ÷ −` work too. In a condition a single `=` also means equal.
* Calls take commas: `max(a, b)`. The compiler writes the semicolon the engine wants.
* Use `abs(x)` for an absolute value, not bars.
* `π` (or `pi`) and `e` are built in. The other constants in the Insert tab (gravity, the speed of
  light, unit weights and so on) are snippets that insert a definition line such as
  `g = 9.80665m/s^2`; until you insert one, `g` is the unit gram. See the
  [reference](../reference/functions.md#constants).

## Vectors and matrices

```sheet
v: [1, 2, 3]
A: [2, -1; -1, 2]
```

`[1, 2, 3]` is a vector; `[1, 2; 3, 4]` is a matrix with columns separated by commas and rows by
semicolons. See [Vectors and matrices](../vectors-matrices.md).

## Inputs: a quantity the reader can change

Put a `?` in front of the value and the quantity becomes an input, with that value as its default:

```sheet
L: ? 6 m | span
w: ? 12 kN/m | design load
M: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum moment
```

In Input mode `L` and `w` are boxes. Everywhere else the lines read as the quantities they are. A
list of options (`[Steel = 200 GPa, Timber = 11 GPa]`, or round brackets for radio buttons) and
`on` or `off` (a checkbox) are inputs too. See [Templates with inputs](../templates.md).

---

Chapter: Prose, LaTeX and tables
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/sheet/prose

# Prose, LaTeX and tables

<!-- description: Write the text of a calculation in Markdown, typeset formulas in LaTeX, add tables and diagrams, and force a line to be read as prose. -->

Anything that is not one of the line kinds is Markdown prose. Use it to say what is being
checked, to state assumptions and to explain results.

## Markdown

Supported Markdown: headings (`#` to `######`), paragraphs, `**bold**`, `*italic*`, bulleted
(`-`) and numbered lists, pipe tables, links, `![alt](file)` images from the library, `` `code` ``
and fenced code blocks. Blank lines between sections are kept.

A plain paragraph, even over several lines, becomes one text line. Only prose that really
contains Markdown (lists, tables, quotes, emphasis, links, code) is passed to the engine's
Markdown renderer.

## LaTeX

`$...$` is an inline formula and `$$...$$` a display formula, in prose, in notes and in the text
of an `if` line. A `$$` alone on a line opens and closes a multi-line formula. `\$` is a dollar
sign, and a `$` before a digit ("$5") is one too.

```sheet
A pipe of diameter $d$ carries a flow $Q$. The mean velocity is

$$v = \frac{4 Q}{\pi d^2}$$

d: 0.2 m
Q: 0.05 m^3/s
v: 4 * Q / (π * d^2) -> m/s
```

```text
A pipe of diameter d carries a flow Q. The mean velocity is

        4Q
   v = ----
        πd²

d = 0.2 m
Q = 0.05 m³/s
v = 4·Q / (π·d²) = 4 · 0.05 m³/s / (3.14 · (0.2 m)²) = 1.59 m/s
```

The page typesets formulas with KaTeX, which is bundled with the app and loaded the first time a
sheet has a formula, so formulas work offline. A formula that cannot be typeset is shown as
its TeX source. In the LaTeX of a sheet, variable names take the same blue as in an equation. In
Word and Excel a formula appears as its TeX source in italics, not as Office Math.

## Tables

A pipe table is prose, with the engine's table styling:

```sheet
| Action     | Symbol | Value |
|------------|--------|-------|
| Permanent  | G      | 4.5 kPa |
| Imposed    | Q      | 3 kPa |

G: 4.5 kPa
Q: 3 kPa
w_uls: 1.2 * G + 1.5 * Q -> kPa | strength combination
```

```text
Action      Symbol   Value
Permanent   G        4.5 kPa
Imposed     Q        3 kPa

G = 4.5 kPa
Q = 3 kPa
w_uls = 1.2·G + 1.5·Q = 1.2 · 4.5 kPa + 1.5 · 3 kPa = 9.9 kPa    strength combination
```

The table is text. It does not feed the calculation, so type the numbers again in quantity lines,
or define the quantities first and mention them in the table text.

In the preview, click a column heading to sort the rows by it (again for descending, a third time
for the source order). It is a view only: the sheet, the printout and the exports keep the order
you wrote. See [Sorting a table](../editing.md#sorting-a-table).

## Diagrams

A fenced block tagged `mermaid` is drawn as a diagram in the results: boxes and arrows, a flow
chart, a sequence or a timeline, written as text in Mermaid's syntax.

````sheet
# Load path

```mermaid
graph TD
  Slab --> Beam
  Beam --> Column
  Column --> Footing
```

G: 4.5 kPa
````

The drawing comes from the text, so editing the fence redraws it. [Diagrams](diagrams.md) starts
from three small examples (a flow chart, a sequence and a state diagram) and gives tips, what
prints and what exports.

## Forcing prose

A line starts with a backslash when it must not be read as a quantity:

```sheet
\L: 5 is shown as text
Note: see the drawing
```

`Note: see the drawing` is already prose, because "see the drawing" is not an expression.

---

Chapter: Diagrams
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/sheet/diagrams

# Diagrams

A diagram is written as text in a fenced block tagged `mermaid`, and the results draw it. Type the
steps, the app draws the boxes and arrows. Edit the text and the drawing follows. The language of
the fence is Mermaid's, and the app bundles Mermaid 12.1.0, which draws more than thirty kinds of
diagram and chart: flow charts, sequence and state diagrams, Gantt charts, pie and XY charts,
Sankey diagrams, mind maps and more.

This chapter is a gallery: one small example of each kind, grouped by what it is for. Copy one
into a sheet to see it drawn, then change it. A kind whose first word ends in `-beta` is new in
the diagram library, and its syntax may still change in a later version. The kinds that are not
available are listed [at the end](#kinds-that-are-not-available), and the [samples](#samples)
show diagrams next to the calculations they describe.

## Starting from the ribbon

The **Diagrams** menu in the **Figures** group of the **Plots & Diagrams** tab of the ribbon inserts a short starter
diagram, so there is no syntax to learn before the first one. Put the caret where the diagram
should go and pick a kind: flowchart, sequence, state, block, architecture, entity relationship,
requirement, tree view, mind map, fishbone, Gantt, timeline, pie, XY chart, quadrant, radar,
Sankey or treemap. In a sheet the starter goes in as a block of its own after the paragraph or
block the caret is in; in a Calcpad worksheet it goes in a `#markdown` block after the caret's
line. Its text is left selected, ready to edit, and Undo takes it out in one step. The menu offers
the kinds engineers use most; the other kinds can be typed by hand, and the gallery below shows
them all.

A diagram does not read the sheet's numbers. Work a value out with a quantity line and type it
into the diagram, as the samples do.

## Processes and behaviour

### Flow chart

`flowchart TD` draws from top to bottom (`LR` draws from left to right). A box is a name and its
label in square brackets, a decision is in braces, and `-->` is an arrow. Text between `--` and
`-->` labels the arrow.

<!-- expect: OK: the section passes. -->
````sheet
# Design check

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Design moment M*] --> B{M* <= phi Ms?}
  B -- yes --> C[Section passes]
  B -- no --> D[Choose a deeper section]
  D --> A
```

Mstar: 54 kN*m | design moment
phiMs: 332 kN*m | design capacity
if Mstar <= phiMs: "OK: the section passes." else: "Fails: choose a deeper section."
````

### Sequence diagram

`sequenceDiagram` draws people or parts side by side and the messages between them, in order from
the top. `->>` is a solid arrow and `-->>` a dashed one.

````sheet
# Review of the calculation

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant D as Designer
  participant C as Checker
  D->>C: Calculation for review
  C-->>D: Comments
  D->>C: Revised calculation
  C-->>D: Approved
```
````

### State diagram

`stateDiagram-v2` draws the states something passes through. `[*]` is the start or the end, and the
text after a colon labels the change.

````sheet
# Status of the calculation

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Draft
  Draft --> Checked: checker signs
  Checked --> Draft: comments
  Checked --> Issued: approved
  Issued --> [*]
```
````

### User journey

`journey` scores each step of a task from 1 (bad) to 5 (good) for the people who take part.

````sheet
# Inspection of a slab pour

```mermaid
journey
  title Site inspection of a slab pour
  section Before the pour
    Check reinforcement: 4: Engineer
    Check cover and chairs: 3: Engineer, Builder
  section The pour
    Slump test: 5: Tester
    Take cylinders: 4: Tester
```
````

### Use case diagram

`usecase-beta` draws actors and the things they do. `actor` names the actors, and
`name(label)` is a use case.

````sheet
# Who does what

```mermaid
usecase-beta
  actor Designer, Checker
  Designer --> design(Design a member)
  Designer --> report(Print the report)
  Checker --> review(Review the calculation)
```
````

### Event model

`eventmodeling` draws a process as frames in time order: `tf` is a time frame with a number, a
kind (`ui`, `cmd`, `evt`, `rmo`) and a name, and `->>` points to the frame it follows.

````sheet
# A check from input to report

```mermaid
eventmodeling
  tf 01 ui InputForm
  tf 02 cmd RunCheck ->> 01
  tf 03 evt CheckPassed ->> 02
  tf 04 rmo DesignReport ->> 03
```
````

## Structure and data

### Class diagram

`classDiagram` draws classes with their fields and methods. `<|--` is inheritance.

````sheet
# Section shapes

```mermaid
classDiagram
  class Section {
    +area() A
    +inertia() I
  }
  class Rectangle {
    +b
    +h
  }
  class Circle {
    +d
  }
  Section <|-- Rectangle
  Section <|-- Circle
```
````

### Entity relationship diagram

`erDiagram` draws a data model. `}o--||` reads "many to exactly one", and the braces list the
attributes of an entity.

````sheet
# Member data model

```mermaid
erDiagram
  MEMBER }o--|| SECTION : uses
  SECTION }o--|| MATERIAL : "made of"
  MEMBER {
    string mark
    float length_m
  }
  SECTION {
    string name
    float area_mm2
  }
  MATERIAL {
    string grade
    float fy_MPa
  }
```
````

### Requirement diagram

`requirementDiagram` ties requirements to the elements that satisfy or verify them.

````sheet
# Traceability

```mermaid
requirementDiagram
  requirement deflection {
    id: R1
    text: Deflection under span over 250
    risk: medium
    verifymethod: analysis
  }
  element beam_check {
    type: sheet
  }
  beam_check - satisfies -> deflection
```
````

### Block diagram

`block-beta` lays blocks out on a grid. `columns 3` sets the grid, `:3` makes a block span three
columns and `space` leaves a gap.

````sheet
# A portal frame in blocks

```mermaid
block-beta
  columns 3
  Roof:3
  Beam1["Beam"] space Beam2["Beam"]
  Col1["Column"] space Col2["Column"]
  Footing:3
```
````

### Architecture diagram

`architecture-beta` draws services with icons (`cloud`, `database`, `disk`, `internet`, `server`)
in groups. `sensors:R -- L:logger` joins the right side of one to the left side of the other.

````sheet
# Monitoring a bridge

```mermaid
architecture-beta
  group site(cloud)[Bridge site]
  service sensors(disk)[Strain gauges] in site
  service logger(server)[Data logger] in site
  service store(database)[Database]
  sensors:R -- L:logger
  logger:R -- L:store
```
````

### C4 diagram

`C4Context` draws a system in its setting, in the C4 model's notation: people, systems and the
relations between them.

````sheet
# Context of a calculation system

```mermaid
C4Context
  title Calculation system
  Person(eng, "Engineer", "Writes the calculation")
  System(app, "Calculation app", "Runs the sheet")
  System_Ext(lib, "Section library", "Section properties")
  Rel(eng, app, "Uses")
  Rel(app, lib, "Reads")
```
````

### Packet diagram

`packet-beta` draws the fields of a data record by bit position.

````sheet
# A logger record

```mermaid
packet-beta
  0-15: "Sensor id"
  16-31: "Strain, microstrain"
  32-47: "Temperature"
  48-63: "Checksum"
```
````

## Plans and time

### Gantt chart

`gantt` draws tasks against dates. `dateFormat` sets how dates are written, `after a1` starts a
task when another ends, and a duration such as `10d` is in days.

````sheet
# Design programme

```mermaid
gantt
  title Design programme
  dateFormat YYYY-MM-DD
  section Design
  Concept       :a1, 2026-11-02, 10d
  Detailed      :a2, after a1, 15d
  section Review
  Check         :b1, after a2, 5d
  Issue         :milestone, after b1, 0d
```
````

### Timeline

`timeline` lists events by period, one line each: `period : event`.

````sheet
# Strength gain

```mermaid
timeline
  title Concrete strength gain
  Day 3 : 15 MPa
  Day 7 : 22 MPa
  Day 28 : 32 MPa
```
````

### Kanban board

`kanban` draws columns of cards. A line indented under a column is a card in it.

````sheet
# Design tasks

```mermaid
kanban
  todo[To do]
    t1[Wind loads]
    t2[Connection design]
  doing[In progress]
    t3[Column check]
  done[Done]
    t4[Gravity loads]
```
````

### Git graph

`gitGraph` draws commits on branches, here the revisions of a calculation and a checker's branch.

````sheet
# Revisions

```mermaid
gitGraph
  commit id: "Rev A"
  branch checker
  commit id: "Comments"
  checkout main
  commit id: "Rev B"
  merge checker
  commit id: "Rev C issued"
```
````

## Charts of numbers

### Pie chart

`pie` draws each value as a slice; `showData` adds the values to the legend.

````sheet
# Dead load share

```mermaid
pie showData
  title Dead load, kPa
  "Slab" : 4.8
  "Screed" : 1.1
  "Services" : 0.5
  "Partitions" : 1.0
```
````

### XY chart

`xychart-beta` draws bars and lines over an x axis of categories or numbers.

````sheet
# Moment along a beam

```mermaid
xychart-beta
  title "Bending moment, kN.m"
  x-axis "x, m" [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
  y-axis "M" 0 --> 60
  bar [0, 30, 48, 54, 48, 30, 0]
  line [0, 30, 48, 54, 48, 30, 0]
```
````

### Quadrant chart

`quadrantChart` places points with coordinates from 0 to 1 in four labelled quadrants.

````sheet
# Risk matrix

```mermaid
quadrantChart
  title Site risks
  x-axis Unlikely --> Likely
  y-axis Minor --> Severe
  quadrant-1 Control first
  quadrant-2 Plan for it
  quadrant-3 Accept
  quadrant-4 Monitor
  Trench collapse: [0.3, 0.9]
  Wet weather: [0.9, 0.5]
```
````

### Radar chart

`radar-beta` compares options over several axes. `max` sets the outer ring.

````sheet
# Floor systems

```mermaid
radar-beta
  title Floor systems
  axis cost["Cost"], speed["Speed"], depth["Shallow depth"], span["Span"]
  curve flat["Flat plate"]{4, 3, 5, 2}
  curve steel["Steel and deck"]{3, 5, 3, 4}
  max 5
```
````

### Sankey diagram

`sankey-beta` draws flows as bands whose width is the value. Each line is `from,to,value`.

````sheet
# Energy through a pump

```mermaid
sankey-beta
Input,Motor,43.3
Motor,Motor losses,3.0
Motor,Pump,40.3
Pump,Pump losses,8.9
Pump,Water,31.4
```
````

### Treemap

`treemap` draws nested rectangles with an area in proportion to the value. Indentation nests an
item in its group.

````sheet
# Cost plan

```mermaid
treemap
"Cost plan"
    "Structure"
        "Frame": 310
        "Floors": 260
    "Envelope"
        "Facade": 280
        "Roof": 90
```
````

## Ideas and analysis

### Mind map

`mindmap` draws a tree from its root; indentation gives the branches. `((text))` draws a circle.

````sheet
# Footbridge brief

```mermaid
mindmap
  root((Footbridge))
    Geometry
      Span 24 m
      Width 2.5 m
    Loads
      Crowd 5 kPa
    Limits
      Deflection L/360
```
````

### Ishikawa (fishbone) diagram

`ishikawa-beta` draws an effect at the head and its causes on the bones. Indentation gives the
categories and the causes in each.

````sheet
# Causes of cracking

```mermaid
ishikawa-beta
  Cracked slab
    Materials
      High water content
    Method
      Late curing
    Design
      Joints too far apart
```
````

### Venn diagram

`venn-beta` draws sets as circles. `set` adds a set, and `union` labels where sets overlap.

````sheet
# Kinds of check

```mermaid
venn-beta
  title Checks
  set S["Strength"]
  set V["Serviceability"]
  union S, V["Both"]
```
````

### Cynefin framework

`cynefin-beta` places items in the five domains (`complex`, `complicated`, `clear`, `chaotic`,
`confusion`). An item is a quoted text, and `-->` shows a move from one domain to another.

````sheet
# Kinds of design problem

```mermaid
cynefin-beta
  complex
    "Novel bracing system"
  complicated
    "Long-span roof"
  clear
    "Standard lintel"
  chaotic
    "Collapse on site"
  chaotic --> complex : "Make safe, then probe"
```
````

### Wardley map

`wardley-beta` maps components by visibility (up) and evolution (across). The coordinates are
`[visibility, evolution]`, from 0 to 1, and `->` joins a component to one it depends on.

````sheet
# Design office

```mermaid
wardley-beta
  title Design office
  anchor Client [0.95, 0.6]
  component Calculation [0.7, 0.5]
  component Section tables [0.4, 0.85]
  Client -> Calculation
  Calculation -> Section tables
```
````

### Tree view

`treeView-beta` draws an indented list as a tree, such as the folders of a project.

````sheet
# Project folders

```mermaid
treeView-beta
  project
    calcs
      beams.sheet
      columns.sheet
    drawings
      general.pdf
```
````

## Grammars: railroad diagrams

A railroad diagram draws the grammar of a language: follow the track from left to right. Each
rule ends with `;`. The same drawing comes from four notations.

### EBNF

`railroad-ebnf-beta`: `,` joins in sequence and `[ ]` is optional. This is the grammar of a
quantity line.

````sheet
# A quantity line

```mermaid
railroad-ebnf-beta
  quantity = name , ":" , expression , [ "->" , unit ] , [ "|" , note ] ;
```
````

### ABNF

`railroad-abnf-beta`: `1*DIGIT` is one or more digits and `[ ]` is optional.

````sheet
# A number

```mermaid
railroad-abnf-beta
  number = 1*DIGIT [ "." 1*DIGIT ] ;
```
````

### PEG

`railroad-peg-beta`: `<-` defines a rule, `+` is one or more and `?` is optional.

````sheet
# A number

```mermaid
railroad-peg-beta
  Number <- Digit+ ("." Digit+)? ;
```
````

### Railroad functions

`railroad-beta` builds a diagram from functions: `sequence`, `choice`, `optional`, `oneOrMore`,
`zeroOrMore`, `terminal` and `nonterminal`.

````sheet
# A quantity line

```mermaid
railroad-beta
  quantity = sequence(nonterminal("name"), terminal(":"), nonterminal("expression"), optional(sequence(terminal("|"), nonterminal("note")))) ;
```
````

## Kinds that are not available

Every kind above was drawn in the app with the bundled Mermaid 12.1.0. These are not available:

| Kind | Why |
| --- | --- |
| ZenUML (`zenuml`) | A separate plugin of the diagram library, not part of the app. The fence shows "No diagram type detected". Use a sequence diagram instead. |
| The `elk` layout (`layout: elk`) | Not shipped; diagrams use the standard layout. |

## Samples

The **Plots and diagrams** group of the Samples dialog (Resources > Samples) has sheets with a
diagram next to the calculation it describes:

* **Design check as a flow diagram** and **Load path and tributary loads** (flow charts)
* **Design states of a steel beam** (state diagram) and **Review and sign-off** (sequence diagram)
* **Construction programme** (Gantt chart), with durations worked out from quantities and rates
* **Dead load share** (pie chart) and **Cost plan** (treemap), with the shares worked out
* **Site risk matrix** (quadrant chart) and **Bending moment along a beam** (XY chart)
* **Energy flow through a pump** (Sankey), from the hydraulic power back to the electrical input
* **Footbridge design brief** (mind map) and **Requirements traceability** (requirement diagram)
* **Concrete strength gain** (timeline) and **Section shapes** (class diagram)

For plots drawn from a function, see [Plots](../plots.md).

## Learning more

Every diagram type and option is described in the Mermaid project's own documentation; what it
shows there can be pasted into a fence here, as long as the kind is in the gallery above.

## Tips

* Keep the text in a box short. A long label wraps onto several lines and makes the box tall.
* A diagram is part of the page, not of the calculation. Names in it are only text: changing `w`
  in a box does not change the load, and a quantity line is still needed for every number.
* In the dark theme a diagram is drawn on a white panel, so it reads the same as on paper.
* A fence that cannot be read shows its text with the reason under it. The usual cause is a
  character the diagram language treats as syntax, such as a bracket or a quote inside a label.

## Printing and exports

Diagrams print and save with the HTML and PDF report as drawings; in Word they appear as their
text. The same fence works inside a `#markdown` block of a Calcpad worksheet. The diagram library
is part of the app and is only loaded when a page has a diagram, so it works offline and costs
nothing on a page without one.

---

Chapter: Folding sections and key results
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/sheet/sections

# Folding sections and key results

A long calculation has a few numbers the reader came for and a lot of working that leads to them. Two markers
let the sheet say which is which, without changing a single result.

## A section that folds

End a heading with `{collapse}` and the section under it is folded away until the reader opens it:

<!-- expect: Beam moment | L = 6 m | = 54 kN · m maximum bending moment | = 0.3 bending utilisation -->
```sheet
# Beam moment

L: 6 m | span
w: 12 kN/m | design load

## Workings {collapse}
The moment at mid-span of a simply supported beam under a uniform load is $w L^2 / 8$.
M: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum bending moment
Ms: 180 kN*m | moment capacity

## Result
utilisation: M / Ms | bending utilisation
```

In the preview and the report the heading shows with a small arrow in front of it. Click the heading to open
the section and click it again to fold it. The lines under a folded heading are still calculated, so `M` is
there for the line after it. The section runs to the next heading of the same level or a higher one, so a
`###` under a `##` is part of it, and it ends at the end of the sheet if no such heading follows.

`{collapse open}` starts the section open. Use it for a section the reader should see at first and may fold away.

Only a heading at the top level of the sheet can fold. A `{collapse}` heading inside an `if`, `for`, `while` or
`repeat` block is ignored, with a warning.

The preview also has a fold arrow beside every other heading (see [Editing](../editing.md)). That fold is only a view
and is not saved in the sheet; a `{collapse}` heading folds by its marker and has no arrow of its own, and "Collapse
all" leaves it as the sheet wrote it.

When you print, or save as PDF, every folded section is opened, so the printed report is complete. The Word and
Excel exports include them too. There is no option to leave a folded section out of an export.

## Key lines

End a quantity or an input line with `{key}` to mark it as one of the numbers that matter:

<!-- expect: L = 6 m span ★ | = 54 kN · m maximum bending moment ★ | = 0.3 bending utilisation ★ -->
```sheet
L: ? 6 m | span {key}
w: 12 kN/m | design load
M: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum bending moment {key}
Ms: 180 kN*m
utilisation: M / Ms | bending utilisation {key}
```

A key line carries a star after it and is highlighted in the preview, the report and the printed page. In Word
and Excel the star is in the line, though the highlight is not. The marker goes last, after the note.

## A list of the key lines

A line that is just `{key results}` becomes a list of the key lines above it, with the values the engine
worked out and their notes:

<!-- expect: Key results | L = 6 m span | M = 54 kN | utilisation = 0.3 -->
```sheet
L: ? 6 m | span {key}
w: 12 kN/m | design load
M: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum bending moment {key}
Ms: 180 kN*m
utilisation: M / Ms | bending utilisation {key}

## Key results
{key results}
```

Put it after the lines it lists: a sheet is calculated from the top, so a key line written below the list has no
value yet and is not in it. A line inside an `if` or `for` block, and a function definition, can be marked but
are not listed.

In the editor, **Text formatting > Fold** inserts a folding heading, **Key results** inserts the heading and the
list, and the **+** between blocks of the preview offers both. Format Document writes the markers as one space
and the marker.

---

Chapter: Conditions and loops
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/sheet/flow

# Conditions and loops

<!-- description: Conditions and loops in a sheet: one-line if checks that print OK or a message, blocks of lines, for and while loops, and their limits. -->

## One-line conditions

```sheet
utilisation: 0.82
if utilisation <= 1: "OK" else: "Fails"
```

The branches are a quoted text or quantities. The text may contain LaTeX. A one-line condition
can also define a quantity: `if a == 2: b: 1`.

## Blocks

A line ending in `:` that starts with `if`, `else if`, `else`, `for`, `while` or `repeat` opens a
block. The body is the lines indented more than the header. A tab counts as four spaces. Blank
lines inside are fine. A line indented no deeper than the header closes the block. A body can hold
anything: quantities, prose, formulas, `>>` lines, and nested blocks.

```sheet
n: 5
if n > 3:
    Large.
else if n > 1:
    Medium.
else:
    Small.
```

```text
n = 5
Large.
```

## Loops

```sheet
for i in 1..3:
    P: 10 kN * i | load at stage $i$
```

```text
P = 10 kN · i = 10 kN · 1 = 10 kN    load at stage 1
P = 10 kN · i = 10 kN · 2 = 20 kN    load at stage 2
P = 10 kN · i = 10 kN · 3 = 30 kN    load at stage 3
```

| Sheet | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `for i in a..b:` | `i` takes a, a+1, ... b. |
| `for i in a..b step s:` | A stepped range. The step may be negative. |
| `for x in v:` | Each element of the vector `v` (a name or a literal). |
| `while c:` | Repeat while the condition holds. |
| `repeat n:` | Repeat n times. |
| `break`, `continue` | Leave the loop, or skip to the next pass. `if c: break` works on one line. |

```sheet
for i in 0..10 step 5:
    s: i
```

```sheet
for x in [2, 4, 6]:
    y: x^2
```

```sheet
n: 3
while n > 0:
    n: n - 1
```

```sheet
total: 0
for i in 1..5:
    total: total + i
    if total > 5: break
```

The last example stops once the total passes 5; it prints the passes with total 1, 3 and 6.

A quantity line in a loop prints on every pass, exactly like a Calcpad loop. Use the loop to build
a vector or to accumulate; if you only need the final value, put the quantity line after the loop.

## Limits

* `repeat` needs a count; for anything else use `>>` lines.
* A loop over a vector cannot have a step.
* A header whose condition is not an expression (`If the load is large:`) is prose. The compiler
  warns if it starts with a keyword.
* An `else` with no matching `if` at the same indentation is read as text, with a warning.

---

Chapter: Functions
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/sheet/functions

# Functions

<!-- description: Define your own functions in a sheet, call the built-in function library, and use numerical commands such as root finding and integration. -->

## Your own functions

A line with an argument list defines a function:

```sheet
f(x, y): sqrt(x^2 + y^2)
g(t): 2 * t
r: f(3, 4) + g(1)
```

```text
f(x; y) = √(x² + y²)
g(t) = 2·t
r = f(3; 4) + g(1) = 7
```

Calls take commas in a sheet; the compiler writes the engine's `;`. Calcpad's own `;` works too,
in a definition and in a call (`f(x; y): x + y`, `max(3; 7)`): inside brackets it means the same as
a comma. Functions can use any quantity defined above them, and may be used in plots
(`plot g(t) for t in 0..5`).

### Keeping functions for reuse

A function defined in a sheet belongs to that sheet. To use it in other sheets, put its definition
in a `.cpd` file and add the file to the library (**File** > Library > Add files to the library,
or drop it on the page). Any sheet then pulls it in with an include line:

```text
>> #include beam_functions.cpd
```

The file holds Calcpad text, so its arguments are separated by `;`:

```text
delta(w; L; E; I) = 5*w*L^4/(384*E*I)
```

Two things to watch in definitions that integrate over time or space:

* The limits of `$Area`, `$Sum` and the other numerical commands must have the same unit.
  `$Area{F(t) @ t = 0ms : 2s}` is fine; a bare `0` against `2s` is an error.
* An angular frequency is a number per second. Write `20 / 1 s`, not `20 rad/s`.

Copying the definition lines into each sheet also works, and keeps the sheet self-contained when you
send it to someone who does not have your library.

## Built-in functions

The engine has more than 200 functions: trigonometric, hyperbolic, logarithmic, rounding,
statistical, interpolation, complex numbers, and a large set for vectors and matrices. The
[function reference](../reference/functions.md) lists them all, with the argument forms, and the
Insert tab in the sidebar finds them as you type.

A few that are used constantly:

```sheet
a: sqrt(2)
b: round(3.14159)
c: max(3, 7, 5)
d: sum([1, 2, 3])
e: interp(2.5, [1, 2, 3], [10, 20, 30])
```

There is no `hypot` in a sheet. For the hypotenuse, or the resultant of any number of components,
use `srss` (square root of the sum of squares), which keeps the unit:

```sheet
a: 3 m
b: 4 m
c: srss(a, b)
```

The result is 5 m, and `srss(3 m, 4 m, 12 m)` is 13 m. (In a Python block `math.hypot` exists.)

A function whose name is also a variable name needs the Calcpad spelling (a name like `gamma`
or `beta` used as a variable only keeps working if you write it the Calcpad way). Function calls
are not renamed unless the sheet defines the function.

## Solving, integrating and slopes

Three numerical operations have a sheet form of their own, written like a `plot` line:

<!-- expect: = 1.41 the positive root | d x = 9 | x = 3 = 6 -->
```sheet
f(x): x^2
x0: solve f(x) = 2 for x in 0..2 | the positive root
A: integral of f(x) for x in 0..3
k: slope of f(x) at x = 3
```

* `solve f(x) = c for x in a..b` finds the `x` between `a` and `b` where both sides are equal
  (Calcpad's `$Root{f(x) = c @ x = a : b}`). Without `= c` it solves `f(x) = 0`. Both sides may
  use the variable (`solve f(x) = g(x) for x in 0..5` finds where two curves cross). The difference
  of the sides must change sign once across the range.
* `integral of f(x) for x in a..b` is the numerical integral (`$Integral`).
* `slope of f(x) at x = a` is the derivative at a point (`$Slope`).

`root(27, 3)` is something else: the cube root of 27. The bounds may carry units, and a bare `0`
takes the unit of the other bound, so `solve x^2 = 4 m^2 for x in 0..5 m -> mm` gives 2000 mm. A
line that starts like one of these but is malformed (`for 2 in 0..5`, two `=` signs) is an error on
its line.

## Numerical commands

The `$Root`, `$Area`, `$Sum`, `$Find` and similar commands are Calcpad commands. Apart from the three
above, in a sheet they go through `>>`:

```sheet
>> f(x) = x^2 - 2
>> x_0 = $Root{f(x) @ x = 0 : 2}
>> I = $Area{x^2 @ x = 0 : 3}
```

The result of the first is 1.41, of the second 9. See [The Calcpad language](../calcpad/index.md).

---

Chapter: Mixing in Calcpad, Show compiled and errors
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/sheet/passthrough

# Mixing in Calcpad, Show compiled and errors

<!-- description: Reach every Calcpad feature from a sheet with >> lines and calcpad fences, see the compiled worksheet, read errors and format the document. -->

Every feature of the Calcpad language stays reachable from a sheet.

## `>>` lines and `calcpad` fences

A line that starts with `>>` is handed to the engine as written. So is everything between a
`calcpad` fence:

````sheet
n: 3 | number of bays
bay: 2.5 m | bay width
>> total = 0 m
```calcpad
#for i = 1 : n
    total = total + bay
#loop
```
len: total * 1 -> m
````

```text
n = 3    number of bays
bay = 2.5 m    bay width
total = 0 m
total = total + bay = 0 m + 2.5 m = 2.5 m
total = total + bay = 2.5 m + 2.5 m = 5 m
total = total + bay = 5 m + 2.5 m = 7.5 m
len = total · 1 = 7.5 m · 1 = 7.5 m
```

Sheet lines and raw lines share one worksheet, so they alternate freely: a raw block reads the
variables defined by sheet lines above it and defines variables that sheet lines below it use.
Prose, quantities, formulas and raw Calcpad can come in any order. To make that work without
remembering renames, an identifier in a raw line that the sheet defines is spelled the way the
sheet spells it (`phi` in a raw line is `φ`). That includes the name that a `>> #UI` line assigns. Text after a `'` or `"` in a raw line is left alone.

A raw block inside a sheet block keeps the block's indentation rules like any other line.

The ribbon uses `>>` for anything with no sheet form: the data grid and the other `#UI` input forms (an entry, drop-down, radio or checkbox has a sheet form, `L: ? 6 m`), `$Map` colour maps,
directives and macros. Those buttons carry a small `>>` mark and a tooltip saying so. See
[The Calcpad language](../calcpad/index.md).

## Python

A fenced block with the language `python` is a Python block. It is explained in
[Python blocks](../python.md).

## Show compiled and Convert to Calcpad

On the Resources tab:

* **Show compiled** opens a panel beside the editor with the Calcpad text the sheet becomes. Its
  line numbers are the sheet's lines.
* **Convert to Calcpad** replaces the sheet with that text. It is one way: there is no
  conversion back to a sheet.

A worked example is in [Your first sheet](../getting-started/first-sheet.md#6-see-what-the-sheet-compiles-to).
Both views give Calcpad as a person would write it, so the sheet is also a way to learn the
Calcpad language.

## Errors

The engine's errors, the report's "on line [n]" links, the error banner, the scroll anchors and
the editor's lint markers all report the *sheet* line, whatever kind of line it was. An undefined
name, for example:

```text
bad: foo + 1

Error in "bad = foo + 1" on line [1]: Undefined variable or units: "foo".
```

The text of an engine message still quotes the compiled Calcpad line (`bad = foo + 1`), which is
what Show compiled displays. The compiler's own problems, such as mixed tab and space indentation,
an `else` with no `if`, an empty block, an unclosed `$$` or a bad `plot` line, are markers on their
lines too. "Unused variable" hints are not shown for sheets, since every quantity is shown.

## Format Document

**Format Document** (Shift+Alt+F) prettifies a sheet: one space around `:`, `|` and `->` and
after `;`, a blank line before each heading, runs of blank lines collapsed, and the colons of a run
of quantity lines aligned. Expressions, prose, `>>` lines, fences and formulas are not touched,
and formatting twice changes nothing.

Other editor help works on the names a sheet defines: **Go to definition** (F12), **find
references**, **hover** (shows the defining line and the Calcpad spelling), and colouring by role.

---

Chapter: The Calcpad language
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/calcpad/

# The Calcpad language

<!-- description: The Calcpad worksheet language that every sheet compiles to: how a worksheet reads, a sheet and its Calcpad side by side, operators and angles. -->

The sheet format is a front end. Underneath, every sheet becomes a **Calcpad worksheet**, the
language of CalcpadCE, and the engine runs that. You can also write Calcpad directly: choose
**File > New Calcpad worksheet** (the second item of the File menu, also on the Resources tab), or
open a `.cpd` file.

Use the Calcpad language when you need something a sheet does not offer on its own: macros that
repeat a block with different arguments, input forms with drop-downs and grids, output control
(hide a block, show only results), the numerical commands, reading and writing data files, or
when you are working with worksheets from the CalcpadCE community.

## How a Calcpad worksheet reads

A worksheet is a list of lines. Each line is one of these.

| First character | Kind | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"` | Heading, a comment shown as a heading | `"Beam check` |
| `'` | Text, a comment shown as written (HTML allowed) | `'Span -'L = 6m` |
| `#` | A directive | `#if`, `#for`, `#def`, `#hide` |
| `$` | A command | `$Plot{x^2 @ x = 0 : 5}` |
| anything else | A calculation | `M = w*L^2/8\|kN*m` |

A single quote also switches between text and calculation inside a line, which is how labels
sit in front of an equation: `'Span -'L = 6m` shows the text "Span -" and then the equation.

```cpd
"Beam check
'Span -'L = 6m
'Load -'w = 12kN/m
'Moment -'M = w*L^2/8|kN*m
#if M < 100kN*m
    'OK
#else
    'Too large
#end if
```

```text
Beam check
Span - L = 6 m
Load - w = 12 kN/m
Moment - M = w·L²/8 = 12 kN/m · (6 m)² / 8 = 54 kN·m
OK
```

## Sheet and Calcpad side by side

| Sheet | Calcpad |
| --- | --- |
| `L: 6 m \| span` | `L = 6m 'span` |
| `M: w*L^2/8 -> kN*m` | `M = w*L^2/8\|kN*m` |
| `# Heading` | `'<h1>Heading</h1>` |
| `Plain paragraph` | `'Plain paragraph` |
| `if u <= 1: "OK" else: "Fails"` | `#if u ≤ 1` ... `#else` ... `#end if` |
| `for i in 1..5:` + indented body | `#for i = 1 : 5` ... `#loop` |
| `f(x, y): x + y` | `f(x; y) = x + y` |
| `[1, 2; 3, 4]` | `[1; 2 \| 3; 4]` |
| `plot f(x) for x in 0..5` | `$Plot{f(x) @ x = 0 : 5}` |
| `phi`, `Mstar` | `φ`, `M_star` |

Function arguments are separated with `;` in Calcpad, matrix rows with `|`, and a unit
conversion is a vertical bar. A sheet writes commas, `->` and brackets, and the compiler does the
translation. To see it for any sheet, use **Show compiled**.

## Operators

`^` power, `*` multiplication, `/` division, `\` integer division, `⦼` modulo (type `%%`), `!`
factorial, `+ - `, comparisons `≡ ≠ < > ≤ ≥` (type `== != <= >=`), logical `∧ ∨ ⊕` (type `&& || `),
`=` assignment, `←` assignment to an outer scope. The editor converts the typed forms when you
open a file. The complete table is in the [reference](../reference/functions.md#operators).

## Angles

Angles are in **degrees** unless you say otherwise. `#rad` switches the rest of the worksheet to
radians, `#gra` to gradians and `#deg` back. This matters whenever you pass π or a plain number to
a trigonometric function. See [Troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md).

## Output control

Directives shape what the report shows without changing the calculation.

```cpd
#hide
k = 3
#show
a = k*2
#val
b = k*3
#equ
#nosub
c = k*4
#varsub
```

```text
a = k·2 = 3 · 2 = 6
9
c = k·4 = 12
```

`#hide` ... `#show` calculates but does not print, `#val` prints only the value, `#nosub` prints
the formula without the numbers put in, `#noc` the formula without the result and `#novar` only
the substituted numbers. `#pre` and `#post` split a document into the part that is filled in on
screen and the part that appears in the report. The complete list is in
[Directives](directives.md).

## What the next pages cover

* [Directives and commands](directives.md): conditions, loops, macros, modules, constants,
  settings, files, numerical commands.
* [Input forms with `#UI`](ui-inputs.md): the `#UI` directive, grids and entry options.
* [Templates with inputs](../templates.md): fill-in forms, and the `?` input lines of a sheet.

**Related pages:** [Calcpad worksheets in the browser](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/calcpad-online/). More pages are in [Calculators and guides](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/).

---

Chapter: Directives and commands
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/calcpad/directives

# Directives and commands

<!-- description: Calcpad directives and commands: conditions, loops, macros, modules, constants, number format, text modes, reading data and numerical commands. -->

A directive starts with `#` and controls the flow of the worksheet. A command starts with `$` and
takes arguments in braces. In a sheet, both are written on `>>` lines (or inside a `calcpad`
fence), except the ones the sheet has its own form for (`if`, `for`, `while`, `repeat`, `plot`).

## Conditions

```cpd
M = 150kN*m
#if M < 100kN*m
    'OK
#else if M < 200kN*m
    'Check again
#else
    'Too large
#end if
```

The condition can be any expression that gives a number: zero is false. A condition that cannot
be evaluated (an undefined name, say) is an error, and the block is left unresolved: no branch
runs. CalcpadCE would silently take the `#else` branch; see
[Deviations from CalcpadCE](../appendix/deviations.md).

## Loops

```cpd
#repeat 3
    y = 2
#loop
```

```cpd
#for i = 1 : 4
    #if i ≡ 3
        #continue
    #end if
    s = i
#loop
```

```text
s = i = 1
s = i = 2
s = i = 4
```

Pass 3 is skipped by `#continue`.

```cpd
n = 0
#while n < 3
    n = n + 1
#loop
```

`#break` leaves the loop and `#continue` skips to the next pass. Every line in the loop prints on
every pass, so use `#hide` around the body when you only want the final value. The commands
`$Sum`, `$Product`, `$Repeat` and `$While` do the same without printing each pass.

## Macros and string variables

Macros are text substituted before the worksheet is calculated. A name ends with `$`.

```cpd
#def twice$(a$) = 2*a$
r = twice$(7)
```

```text
r = 2·7 = 14
```

A multi-line macro repeats a whole block with different values:

```cpd
#def beam$(span$; load$)
    M = load$*span$^2/8
    V = load$*span$/2
#end def
beam$(6m; 12kN/m)
```

```text
M = 12 kN/m · (6 m)² / 8 = 9 kN·m
V = 12 kN/m · 6 m / 2 = 36 kN
```

The macro text does not have to be valid Calcpad by itself. It is substituted first and parsed
after. **Unwrapped** in the results views shows the text after substitution, which is the place to
look when a macro misbehaves. A macro cannot contain another definition; it can use an earlier
one.

## Modules

`#include name.cpd` pulls in a file from the library (see [Saving](../getting-started/saving.md)).
Put shared definitions in a file with a `#global` section and keep the worksheet-specific part in
`#local`: only the global part is included when the file is imported.

## Constants

```cpd
#const g_n = 9.81m/s^2
F = 70kg*g_n|N
```

A `#const` cannot be changed later.

## Number format

`#round n` rounds output to n digits, `#round default` goes back; `#format spec` sets a custom
format string (for example `#format 0.00`). The **Decimals** setting sets the default.
`#settings {"decimals": 4}` overrides engine settings for the lines that follow.

## Text modes

`#md on` and `#md off` turn Markdown on and off in comment lines. `#markdown` ... `#end markdown`
and `#html` ... `#end html` switch to a block of Markdown or raw HTML, and `#cpd` goes back to
calculation inside one.

```cpd
#markdown
## Section

* one
* two
#end markdown
```

## Reading and writing data

`#read M from file.csv`, `#write M to file.csv` and `#append M to file.csv` move a matrix
between the worksheet and a text, CSV or Excel file in the library. Options choose the cell range
(`@R1C1:R2C2` for text, `@Sheet1!A1:B2` for Excel), the matrix type and the separator. The full
forms are in the [reference](../reference/functions.md#directives).

A worksheet that writes files saves them into the library and downloads them when their content
changes.

## Numerical commands

```cpd
#rad
f(x) = x^3 - 2*x - 5
r = $Root{f(x) @ x = 2 : 3}
A = $Area{sin(x) @ x = 0 : π}
m = $Slope{x^3 @ x = 2}
hi = $Sup{sin(x) @ x = 0 : 3}
S = $Sum{1/k^2 @ k = 1 : 100}
P = $Product{k @ k = 1 : 5}
```

```text
r = $Root{f(x) = 0; x ∈ [2; 3]} = 2.09
A = ∫ sin(x) dx from 0 to π = 2
m = d/dx x³ at x = 2 = 12
hi = $Sup{sin(x); x ∈ [0; 3]} = 1
S = Σ 1/k² for k = 1 to 100 = 1.63
P = Π k for k = 1 to 5 = 120
```

| Command | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `$Root{f(x) @ x = a : b}` | A root of f in the interval. `$Root{f(x) = c @ ...}` solves f(x) = c. |
| `$Find{f(x) @ x = a : b}` | An approximate solution, when the exact value is not needed. |
| `$Sup`, `$Inf` | Local maximum or minimum. |
| `$Area` | Numerical integral (adaptive Gauss-Lobatto). |
| `$Integral` | Numerical integral (tanh-sinh). |
| `$Slope{f(x) @ x = a}` | Derivative at a point. |
| `$Sum`, `$Product` | Iterative sum and product. |
| `$Repeat`, `$While`, `$Block`, `$Inline` | Iterative expression blocks. |
| `$Plot`, `$Map` | Plots; see [Plots](../plots.md). |

The relative precision of the numerical methods is the `Precision` setting (default 1e-12).

## Python

`#python` ... `#end python` is a Python block. In a sheet it is a fenced `python` block. See
[Python blocks](../python.md).

## Input forms

`#UI` turns an assignment into an input control. See [Input forms with `#UI`](ui-inputs.md). In a sheet, most inputs are written as `L: ? 6 m` lines instead; see [Templates with inputs](../templates.md).

## Not available in the browser

`#pause` and `#input` (step-by-step execution) are not supported in the web version, and neither
are raster (PNG) plots or compiled `.cpdz` worksheets. See
[Deviations from CalcpadCE](../appendix/deviations.md).

---

Chapter: Input forms with #UI
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/calcpad/ui-inputs

# Input forms with `#UI`

<!-- description: Turn Calcpad assignments into input controls with #UI: text boxes, drop-downs, radio buttons, checkboxes and editable grids in Input mode. -->

`#UI` is the Calcpad language's own input directive. It turns the assignment that follows it into an
input control in Input mode: a text box, a drop-down, radio buttons, a checkbox or an editable grid.

In a **sheet**, most inputs do not need it. A line such as `L: ? 6 m | span` is an input, and the
sheet compiler writes the `#UI` line for you. See [Templates with inputs](../templates.md), which
also covers the Input mode, saving values and sharing a template. Write `#UI` yourself when:

* you work in a Calcpad worksheet (`.cpd`);
* you need a data grid, a vector or matrix input, or one of the entry options below, which the `?`
  form has no way to say.

In a sheet, a `#UI` line is a Calcpad line, so it starts with `>>`.

## The input line

```text
>> #UI 'Span, 'L = 6m
```

* `>>` hands the line to the engine as written (leave it out in a `.cpd` worksheet).
* `#UI` says "show the next assignment as an input control in Input mode".
* `'Span, 'L = 6m`: an optional label (`'Span, ` is text) and then the assignment. `L = 6m` is the
  name and the default value, with its unit.

In Preview and in a report this line shows as a plain line (`Span, L = 6 m`). In Input mode the
`6` becomes a text box with `m` beside it.

### What may be on the right of the `=`

| Right-hand side | Allowed | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A number, with or without a unit | Yes | `#UI L = 10m`, `#UI n = 4`, `#UI q = 3kN/m` |
| A vector or matrix literal | Yes | `#UI v = [1; 2; 3]`, `#UI M = [1; 2 \| 3; 4]` |
| `vector(n)` or `matrix(r; c)` | Yes | `#UI Z = vector(5)` |
| An expression | Only with `allowExpression` | `#UI {"allowExpression": true} h = L/2` |
| Text | No | |

## A sheet with `#UI` lines

The beam check as a sheet whose inputs are `#UI` lines. Names such as `phi` or `Delta_T` work in a `#UI` line as in any other line (the first is shown as
`φ`). A dotted name does not: a dot is the index operator.

<!-- expect: Span, L = 6 m | M _star = w · L ^2 8 = 12 kN ∕ m · ( 6 m ) ^2 8 = 54 kN · m | = 0.163 | OK: the section passes. -->
```sheet
# Beam bending check

Fill in the inputs, then read the check below.

## Inputs
>> #UI 'Span, 'L = 6m
>> #UI 'Design load, 'w = 12kN/m
>> #UI 'Yield stress, 'f_y = 300MPa
>> #UI 'Section modulus, 'Z_e = 1230000mm^3
>> #UI 'Capacity factor, 'cf = 0.9

## Check
Mstar: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum moment
Mcap: cf * f_y * Z_e -> kN*m | design capacity
ratio: Mstar / Mcap | utilisation
if ratio <= 1: "OK: the section passes." else: "Fails: increase the section."
```

Change the span to 10 and the load to 20 in the form: the moment is 250 kN·m, the ratio 0.753 and
the message still reads OK.

## Controls

The `type` property picks the control. When it is left out, the engine picks one from the right-hand
side.

```text
>> #UI {"type": "dropdown", "keys": ["Soft clay", "Stiff clay", "Dense sand"], "values": ["75kPa", "150kPa", "300kPa"]} 'Soil allowable bearing, 'q_a = 150kPa
>> #UI {"type": "radio", "keys": ["Concrete", "Steel"], "values": ["25", "78.5"]} 'Column unit weight in kN/m3, 'unit_weight = 25
>> #UI {"type": "checkbox"} 'Include footing weight (1 = yes), 'add_weight = 1
```

* A drop-down or radio group shows the `keys` and works by the matching `values` entry. A value can
  carry its own unit, so a menu can switch units as well as magnitudes (`"values": ["1m", "3.281ft"]`).
* A checkbox is `1` when ticked and `0` when not.
* Use the `?` form of a sheet for these when you can: `E: ? [Steel = 200 GPa, *Timber = 11 GPa]`
  writes this JSON for you.

### A grid and a radio group together

<!-- expect: levels = n_rows(loads) = 3 | = 3240 kN | = 1260 kN | G _column = unit _weight -->
```sheet
# Column load take-down

A column carries the tributary area of each level. Choose the column material, set the sizes and fill in the floor loads, one row per level.

## Inputs
>> #UI 'Tributary area per level, 'A_t = 36m^2
>> #UI 'Column section area, 'A_c = 0.09m^2
>> #UI 'Storey height, 'H = 3.5m
>> #UI {"type": "radio", "keys": ["Concrete", "Steel"], "values": ["25", "78.5"]} 'Column unit weight in kN/m3, 'unit_weight = 25
>> #UI {"type": "datagrid", "columnHeaders": ["Dead", "Live"], "rowHeaders": ["Roof", "Level 2", "Level 1"]} loads = [20; 5 | 35; 15 | 35; 15]

## Loads at the base of the column
levels: n_rows(loads)
G_floors: sum(col(loads, 1)) * 1 kPa * A_t -> kN | dead load from the floors
Q_floors: sum(col(loads, 2)) * 1 kPa * A_t -> kN | live load from the floors
G_column: unit_weight * 1 kN/m^3 * A_c * H * levels -> kN | weight of the column
Nstar: 1.2 * (G_floors + G_column) + 1.5 * Q_floors -> kN | factored axial load
```

The grid is a small spreadsheet of three rows and two columns with its own headers. Its default
(`[20; 5 | 35; 15 | 35; 15]`, with `|` between rows) fills the cells. Click a cell, type a number
and press Enter, and every line that uses `loads` follows. At the defaults:

```text
levels = n_rows(loads) = 3
G_floors = sum(col(loads; 1)) · 1 kPa · A_t = ... = 3240 kN    dead load from the floors
Q_floors = sum(col(loads; 2)) · 1 kPa · A_t = ... = 1260 kN    live load from the floors
G_column = unit_weight · 1 kN/m³ · A_c · H · levels = 25 · 1 kN/m³ · 0.09 m² · 3.5 m · 3 = 23.62 kN
N_star = 1.2·(G_floors + G_column) + 1.5·Q_floors = 1.2 · (3240 kN + 23.62 kN) + 1.5 · 1260 kN = 5806.35 kN
```

Choose **Steel**: `unit_weight` becomes 78.5, `G_column` 74.18 kN and `N_star` 5867.02 kN.

* A grid holds numbers only. To give them units, multiply in the sheet (`* 1 kPa` above) or write
  the units in the headers (`"Dead (kPa)"`).
* The grid size comes from the default value (or the `rows` and `columns` properties). Rows and
  columns cannot be added in the form.
* One `#UI` line per name is the stable arrangement. Rename an input and a value saved under the old
  name is not used any more.

## Entry options

A JSON object between `#UI` and the label sets properties:

```text
>> #UI {"forceUnits": false} 'Line load, 'q = 3kN/m
>> #UI {"allowExpression": true} 'Half span, 'h = L/2
```

* `forceUnits: false` puts the unit inside the box (`3kN/m`), so the user can type another unit.
* `allowExpression: true` accepts a formula as typed, and keeps it a formula across edits. Nothing
  is validated as you type: an entry the engine cannot read leaves the control in place and shows
  the error on the line.

Both were run in the form: the first box held `3kN/m` and `5kN/m` gave a moment of 22.5 kN·m; the
second held `L/2`.

### All the properties

| Property | Applies to | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | all | `entry`, `datagrid`, `dropdown`, `radio`, `checkbox`. Found from the right-hand side when omitted. |
| `forceUnits` | entry, grid | Default `true`: the unit stays in the document and only the number is editable. |
| `allowExpression` | entry, grid | Default `false`. Accepts any expression. Implies `forceUnits: false`. |
| `keys`, `values` | dropdown, radio | The labels shown and the values used. Both are required and must be the same length. |
| `rows`, `columns` | grid | The grid size. A literal is cut or padded with zeros to fit. |
| `rowHeaders`, `columnHeaders` | grid | Header labels. |
| `width`, `rowHeaderWidth`, `columnWidths` | grid | Sizes in pixels, or a percentage for `width`. |
| `style`, `reportStyle` | all | A CSS class for the control, or for its line in the report. |

The ribbon's Input/Output tab inserts a starting line for each control. In a sheet, Entry,
Dropdown, Radio and Checkbox insert the `?` form. Data grid and **More input forms** (the labelled,
vector, matrix and formula forms) insert `>> #UI` lines.

## The views, `#pre` and `#post`

`#pre` and `#post` let one file serve two audiences: an instruction ("fill in the values below")
that only the person at the form sees, and a note ("values used in this report") that only the
report carries. See the table of views in [Templates with inputs](../templates.md#using-the-form).
In a sheet they go in a `calcpad` fence:

````text
```calcpad
#pre
'<p>Fill in the values below, then press Report.</p>
#end pre
```
````

## In a Calcpad worksheet

A worksheet takes the lines as they are and has no renaming issue. The beam check as a `.cpd`:

```cpd
"Beam bending check
#UI 'Span, 'L = 6m
#UI 'Design load, 'w = 12kN/m
#UI 'Yield stress, 'f_y = 300MPa
#UI 'Section modulus, 'Z_e = 1230000mm^3
#UI 'Capacity factor, 'φ = 0.9
M_star = w*L^2/8|kN*m
M_cap = φ*f_y*Z_e|kN*m
ratio = M_star/M_cap
```
