```cpd
#if ratio ≤ 1
    'OK
#else
    'Fails
#end if
```

In a worksheet, **Save values** writes the entered values into a comment on the first line, and the
browser opens the form only when you press **Input**. The Excel export has an **Inputs** sheet
listing the variables set by input fields.

## Known limits

Workarounds for behaviour that is to be fixed. This is the only list of them on this page.

* **Superscript units and exponent notation in a `#UI` line.** The engine's own `#UI` line takes
  only the `^` and `*` spellings. `1230000mm³` is an error there (`Error parsing "mm³" as
  units`), and so is `1.23e6`. Write `1230000mm^3`. A `?` line has no such limit: it takes `mm³`,
  `kN·m`, `N/mm²`, `°` and `%`, and writes the engine's spelling for you.
* **A default should be one of the options.** In a raw line the default of a drop-down or radio
  group should be one of its `values`. A default that matches none still shows the first label
  while the calculation keeps using the default, so the control and the numbers disagree. (The
  `?` form cannot do this: its default is always one of the options.) A match is by value, so a
  default such as `25kN/m` finds the option written `25 kN/m`.
* **Two options cannot have the same value** in a `?` line. It is an error on that line.

---

Chapter: Units
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/units

# Units

<!-- description: Units are part of every value: attach SI and US units, use prefixes, let unit errors catch mistakes, show percentages and define your own units. -->

<p><strong>Video:</strong> Units and results</p>
<video controls preload="none" poster="videos/02-units-and-results.jpg" style="width:100%;max-width:960px" src="videos/02-units-and-results.mp4"></video>

Units are part of the value. The engine carries them through every operation, converts between
them, and stops with an error when a formula does not add up dimensionally.

## Attaching units

Write the unit after a number, with or without a space: `15 kg`, `12kN/m`, `1230000 mm³`.

```sheet
a: 1.23 m + 35 cm + 12 mm -> cm
v: 10 m/s -> km/h
P: 2.5 kN / (50 mm * 200 mm) -> MPa
g0: 9.81 m/s²
m: 70 kg
W: m * g0 -> N
```

```text
a = 1.23 m + 35 cm + 12 mm = 159.2 cm
v = 10 m/s = 36 km/h
P = 2.5 kN / (50 mm · 200 mm) = 0.25 MPa
g0 = 9.81 m/s²
m = 70 kg
W = m·g0 = 70 kg · 9.81 m/s² = 686.7 N
```

Without `->`, a sum comes out in the first unit it meets. With `-> unit` the result is converted
to the unit you choose. In the Calcpad language the same conversion is a vertical bar:
`a = 1.23m + 35cm + 12mm | cm`.

Prefixes work on every unit that takes them: `kN` is 10³ N, `MPa` is 10⁶ Pa, `mm` is 10⁻³ m. See
"Prefixes" below for the full list.

## Prefixes

Any SI prefix goes in front of any SI unit that takes one, so `3 mN`, `2 GPa`, `5 µm`, `40 nF` and `1.2 kΩ`
all work.

| Prefix | Symbol | Factor | | Prefix | Symbol | Factor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| yotta | `Y` | 10²⁴ | | deci | `d` | 10⁻¹ |
| zetta | `Z` | 10²¹ | | centi | `c` | 10⁻² |
| exa | `E` | 10¹⁸ | | milli | `m` | 10⁻³ |
| peta | `P` | 10¹⁵ | | micro | `μ`, `µ` or `u` | 10⁻⁶ |
| tera | `T` | 10¹² | | nano | `n` | 10⁻⁹ |
| giga | `G` | 10⁹ | | pico | `p` | 10⁻¹² |
| mega | `M` | 10⁶ | | femto | `f` | 10⁻¹⁵ |
| kilo | `k` | 10³ | | atto | `a` | 10⁻¹⁸ |
| hecto | `h` | 10² | | zepto | `z` | 10⁻²¹ |
| deca | `da` | 10¹ | | yocto | `y` | 10⁻²⁴ |

Micro can be typed as the Greek mu `μ`, the micro sign `µ` (what a keyboard gives) or a plain `u`; the result
shows `μ`. The units that take a prefix are `g`, `m`, `s`, `A`, `mol`, `cd`, `rad`, `L`, `N`, `Nm`, `Pa`, `bar`,
`J`, `W`, `Wh`, `VA`, `VAR`, `Hz`, `V`, `C`, `F`, `Ω`, `S`, `Wb`, `T`, `H`, `Bq`, `Gy`, `Sv`, `lm`, `lx`, `kat`,
`eV`, `Ah` and `Da`. Everything else stays as it was: `min`, `h`, `d`, `ft`, `in`, `lb`, `psi`, `°C` and the
other non-SI units take no prefix (`kft` and `mmin` are errors), the kilogram is `kg` (`Mg` is a megagram, not
`kkg`), and kelvin `K` takes none either.

A name the unit list already had keeps its meaning, and the list is read first. So `min` is the minute (not a
milli-inch), `mm` is the millimetre, `Pa` the pascal, `cd` the candela, `ft` the foot, `h` the hour, `d` the day,
`T` the tesla and `u` the atomic mass unit; `da` alone is not a unit, and `dam` is the decametre. The prefix
spellings that read as another unit are told apart by their case: `fT` is a femtotesla and `ft` a foot, `mS` is
a millisiemens and `ms` a millisecond. One name is shadowed: `ks` has always been the metric horsepower, so a
kilosecond is written `1000 s`. A variable you define always wins over a unit of the same
name, so a sheet that has a variable called `mN` still works.

<!-- expect: F _n = F = 3 mN = 0.003 N | E _m = E = 2 GPa = 2000 MPa | t _n = t = 5 μm = 5000 nm -->
```sheet
F: 3 mN
F_n: F -> N
E: 2 GPa
E_m: E -> MPa
t: 5 µm
t_n: t -> nm
```

```text
F_n = F = 3 mN = 0.003 N
E_m = E = 2 GPa = 2000 MPa
t_n = t = 5 μm = 5000 nm
```

## Errors you want

```sheet
x: 6 m
t: 2 s
speed: x / t
```

```text
speed = x/t = 6 m / 2 s = 3 m/s
```

Dividing a length by a time is fine. Adding them is not:

```text
x: 6 m
t: 2 s
speed: x / t
len: x + t

Error in "len = x + t" on line [4]: Inconsistent units: "m + s".
```

That is the engine doing its job. A unit slip is the most common mistake in hand calculations, and
here it stops the sheet and names the line.

## Which units exist

The built-in list is long. The groups are:

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Dimensionless | `%`, `‰`, `ppm`, angles `°`, `rad`, `grad`, `rev` |
| Mass | `g`, `kg`, `t`, `mg`, `lb`, `oz`, `slug` |
| Length | `m`, `km`, `mm`, `μm`, `in`, `ft`, `yd`, `mi`, `nmi` |
| Time and frequency | `s`, `ms`, `min`, `h`, `d`, `Hz`, `rpm` |
| Force | `N`, `kN`, `MN`, `kgf`, `lbf`, `kip` |
| Pressure | `Pa`, `kPa`, `MPa`, `bar`, `atm`, `psi`, `ksi` |
| Energy and power | `J`, `kJ`, `Wh`, `kWh`, `cal`, `BTU`, `W`, `kW`, `hp` |
| Area and volume | `a`, `ha`, `ac`, `L`, `mL`, `gal`, `bbl` |
| Temperature | `K`, `°C`, `°F`, `°R` |
| Electrical | `A`, `V`, `Ω`, `F`, `H`, `C`, `S`, `T`, `Wb` |
| Other | `mol`, `cd`, `lm`, `lx`, `Bq`, `Gy`, `Sv`, `kat` |

The Insert tab in the sidebar lists all 400 or so, grouped, and a click inserts one. The Math
tab has a **Units** palette organised by dimension.

### Angles

Angle units are accepted by trigonometric functions and override every other setting.
`sin(30 deg)` is 0.5 whatever the angle setting is. A bare number follows the setting: degrees by
default, changed on the Math Formatting tab (`#deg`, `#rad`, `#gra` in Calcpad). Inverse
trigonometric functions return a plain number unless you define `ReturnAngleUnits = 1`
(Calcpad line) first:

```cpd
a = asin(0.5)
ReturnAngleUnits = 1
b = asin(0.5)
```

```text
a = asin(0.5) = 30
ReturnAngleUnits = 1
b = asin(0.5) = 30°
```

### Temperatures

`20 °C` is a temperature; `300 K` is another, and the difference of two temperatures is a
difference:

```sheet
T1: 20 °C
T2: 300 K
d: T2 - T1
```

```text
d = T2 − T1 = 300 K − 20 °C = 280 K
```

### US and UK names

A few bare names mean different things in the US and UK systems (`gal`, `ton`, `pt`, `qt`, `bbl`,
`cwt`, `therm`). The setting **Non-metric units** picks one. Write the explicit suffix
(`gal_US`, `gal_UK`) when a sheet must not depend on the setting.

## Percentages

A ratio has no unit, so it comes out as a plain number. Convert it with `-> %` to show it as a
percentage, and write `%` after a number to enter one. `‰` (per mille) works the same way.

<!-- expect: 355.1 kN = 0.691 | util = ratio = 0.691 = 69.07 % | f = Ed · r = 245.25 kN · 4 % = 9.81 kN -->
```sheet
Ed: 245.25 kN
Rd: 355.1 kN
ratio: Ed / Rd
util: ratio -> %
r: 4%
f: Ed * r
slope: 1 / 40 -> ‰
```

```text
ratio = Ed / Rd = 245.25 kN / 355.1 kN = 0.691
util = ratio = 0.691 = 69.07 %
r = 4 %
f = Ed · r = 245.25 kN · 4 % = 9.81 kN
slope = 1 / 40 = 25 ‰
```

The value itself does not change, only the way it is shown: `util` is the same number as
`ratio`, and `r` is 0.04 in every formula. A result in percent is rounded to the decimals set on the
Math Formatting tab like any other result, and the rounded figure typed back in (`69.07%`) is the
same ratio to that many digits. An input works the same way: `rate: ? 12.5 %` shows a box holding
12.5 with `%` after it, and the name is 0.125 in the formulas.

A percentage times a plain number is a plain number (`4 % · 2` is `0.08`); add `-> %` to the line
to keep it as a percentage.

## Your own units

A sheet defines a unit of its own with a `#unit` line: the name, `=`, and its value in units
the engine knows or in units defined above it. Later lines use it after a number and after `->`,
like any other unit.

<!-- expect: bag = 25 kg cement bag | load = 3 pallet = 3 t | n = 1000 kg = 40 bag -->
```sheet
#unit bag = 25 kg | cement bag
#unit pallet = 40 bag
load: 3 pallet -> t
n: 1000 kg -> bag
rate: 6 bag / 1 m³ -> kg/m³
```

```text
bag = 25 kg   cement bag
pallet = 40 bag
load = 3 pallet = 3 t
n = 1000 kg = 40 bag
rate = 6 bag / 1 m³ = 150 kg/m³
```

A unit name is letters and `_` only (`bag`, `ton_short`), with no digits; a name with a digit is an
error on its line. The value can use the usual spellings (`m²`, `kN·m`) and can have a note after
`|`. A built-in unit cannot be redefined: `#unit slug = 14.6 kg` is an error, because `slug` is
already a unit. In the Calcpad language, and in a `>>` line of a sheet, the same unit is a line
with a dot in front of the name: `.bag = 25kg`.

Currency and information units are defined as dimensionless units, the first as 1 and the others
as multiples:

```sheet
#unit USD = 1
#unit AUD = 0.65 USD
price: 200 AUD -> USD
```

```text
USD = 1
AUD = 0.65 USD
price = 200 AUD = 130 USD
```

Two families of dimensionless custom units in one sheet share a dimension, so do not mix them.

## Units and names

A word that follows a number immediately is a unit (`2 m`). A standalone word is a variable if you
defined one with that name, and a unit otherwise. Put a dot in front to force a unit even when a
variable has the same name. In a sheet this rarely matters, but it explains one surprise: if you
name a variable `m` and later write `5 m`, the `m` after the number is still the unit.

## Removing and reading units

The functions `getunits(x)`, `clrunits(x)` and `setunits(x, u)` read, strip and attach units. They
are in the [function reference](reference/functions.md).

```sheet
q: setunits(5, kN)
F: 5 kN
n: F / 1 kN
```

```text
q = setunits(5; kN) = 5 kN
F = 5 kN
n = F / 1 kN = 5 kN / 1 kN = 5
```

Use `clrunits` sparingly. A value without a unit is a value the engine can no longer check.

## Units in vectors and matrices

A vector or matrix whose elements all carry the same unit shows the unit once after the
bracket. See [Vectors and matrices](vectors-matrices.md).

**Related pages:** [Calculations with units](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/engineering-calculations-with-units/), [Simply supported beam](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/simply-supported-beam-calculator/), [Pipe flow, Darcy-Weisbach](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/pipe-flow-darcy-weisbach-calculator/). More pages are in [Calculators and guides](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/).

---

Chapter: Vectors and matrices
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/vectors-matrices

# Vectors and matrices

<!-- description: Vectors and matrices in a sheet: write them with brackets, do arithmetic, solve and decompose, find eigenvalues and read or write data files. -->

## Writing them

In a sheet, a bracket makes a vector or a matrix. Elements are separated by commas or semicolons
and rows by semicolons:

| You write | You get |
| --- | --- |
| `[1, 2, 3]` or `[1; 2; 3]` | a vector with three elements |
| `[1, 2; 3, 4]` | a 2 by 2 matrix: columns separated by commas, rows by semicolons |

Rows must have equal length and elements can be expressions. (In the Calcpad language the same
matrix is `[1; 2 | 3; 4]`, with `|` between rows.)

```sheet
v: [1, 2, 3]
A: [2, -1; -1, 2]
b: [1; 0]
x: lsolve(A, b)
d: det(A)
e: v.2
f: A.(1, 2)
```

```text
v = [1; 2; 3] = [1 2 3]
A = [2; -1 | -1; 2] = | 2 -1 |
                      | -1 2 |
b = [1; 0] = [1 0]
x = lsolve(A; b) = [0.667 0.333]
d = det(A) = 3
e = v.2 = 2
f = A.(1; 2) = -1
```

An element is reached with a dot: `v.2` is the second element of the vector `v`, and `A.(1, 2)` is
row 1, column 2 of `A`. Indexes start at 1.

Vector and matrix names show an arrow over a vector in the report.

## Arithmetic

```sheet
A: [1, 2; 3, 4]
B: A * A
C: A + 2
D: A - [1, 1; 1, 1]
At: transp(A)
v: [1; 2]
Av: A * v
r: rank(A)
tr: trace(A)
```

```text
B = A·A = | 7 10 |
          | 15 22 |
C = A + 2 = | 3 4 |
            | 5 6 |
Av = A·v = [5 11]
rank(A) = 2     trace(A) = 5
```

A matrix times a matrix is the matrix product. A matrix plus or minus a number applies to every
element. A power applies to every element of a vector (`x^2` above squares each element), and
`hprod(A, B)` is the element-by-element product of two matrices.

## Solving and decomposing

```sheet
K: [4, -2; -2, 3]
F: [10; 0]
u: lsolve(K, F)
```

```text
u = lsolve(K; F) = [3.75 2.5]
```

`lsolve(A, b)` solves A x = b with an LDLᵀ factorisation for a symmetric matrix and an LU
factorisation otherwise. `clsolve` uses Cholesky and `slsolve` an iterative method for large
sparse systems. `msolve` solves for several right-hand sides at once. `inverse`, `det`, `rank`,
`cond`, `lu`, `qr`, `svd`, `cholesky`, `eigenvals`, `eigenvecs` and `eigen` are there too.

## Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

```sheet
K: [4, -2; -2, 3]
lam: eigenvals(K)
V: eigenvecs(K)
E: eigen(K)
```

```text
lam = eigenvals(K) = [1.44 5.56]
V = eigenvecs(K) = | -0.615 -0.788 |
                   | -0.788  0.615 |
E = eigen(K) = | 1.44 -0.615 -0.788 |
               | 5.56 -0.788  0.615 |
```

`eigenvals(M)` returns the eigenvalues of a square matrix in ascending order.
`eigenvecs(M)` returns one unit eigenvector per **row**, in the same order, and `eigen(M)` gives
both at once with the eigenvalue in the first column. A second argument keeps only some of them:
`eigenvals(M, 2)` is the two smallest and `eigenvals(M, -1)` the largest. Units carry over, so a
stress tensor in MPa has principal stresses in MPa.

The matrix does not have to be symmetric:

<!-- expect: eigenvals(A) = [2 5] | eigenvals(A; -1) = [5] -->
```sheet
A: [4, 1; 2, 3]
lam: eigenvals(A)
V: eigenvecs(A)
lmax: eigenvals(A, -1)
```

```text
lam = eigenvals(A) = [2 5]
V = eigenvecs(A) = | -0.447 0.894 |
                   |  0.707 0.707 |
lmax = eigenvals(A; -1) = [5]
```

A symmetric matrix uses the symmetric solver. Any other square matrix is reduced to Hessenberg form
and solved with the shifted QR iteration; each eigenvector is scaled to unit length with its largest
component positive.

### Complex eigenvalues

A real matrix that is not symmetric can have complex eigenvalues, which a vector cannot hold.
`eigenvals` then stops with `The matrix has complex eigenvalues.` Use `ceigenvals` and
`ceigenvecs`, which write each complex number as a real part and an imaginary part, the same
layout `fft` uses:

<!-- expect: ceigenvals(R) = 1 1 -2 2 -->
```sheet
R: [1, -2; 2, 1]
C: ceigenvals(R)
W: ceigenvecs(R)
```

```text
C = ceigenvals(R) = |  1 1 |
                    | -2 2 |
W = ceigenvecs(R) = | 0.707     0 |
                    |     0 0.707 |
                    | 0.707     0 |
                    |     0 -0.707 |
```

Column k of `ceigenvals` is eigenvalue k: row 1 is the real part and row 2 the imaginary part,
so the eigenvalues above are 1 - 2i and 1 + 2i. In `ceigenvecs` eigenvector k is row 2k - 1
(real parts) plus row 2k (imaginary parts): the first one is [0.707, 0.707i]. They are sorted by
real part, then imaginary part.

For the polar form, magnitude and angle, use the two rows:

```sheet
R: [1, -2; 2, 1]
C: ceigenvals(R)
mag: sqrt(row(C, 1)^2 + row(C, 2)^2)
ang: atan2(row(C, 1), row(C, 2))
```

```text
mag = [2.24 2.24]
ang = atan2(row(C; 1); row(C; 2)) = [-63.43 63.43]
```

In a Calcpad document with complex numbers switched on in Settings, `#phasor` shows every
complex result as magnitude∠angle, and `#complex` switches back to a + bi.

### Natural frequencies: K x = λ M x

Give `eigenvals`, `eigenvecs` or `eigen` a second matrix and they solve the generalized problem
K x = λ M x. With a stiffness matrix K and a mass matrix M, each λ is ω², the square of a natural
circular frequency:

<!-- expect: eigenvals(K; M) = [585.79 3414.21] | = 3.85 Hz | row(Φ; 1)) = 1 -->
```sheet
k: 20000 kN/m
m: 10 t
K: [2*k, -k; -k, k]
M: [2*m, 0 t; 0 t, m]
λ: eigenvals(K, M)
f_1: sqrt(λ.1)/(2*π) -> Hz
Phi: eigenvecs(K, M)
m_1: dot(row(Phi, 1), M*row(Phi, 1))
```

```text
λ = eigenvals(K; M) = [585.79 3414.21] s⁻²
f_1 = 3.85 Hz
Φ = eigenvecs(K; M) = |  0.158 0.224 | t^-0.5
                      | -0.158 0.224 |
m_1 = 1
```

K must be symmetric and M symmetric positive definite, both square and the same size; anything
else stops with a message that says which matrix is wrong. The eigenvalues come in ascending order
with the units of K/M (kN/m over t is s⁻²). Each mode shape is a row of `eigenvecs(K, M)`, scaled so
that xᵀ M x = 1 and turned so that its largest component is positive; its units are those of
M^-0.5, so the modal mass `m_1` above is exactly 1. Divide a row by one of its components to scale
it to 1 at that point instead. Internally M is factored by Cholesky (M = L Lᵀ), the problem is
turned into the symmetric one of L⁻¹ K L⁻ᵀ, solved with the symmetric solver, and transformed back.
To keep only the lowest modes, take them from the result: `first(eigenvals(K, M), 3)`.

The samples *Principal stresses* (a plane and a 3D stress tensor, checked with Mohr's circle) and
*Shear frame natural frequencies* (the frequencies and mode shapes of a two storey frame from
`eigenvals(K, M)`) use these functions.

## Building vectors and matrices

```sheet
x: range(0, 10, 2.5)
y: x^2
s: sum(y)
mx: max(y)
w: linspace(0, 1, 5)
```

```text
x = range(0; 10; 2.5) = [0 2.5 5 7.5 10]
y = x ^ 2 = [0 6.25 25 56.25 100]
s = sum(y) = 187.5
mx = max(y) = 100
w = linspace(0; 1; 5) = [0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1]
```

Constructors: `vector(n)`, `matrix(m, n)`, `identity(n)`, `diagonal(n, d)`, `column(m, c)`,
`utriang(n)`, `ltriang(n)`, `symmetric(n)`, `join_cols`, `join_rows`, `augment`, `stack`.
Pieces: `row`, `col`, `submatrix`, `slice`, `first`, `last`, `extract`, `diag2vec`. Sorting and
searching: `sort`, `rsort`, `order`, `find`, `lookup`, `hlookup`, `vlookup`. Statistics and
interpolation: `average`, `median`, `stdev`, `var`, `take`, `line`, `spline`, `interp`, `linterp`,
`polyfit`.

```sheet
A2: [1, 2, 3; 4, 5, 6]
r1: row(A2, 1)
c2: col(A2, 2)
sm: submatrix(A2, 1, 2, 2, 3)
```

```text
r1 = row(A2; 1) = [1 2 3]
c2 = col(A2; 2) = [2 5]
sm = submatrix(A2; 1; 2; 2; 3) = | 2 3 |
                                 | 5 6 |
```

The whole list is in the [function reference](reference/functions.md). The large high-performance
variants (`matrix_hp` and so on) are for big numerical models: they store the numbers more
compactly and are faster, and they behave like the ordinary ones in a calculation.

## Units in vectors and matrices

A vector or matrix whose elements all have the same unit shows the unit once, after the closing
bracket:

```sheet
P: [16 ft; 12 ft]
Q: [3 m; 40 cm]
```

```text
P = [16; 12] ft = [16 12] ft
Q = [3 m; 40 cm] = [3 0.4] m
```

Elements in another unit of the same dimension are converted to the first element's unit in the
result. An element that is an expression, has no unit, or has another dimension keeps its own
unit. To write the unit on every element, put a `>>` line in the sheet:

```sheet
>> #settings {"unitPerElement": true}
P: [16 ft; 12 ft]
```

You cannot write a unit after a bracket (`[1, 2] kN`). Put it on the elements.

## Reading and writing files

`#read` brings a matrix in from a text, CSV or Excel file in the library, and `#write` and
`#append` save one. They are Calcpad directives, so in a sheet they are `>>` lines:

```text
>> #read M from loads.csv
>> #write M to results.csv
```

Add the files to the library first (File > Open, or drag them onto the page). The options for
cell ranges and separators are in the [directive list](reference/functions.md#directives).

**Related calculators:** [Principal stresses](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/principal-stress-calculator/), [Principal axes of a section](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/section-principal-axes-calculator/), [Shear frame frequencies](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/shear-frame-natural-frequencies/). More pages are in [Calculators and guides](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/).

Chapter: Function and command reference
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/reference/functions

# Function and command reference

This page is generated from the editor's own snippet library (`book/gen-reference.py`), so it
lists what the Insert tab and the ribbon offer. In the Calcpad language, arguments are separated
with `;`, as shown here. In a sheet, write commas: `max(a, b)`.

Names are case sensitive. Greek letters, subscripts (`x_1`) and primes can be part of a name.

## Constants

`π` (also `pi`) and `e` are built in. The others are snippets that insert a definition line; until the line is in the worksheet the name means whatever it meant before (`g` is the unit gram).

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `π` | Pi - ratio of circumference to diameter |
| `pi` | Pi - ratio of circumference to diameter (spelled out) |
| `e` | Euler's number - base of natural logarithm |
| `φ = 1.618033988749894` | Golden ratio |
| `γ = 0.5772156649015328` | Euler-Mascheroni constant |
| `g = 9.80665m/s^2` | Standard gravitational acceleration |
| `G = 6.67430*10^-11*(m^3/(kg*s^2))` | Gravitational constant |
| `M_E = 5.9722*10^24*kg` | Earth mass |
| `M_S = 1.98847*10^30*kg` | Solar mass |
| `c = 299792458m/s` | Speed of light in vacuum |
| `h = 6.62607015*10^-34*J/Hz` | Planck constant |
| `μ_0 = 1.25663706212*10^-6*N/A^2` | Vacuum permeability |
| `ε_0 = 8.8541878128*10^-12*F/m` | Vacuum permittivity |
| `k_e = 8.9875517923*10^9*N*m^2/C^2` | Coulomb constant |
| `e = 1.602176634*10^-19*C` | Elementary charge |
| `m_e = 9.1093837015*10^-31*kg` | Electron mass |
| `m_p = 1.67262192369*10^-27*kg` | Proton mass |
| `m_n = 1.67492749804*10^-27*kg` | Neutron mass |
| `N_A = 6.02214076*10^23*mol^-1` | Avogadro constant |
| `σ = 5.670374419*10^-8*W*m^-2*K^-4` | Stefan-Boltzmann constant |
| `k_B = 1.380649*10^-23*J/K` | Boltzmann constant |
| `R = 8.31446261815324*(J/(mol*K))` | Molar gas constant |
| `F = 96485.33212331C/mol` | Faraday constant |
| `γ_c = 25kN/m^3` | Unit weight of concrete |
| `γ_s = 78.5kN/m^3` | Unit weight of steel |
| `γ_a = 27kN/m^3` | Unit weight of aluminium |
| `γ_g = 25kN/m^3` | Unit weight of glass |
| `γ_w = 10kN/m^3` | Unit weight of water |

## Matrix functions

Functions marked `_hp` use the high-performance storage; they behave like the ordinary ones.

| `column_hp(a; b)` | Creates a high-performance column matrix m x 1 |

### Data

| Form | Meaning |

| `mfind_ne(a; b)` | Indexes of elements != x |
| `mfind_lt(a; b)` | Indexes of elements < x |
| `mfind_le(a; b)` | Indexes of elements <= x |
| `mfind_gt(a; b)` | Indexes of elements > x |
| `mfind_ge(a; b)` | Indexes of elements >= x |
| `hlookup(a; b; c; d)` | Values from row i2 where row i1 elements = x |
| `hlookup_eq(a; b; c; d)` | Values from row i2 where row i1 = x |
| `hlookup_ne(a; b; c; d)` | Values from row i2 where row i1 != x |
| `hlookup_lt(a; b; c; d)` | Values from row i2 where row i1 < x |
| `hlookup_le(a; b; c; d)` | Values from row i2 where row i1 <= x |
| `hlookup_gt(a; b; c; d)` | Values from row i2 where row i1 > x |
| `hlookup_ge(a; b; c; d)` | Values from row i2 where row i1 >= x |
| `vlookup(a; b; c; d)` | Values from column j2 where column j1 = x |
| `vlookup_eq(a; b; c; d)` | Values from column j2 where column j1 = x |
| `vlookup_ne(a; b; c; d)` | Values from column j2 where column j1 != x |
| `vlookup_lt(a; b; c; d)` | Values from column j2 where column j1 < x |
| `vlookup_le(a; b; c; d)` | Values from column j2 where column j1 <= x |
| `vlookup_gt(a; b; c; d)` | Values from column j2 where column j1 > x |
| `vlookup_ge(a; b; c; d)` | Values from column j2 where column j1 >= x |

### Math

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `hprod(a; b)` | Hadamard (element-wise) product of matrices A and B |
| `fprod(a; b)` | Frobenius product of matrices A and B |
| `kprod(a; b)` | Kronecker product of matrices A and B |
| `mnorm(x)` | L2 norm of matrix M |
| `mnorm_1(x)` | L1 norm of matrix M |
| `mnorm_2(x)` | L2 norm of matrix M |
| `mnorm_e(x)` | Frobenius norm of matrix M |
| `mnorm_i(x)` | L-infinity norm of matrix M |
| `cond(x)` | Condition number based on L2 norm |
| `cond_1(x)` | Condition number based on L1 norm |
| `cond_2(x)` | Condition number based on L2 norm |
| `cond_e(x)` | Condition number based on Frobenius norm |
| `cond_i(x)` | Condition number based on L-infinity norm |
| `det(x)` | Determinant of matrix M |
| `rank(x)` | Rank of matrix M |
| `trace(x)` | Trace of matrix M (sum of diagonal elements) |
| `transp(x)` | Transpose of matrix M |
| `adj(x)` | Adjugate of matrix M |
| `cofactor(x)` | Cofactor matrix of M |
| `polyroots(x)` | Real roots of a polynomial |
| `eigenvals(a; b)` | First ne eigenvalues of matrix M (or all if omitted), or of K x = λ M x |
| `eigenvecs(a; b)` | First ne eigenvectors of matrix M (or all if omitted), or of K x = λ M x |
| `eigen(a; b)` | First ne eigenvalues and eigenvectors (or all if omitted) |
| `ceigenvals(x)` | Complex eigenvalues of matrix M |
| `ceigenvecs(x)` | Complex eigenvectors of matrix M |
| `cholesky(x)` | Cholesky decomposition of symmetric positive-definite matrix |
| `lu(x)` | LU decomposition of matrix M |
| `qr(x)` | QR decomposition of matrix M |
| `svd(x)` | Singular value decomposition of M |
| `inverse(x)` | Inverse of matrix M |
| `lsolve(a; b)` | Solves Ax = b using LDLT (symmetric) or LU decomposition |
| `clsolve(a; b)` | Solves Ax = b using Cholesky decomposition |
| `slsolve(a; b)` | Solves Ax = b using preconditioned conjugate gradient |
| `msolve(a; b)` | Solves AX = B using LDLT or LU decomposition |
| `cmsolve(a; b)` | Solves AX = B using Cholesky decomposition |
| `smsolve(a; b)` | Solves AX = B using preconditioned conjugate gradient |
| `fft(x)` | Fast Fourier transform (1 row for real, 2 for complex) |
| `ift(x)` | Inverse Fourier transform (1 row for real, 2 for complex) |
| `take(a; b; c)` | Returns element of matrix M at indexes x and y |
| `line(a; b; c)` | Double linear interpolation from matrix M |
| `spline(a; b; c)` | Double Hermite spline interpolation from matrix M |

## Commands

Commands start with `$` and take their arguments in braces. `@` separates the expression from the variable and its interval `a : b`. In a sheet, write them on a `>>` line, except plots, which have the `plot` line.

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `$Root{a @ b = c : d}` | Root finding for f(x) = 0 |
| `$Root{a = b @ c = d : e}` | Root finding for f(x) = const |
| `$Find{a @ b = c : d}` | Find approximate solution (x not required to be precise) |
| `$Sup{a @ b = c : d}` | Find local maximum of a function |
| `$Inf{a @ b = c : d}` | Find local minimum of a function |
| `$Area{a @ b = c : d}` | Numerical integration (adaptive Gauss-Lobatto) |
| `$Integral{a @ b = c : d}` | Numerical integration (Tanh-Sinh) |
| `$Slope{a @ b = c}` | Numerical differentiation (slope at point) |
| `$Sum{a @ b = c : d}` | Iterative sum |
| `$Product{a @ b = c : d}` | Iterative product |
| `$Repeat{a @ b = c : d}` | Iterative expression block with counter |
| `$While{a; b}` | Iterative expression block with condition |
| `$Block{x}` | Multiline expression block |
| `$Inline{x}` | Inline expression block |
| `$Plot{a @ b = c : d}` | Simple function plot |
| `$Plot{a \| b @ c = d : e}` | Parametric plot |
| `$Plot{a & b @ c = d : e}` | Multiple function plot |
| `$Map{a @ b = c : d & e = f : g}` | 2D color map of a 3D surface |

## Directives

Directives start with `#`. The block forms (`#if` ... `#end if`) are listed once, by their opening word.

### Program Flow Control

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#if` | If condition |
| `#else if condition` | Else If clause |
| `#else` | Else clause |

### Iteration Blocks

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#repeat` | Repeat loop start |
| `#for` | For loop start |
| `#while` | While loop start |
| `#loop` | End of loop block |
| `#break` | Break out of current loop |
| `#continue` | Continue to next iteration |

### Modules and Macros

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#include filename` | Include external file (module). Path is relative to the current file or the library path. |
| `#ProjectPath path` | Declares the folder {project} stands for in #include, #read, #write and image paths below this line. |
| `#LibraryPath path` | Declares the folder {library} stands for in #include, #read, #write and image paths below this line. |
| `#local` | Start local section (not included when file is imported) |
| `#global` | Start global section (included when file is imported) |
| `#def` | Define macro or string variable |
| `#def name$ = expression` | Inline string variable definition |
| `#def name$(param$) = expression` | Inline macro with parameters |

### External Data

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#read M from filename` | Read matrix from text/CSV or Excel file |
| `#read M from filename.csv@R1C1:R2C2 TYPE=R SEP=','` | Read matrix from a CSV/text file with all options. @R1C1:R2C2 = cell range (row, column). TYPE: R=Raw (default), D=Diagonal, C=Column, L=Lower triangular, U=Upper triangular, S=Symmetric, V=Vector. SEP: column separator character (default ','). |
| `#read M from filename.xlsx@Sheet1!A1:B2 TYPE=R` | Read matrix from an Excel file (.xlsx/.xlsm) with all options. @Sheet!A1:B2 = sheet name and cell range. TYPE: R=Raw (default), D=Diagonal, C=Column, L=Lower triangular, U=Upper triangular, S=Symmetric, V=Vector. |
| `#write M to filename` | Write matrix to text/CSV or Excel file |
| `#write M to filename.csv@R1C1:R2C2 TYPE=N SEP=','` | Write matrix to a CSV/text file with all options. @R1C1:R2C2 = cell range (row, column). TYPE: Y=Compact (transpose special matrix types), N=Normal (default). SEP: column separator character (default ','). |
| `#write M to filename.xlsx@Sheet1!A1:B2 TYPE=N` | Write matrix to an Excel file (.xlsx/.xlsm) with all options. @Sheet!A1:B2 = sheet name and cell range. TYPE: Y=Compact (transpose special matrix types), N=Normal (default). |
| `#append M to filename` | Append matrix to text/CSV or Excel file |
| `#append M to filename.csv@R1C1:R2C2 TYPE=N SEP=','` | Append matrix to a CSV/text file with all options. @R1C1:R2C2 = cell range (row, column). TYPE: Y=Compact (transpose special matrix types), N=Normal (default). SEP: column separator character (default ','). |
| `#append M to filename.xlsx@Sheet1!A1:B2 TYPE=N` | Append matrix to an Excel file (.xlsx/.xlsm) with all options. @Sheet!A1:B2 = sheet name and cell range. TYPE: Y=Compact (transpose special matrix types), N=Normal (default). |

### Read Only

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#const` | Define a constant (readonly) variable or function |
| `#const name = value` | Define a constant variable |
| `#const f(x) = expression` | Define a constant function |

### Output Control

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#show` | Show the output contents (default). Optionally takes a condition, e.g. '#show x == 5'. Applies to the rest of the document, or up to a matching #end show. |
| `#hide` | Hide the output contents. Optionally takes a condition, e.g. '#hide x == 5'. Applies to the rest of the document, or up to a matching #end hide. |
| `#pre` | Show contents on screen only - hidden when printing/exporting to PDF. Optionally takes a condition. Applies to the rest of the document, or up to a matching #end pre. |
| `#post` | Show contents in the preview and when printing/exporting to PDF - hidden in UI mode. Optionally takes a condition. Applies to the rest of the document, or up to a matching #end post. |
| `#val` | Show only the result, without the equation. Optionally takes a condition. Applies to the rest of the document, or up to a matching #end val. |
| `#equ` | Show complete equations and results (default). Optionally takes a condition. Applies to the rest of the document, or up to a matching #end equ. |
| `#noc` | Show equations without results (no calculations). Optionally takes a condition. Applies to the rest of the document, or up to a matching #end noc. |
| `#varsub` | Show equations with both variable names and their substituted values (default). Optionally takes a condition. Applies to the rest of the document, or up to a matching #end varsub. |
| `#nosub` | Show equations with variable names only, without substituted values. Optionally takes a condition. Applies to the rest of the document, or up to a matching #end nosub. |
| `#novar` | Show equations with substituted values only, without variable names. Optionally takes a condition. Applies to the rest of the document, or up to a matching #end novar. |
| `#split` | Split long equations after the "=" symbol onto a new indented line. Applies to the rest of the document; takes no condition and has no #end form - switch back with #wrap. |
| `#wrap` | Wrap long equations at the end of the line (default). Applies to the rest of the document; takes no condition and has no #end form - switch back with #split. |
| `#format spec` | Specify custom format string |
| `#format default` | Restore default formatting |
| `#phasor` | Set complex number output to polar phasor (A angle phi) |
| `#complex` | Set complex number output to cartesian algebraic (a + ib) |
| `#md on` | Enable markdown in comments |
| `#md off` | Disable markdown in comments |
| `#html` | Output the following lines as raw HTML. Only #cpd, #markdown and the #end forms are allowed inside; macros still expand. Optionally takes a condition, e.g. '#html x > 3', that skips the block when false. Applies up to a matching #end html, or until the next mode directive. |
| `#markdown` | Render the following lines as Markdown, including tables, lists and code blocks. Only #cpd, #html and the #end forms are allowed inside; macros still expand. Optionally takes a condition, e.g. '#markdown x > 3', that skips the block when false. Applies up to a matching #end markdown, or until the next mode directive. |
| `#cpd` | Parse the following lines as Calcpad (the default mode), e.g. to calculate inside an #html block. Optionally takes a condition, e.g. '#cpd x > 3', that skips the block when false. Applies up to a matching #end cpd, or until the next mode directive. |

### UI Inputs

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#UI L = 10m` | Expose the following assignment as an input control in UI mode. Ignored when rendering a report. |
| `#UI {"type": "datagrid", "rows": 2, "columns": 3, "columnHeaders": ["a", "b", "c"]} M = [1; 2; 3 \| 4; 5; 6]` | Editable grid for a vector or matrix. Rows and columns are auto-detected from the right hand side when omitted. |
| `#UI v = [1; 2; 3]` | Editable grid whose size is auto-detected from the vector or matrix assigned to it. |
| `#UI {"type": "datagrid", "width": "100%", "rowHeaderWidth": 120, "columnWidths": [2, 1, 1]} M = matrix(2; 3)` | Sized grid. 'width' is the total in pixels or "100%" to fill the line; 'columnWidths' are shared out in proportion. |
| `#UI {"forceUnits": false} q = 3kN/m` | Put the unit in the input box, so the whole value - number and unit - is editable. |
| `#UI {"allowExpression": true} k = 2*L` | Accept any expression, written to the document as typed. The line's own errors report what it cannot read. |
| `#UI {"type": "dropdown", "keys": ["Low", "High"], "values": ["1", "2"]} x = 1` | Drop-down list. 'keys' are the labels shown, 'values' are substituted into the calculation. |
| `#UI {"type": "radio", "keys": ["Steel", "Concrete"], "values": ["200GPa", "25GPa"]} E = 200GPa` | Radio button group. 'keys' are the labels shown, 'values' are substituted into the calculation. |
| `#UI {"type": "checkbox"} b = 1` | Checkbox toggling the value between 1 and 0. |

### Settings/Rounding

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#round digits` | Round output to n digits after decimal point |
| `#round default` | Restore rounding to default settings |

### Settings/Overrides

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#settings {"decimals": 4, "substitute": false}` | Override engine settings for subsequent lines via JSON. Use the Properties panel to see the available settings and edit them. |

### Breakpoints

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#pause` | Pause calculation and wait for user to resume. Not supported in Calcpad.Web. |
| `#input` | Render input form and wait for user input. Not supported in Calcpad.Web. |

### Settings/Angle Units

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#deg` | Set angle units to degrees |
| `#rad` | Set angle units to radians |
| `#gra` | Set angle units to gradians |

## Worksheet settings

Written as an assignment on a line of their own. In a sheet, use a `>>` line.

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `PlotHeight = 400` | Height of plot area in pixels |
| `PlotWidth = 800` | Width of plot area in pixels |
| `PlotSVG = 1` | Draw plots in SVG (1) or PNG (0) format |
| `PlotAdaptive = 1` | Use adaptive mesh (1) or uniform (0) |
| `PlotStep = 0` | Mesh size for map plotting |
| `PlotPalette = 0` | Color palette number (0-9) for surface plots |
| `PlotShadows = 1` | Draw surface plots with shadows |
| `PlotSmooth = 1` | Smooth gradient (1) or isobands (0) for surface plots |
| `PlotLightDir = 0` | Direction to light source (0-7) clockwise |
| `Precision = 1e-12` | Relative precision for numerical methods (10^-2 to 10^-16) |
| `Tol = 1e-8` | Target tolerance for iterative PCG solver |

## Number format strings

Used after `#format`, or at the end of an equation to format one result.

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `:e` | Exponential notation, default precision |
| `:e3` | Exponential notation with 3 mantissa digits |
| `:f` | Fixed-point notation, default precision |
| `:f3` | Fixed-point notation with 3 decimal digits |
| `:g` | General notation, default precision |
| `:g3` | General notation with 3 significant digits |
| `:n` | Number with digit grouping, default precision |
| `:n3` | Number with digit grouping and 3 decimal digits |
| `:c` | Currency notation, default precision |
| `:c3` | Currency notation with 3 decimal digits |
| `:0.000` | Custom format - fixed decimal places, zero-padded |
| `:#,#.00` | Custom format - digit grouping with optional leading digits |
| `:0.00e+00` | Custom format - explicit exponential notation |

## Units

The predefined units by group. Prefixes (k, M, G, m, μ and so on) are listed where they apply. The names, not the descriptions, are what you type.

* **Dimensionless**: `%`, `‰`, `‱`, `pcm`, `ppm`, `ppb`, `ppt`, `ppq`
* **Angles**: `°`, `′`, `″`, `deg`, `rad`, `grad`, `rev`
* **Metric/Mass**: `g`, `dag`, `hg`, `kg`, `t`, `kt`, `Mt`, `Gt`, `dg`, `cg`, `mg`, `μg`, `ng`, `pg`, `Da`, `u`
* **Metric/Length**: `m`, `km`, `dm`, `cm`, `mm`, `μm`, `nm`, `pm`, `AU`, `ly`
* **Metric/Area**: `a`, `daa`, `ha`
* **Metric/Volume**: `L`, `daL`, `hL`, `dL`, `cL`, `mL`, `μL`, `nL`, `pL`
* **Time**: `s`, `ms`, `μs`, `ns`, `ps`, `min`, `h`, `d`, `w`, `y`
* **Frequency**: `Hz`, `kHz`, `MHz`, `GHz`, `THz`, `mHz`, `μHz`, `nHz`, `pHz`, `rpm`
* **Speed**: `kmh`
* **Temperature**: `°C`, `Δ°C`, `K`
* **Metric/Force**: `N`, `daN`, `hN`, `kN`, `MN`, `GN`, `TN`, `gf`, `kgf`, `tf`, `dyn`
* **Metric/Moment**: `Nm`, `kNm`
* **Metric/Pressure**: `Pa`, `daPa`, `hPa`, `kPa`, `MPa`, `GPa`, `TPa`, `dPa`, `cPa`, `mPa`, `μPa`, `nPa`, `pPa`, `bar`, `mbar`, `μbar`, `atm`, `at`, `Torr`, `mmHg`
* **Metric/Viscosity**: `P`, `cP`, `St`, `cSt`
* **Metric/Energy**: `J`, `kJ`, `MJ`, `GJ`, `TJ`, `mJ`, `μJ`, `nJ`, `pJ`, `Wh`, `kWh`, `MWh`, `GWh`, `TWh`, `mWh`, `μWh`, `nWh`, `pWh`, `VAh`, `kVAh`, `MVAh`, `GVAh`, `VARh`, `kVARh`, `MVARh`, `GVARh`, `eV`, `keV`, `MeV`, `GeV`, `TeV`, `PeV`, `EeV`, `cal`, `kcal`, `erg`
* **Metric/Power**: `W`, `kW`, `MW`, `GW`, `TW`, `mW`, `μW`, `nW`, `pW`, `VA`, `kVA`, `MVA`, `GVA`, `TVA`, `mVA`, `μVA`, `nVA`, `pVA`, `VAR`, `kVAR`, `MVAR`, `GVAR`, `TVAR`, `mVAR`, `μVAR`, `nVAR`, `pVAR`
* **Electrical/Current**: `A`, `kA`, `MA`, `GA`, `TA`, `mA`, `μA`, `nA`, `pA`
* **Electrical/Charge**: `C`, `kC`, `MC`, `GC`, `TC`, `mC`, `μC`, `nC`, `pC`, `Ah`, `mAh`
* **Electrical/Potential**: `V`, `kV`, `MV`, `GV`, `TV`, `mV`, `μV`, `nV`, `pV`
* **Electrical/Capacitance**: `F`, `kF`, `MF`, `GF`, `TF`, `mF`, `μF`, `nF`, `pF`
* **Electrical/Resistance**: `Ω`, `kΩ`, `MΩ`, `GΩ`, `TΩ`, `mΩ`, `μΩ`, `nΩ`, `pΩ`
* **Electrical/Conductance**: `S`, `kS`, `MS`, `GS`, `TS`, `mS`, `μS`, `nS`, `pS`, `℧`, `k℧`, `M℧`, `G℧`, `T℧`, `m℧`, `μ℧`, `n℧`, `p℧`
* **Electrical/Magnetic Flux**: `Wb`, `kWb`, `MWb`, `GWb`, `TWb`, `mWb`, `μWb`, `nWb`, `pWb`
* **Electrical/Magnetic Flux Density**: `T`, `kT`, `MT`, `GT`, `TT`, `mT`, `μT`, `nT`, `pT`
* **Electrical/Inductance**: `H`, `kH`, `MH`, `GH`, `TH`, `mH`, `μH`, `nH`, `pH`
* **Luminous**: `cd`, `lm`, `lx`
* **Radioactivity**: `Bq`, `kBq`, `MBq`, `GBq`, `TBq`, `mBq`, `μBq`, `nBq`, `pBq`, `Ci`, `Rd`
* **Dose/Absorbed**: `Gy`, `kGy`, `MGy`, `GGy`, `TGy`, `mGy`, `μGy`, `nGy`, `pGy`

Chapter: Plots
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/plots

# Plots

<p><strong>Video:</strong> Plots in the sheet format</p>
<video controls preload="none" poster="videos/03-plots-in-sheets.jpg" style="width:100%;max-width:960px" src="videos/03-plots-in-sheets.mp4"></video>

There are three ways to draw: the `plot` line of the sheet format, the Calcpad `$Plot` and `$Map`
commands, and Python blocks, which are covered in [Python blocks](python.md). All three can sit in
the same sheet.

Charts that are not drawn from a function, such as a pie chart, a Gantt chart, a Sankey diagram or a
bar chart of values you type, are diagrams written as text. See [Diagrams](sheet/diagrams.md) for a
gallery of every kind, and the **Plots and diagrams** group of the samples.

## The `plot` line

```sheet
L: 6
w: 12
M(x): w * x * (L - x) / 2
plot M(x) for x in 0..L
```

The line is `plot expression for variable in from..to`. It becomes `$Plot{ M(x) @ x = 0 : L }`. The
expression can be a function you defined, or any expression of the variable:

```sheet
>> #rad
plot sin(x), cos(x) for x in 0..2*π
```

Several expressions, separated by commas, are drawn together, each in its own colour. An optional
`y =` before the expressions is dropped (`plot y = f(x) for x in 0..10`). A malformed `plot` line
is reported on its line in the report and in the editor.

### A legend

Give a curve a name with `as "name"` after its expression, and the plot gets a legend in its top
right corner: a colour swatch and the name of each curve.

```sheet
>> #rad
plot sin(x) as "sine", cos(x) as "cosine" for x in 0..2*π
```

A curve without a name is listed by its expression, and a plot where no curve has a name has no
legend, as before. A name cannot contain quotes, `&`, `|`, `@` or braces. The legend is part of the
SVG, so it is in the printout and the PDF and in the Word picture; in Excel the names are the
series names of the chart. In Calcpad text the name follows the expression in double quotes,
`$Plot{sin(x) "sine" & cos(x) "cosine" @ x = 0 : 2*π}` (this is not in CalcpadCE).

The plot is an SVG drawing. It is sharp at any zoom, it prints well, and its data is exported to
Excel as a native chart.

### Radians, not degrees

Angles are in degrees by default. `sin(x)` over `0..2*π` is then the sine of the first six
degrees, which is a nearly flat line. Put `>> #rad` in the sheet before the plot, as above, or
plot over degrees (`0..360`).

### Plotting a function with units

The plotted variable must be a plain number. If `L` is `6 m`, then `for x in 0..L` stops with
`Inconsistent units`. Give the variable the unit inside the expression instead:

```sheet
L: 6 m
w: 12 kN/m
M(x): w * x * (L - x) / 2
plot M(x * 1 m) for x in 0..6
```

The axes are labelled with the variable names, and the end points of the curve are marked with
their values.

## Other kinds of plot: `$Plot` and `$Map`

A sheet reaches the rest of the plotting commands through `>>` lines.

```sheet
>> #rad
>> $Plot{cos(t) | sin(t) @ t = 0 : 2*π}
>> $Plot{cos(t) | sin(t) & 2*cos(t) | 2*sin(t) @ t = 0 : 2*π}
>> $Map{x*y @ x = -1 : 1 & y = -1 : 1}
```

| Form | Draws |
| --- | --- |
| `$Plot{y(x) @ x = a : b}` | A function of one variable. |
| `$Plot{y1(x) & y2(x) @ x = a : b}` | Several functions on one plot. |
| `$Plot{y1(x) "name 1" & y2(x) "name 2" @ x = a : b}` | The same, with a legend. |
| `$Plot{x(t) \| y(t) @ t = a : b}` | A parametric curve. |
| `$Plot{x1(t) \| y1(t) & x2(t) \| y2(t) @ t = a : b}` | Several parametric curves. |
| `$Map{f(x; y) @ x = a : b & y = c : d}` | A colour map of a surface. |

`$Plot` must be the first thing on its line. Anything after the closing brace is ignored. Plotting
supports real numbers only.

## Size and style

Set these by assigning them on a line of their own (in a sheet, a `>>` line), before the plot:

```sheet
L: 6
w: 12
M(x): w * x * (L - x) / 2
>> PlotWidth = 600
>> PlotHeight = 300
plot M(x) for x in 0..L
```

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `PlotWidth`, `PlotHeight` | Size of the plot area in pixels. |
| `PlotSVG` | 1 for vector (SVG), 0 for raster. The web version draws SVG only. |
| `PlotAdaptive` | 1 to concentrate sample points where the curve bends (the default). Turn it off for rapidly oscillating functions, which can lose peaks. |
| `PlotStep` | Mesh size for colour maps. |
| `PlotPalette` | Colour palette 0 to 9 for colour maps. |
| `PlotSmooth` | 1 for a smooth gradient, 0 for isobands. |
| `PlotShadows` | 1 to shade colour maps. |
| `PlotLightDir` | Direction of the light, 0 to 7 clockwise from north. |

The same settings are on the Calculation tab of the Settings dialog, which sets the defaults for every
worksheet. The Plots & Diagrams tab of the ribbon has buttons for each form and for these lines.

## The buttons under a plot

In the preview, a plot has a row of small buttons. They are not part of a printout or an export.

| Plot made by | Buttons |
| --- | --- |
| A `plot` line or `$Plot` | Copy data, PNG, SVG |
| Python (matplotlib style) | Log x, Log y, 1:1, Copy data, PNG, SVG |
| Python (3D scene) | Copy data, PNG |

**Copy data** puts the plotted points on the clipboard. For a `plot` line the data is read back
from the drawing, through the axis labels, so it is correct to about four figures. **PNG** and
**SVG** save the picture.

## Plots in exports

* **Word**: plots are pictures. The SVG is rasterised for Word and kept beside the picture.
* **Excel**: a `$Plot` or `plot` becomes a native, editable XY chart with its data on a "Plot data"
  sheet. A colour map becomes a picture.
* **PDF**: the printed page has the plot as drawn.

See [Exporting](exporting.md).

## Python plots

For interactive charts, subplots, 3D surfaces and plots of computed arrays, use a Python block.
See [Python blocks](python.md). For a chart that redraws while you drag a slider, see
[Interactive panels](python-panels.md).

**Related calculators:** [Moment and shear diagrams](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/bending-moment-shear-force-diagram/), [Pump operating point](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/pump-operating-point-calculator/), [Concrete strength gain](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/concrete-strength-gain-calculator/). More pages are in [Calculators and guides](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/).

Chapter: Python blocks
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/python

# Python blocks

<!-- description: Run small Python programs inside a sheet: numpy-style arrays and linear algebra, matplotlib-style and Plotly-style charts and 3D plots, sandboxed. -->

<p><strong>Video:</strong> Plots from Python, Plotly and matplotlib style</p>
<video controls preload="none" poster="videos/04-plots-from-python.jpg" style="width:100%;max-width:960px" src="videos/04-plots-from-python.mp4"></video>

A sheet can hold small Python programs. They run in the page, in a sandbox, on a compact Python
interpreter (MicroPython) with small stand-ins for numpy, matplotlib and Plotly. What a block prints,
draws and exports becomes part of the sheet, and the numbers it exports can be used by the
quantity lines that follow.

Nothing is downloaded for a sheet without Python. The first time a sheet with a Python block is
calculated, the page asks "This worksheet runs Python code" (**Run Python** or **Not now**). The
answer is remembered for that tab. About 0.6 MB is fetched the first time and cached afterwards.

## The block

A Python block is a fenced code block with the language `python`:

````sheet python
# Moment diagram with matplotlib

L: 6 m | span
w: 12 kN/m | design load

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

L_m, w_k = 6.0, 12.0
x = np.linspace(0, L_m, 61)
M = w_k * x * (L_m - x) / 2

print("Maximum moment", round(float(M.max()), 2), "kN.m at", round(float(x[np.argmax(M)]), 2), "m")

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3))
plt.plot(x, M, "b-", label="M(x)")
plt.fill_between(x, M, alpha=0.2)
plt.xlabel("x (m)")
plt.ylabel("M (kN.m)")
plt.title("Simply supported beam")
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.show()

export(M_peak=float(M.max()))
```

Mmax: M_peak * 1 kN*m
Mcheck: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m
````

The result shows the printed line, the figure where `plt.show()` was called, and then the two
quantity lines:

```text
Maximum moment 54.0 kN.m at 3.0 m
[figure: the parabolic moment diagram]
M_peak = 54
Mmax = M_peak · 1 kN·m = 54 · 1 kN·m = 54 kN·m
Mcheck = w·L²/8 = 12 kN/m · (6 m)² / 8 = 54 kN·m
```

The two numbers agree, which is the point of mixing: Python draws and explores, the sheet
carries the units and the check.

| In the block | In the sheet |
| --- | --- |
| `print(...)` | A monospace paragraph. |
| `plt.show()` or `plt.savefig(...)` | An inline SVG figure at that point. |
| `fig.show()` on a Plotly figure | An interactive chart at that point. |
| `export(name=value, ...)` | A definition `name = value`, a vector for a list or 1-D array, a matrix for a list of lists. |
| `export_data(name=value, ...)` | Like `export` but nothing is printed; for large arrays. |
| An exception | One red error line naming the Python line and the exception type. The rest of the sheet still calculates. |

Rules worth knowing:

* All blocks of a sheet run in order in one interpreter, before the engine. A later block sees
  the earlier blocks' variables.
* Variables are exported **explicitly**, so a loop variable never collides with a unit name such
  as `m` or `s`. Exported numbers are unitless; attach the unit in the sheet, as `Mmax` does above.
* Names in `export` are written the way the sheet spells them: `export(sigma_c=2)` is σ_c below the
  block.
* Python cannot read the sheet's quantities. Pass numbers in by writing them in the block.
* Several names in one `export` call arrive in no promised order. Use separate calls where
  order matters.

## Which numpy and matplotlib

The stand-ins are small subsets that mimic those packages. What works:

* numpy: `array`, `linspace`, `arange`, `zeros`, `ones`, `full`, arithmetic and `**`, `@`, `dot`,
  `sum`, `mean`, `max`, `argmax`, `cumsum`, `abs`, `clip`, `maximum`, `where`, `sqrt`, `exp`,
  `sin`, `cos`, `diff`, `trapz`, `eye`, boolean masks, and for plotting `hypot`, `arctan2`,
  `meshgrid` (`indexing="xy"` or `"ij"`), `outer`, `interp`, `polyfit`, `polyval`.
* math: everything in MicroPython's `math`, plus `hypot`, `dist`, `prod`, `fsum`, `isqrt`, `comb`,
  `perm`, `gcd` and `lcm`, which the page adds.
* numpy.linalg and scipy.linalg: `solve`, `inv`, `det`, `cholesky`, `eigh`, `svd`, `matrix_rank`,
  `cond`, `pinv`, `norm`. The numbers come from the same engine as the sheet's `lsolve`, `inverse`
  and `det`.
* matplotlib: `plot`, `scatter`, `bar`, `fill_between`, `axhline`, `axvline`, `text`, `xlabel`,
  `ylabel`, `title`, `legend`, `grid`, `xlim`, `ylim`, `figure(figsize)`, `subplots`, `tight_layout`,
  `suptitle`, `axis("equal")`, log axes, `show`, `savefig`.

Missing functions raise a named error rather than a wrong answer. Not available: `vstack`, `hstack`,
`reshape`, `sort`, `random`, `poly1d`, `roots` in numpy; `hist`, `pie`, `errorbar`,
`step`, `annotate`, `imshow`, `contour`, `twinx` in matplotlib; non-symmetric `eig` and `lstsq` in
linalg.

```text
NotImplementedError: numpy.linalg.lstsq is not available in the light Python stand-in
```

A singular matrix raises `LinAlgError: Matrix is singular.` on the Python line that made the call.
A list written out in the source can hold up to 16,000 numbers; a longer one is refused with
an error that says what to do instead. For thousands of values, build the list in a loop or
parse a text string (`[float(v) for v in "1.5 2.5 3.5".split()]`), which is also much faster.

````sheet python
# Linear algebra in a block

```python
import numpy as np

K = np.array([[4.0, -2.0], [-2.0, 3.0]])
u = np.linalg.solve(K, np.array([10.0, 0.0]))
print("u =", [round(float(v), 4) for v in u])
export(u1=float(u[0]), u2=float(u[1]))
```

total: u1 + u2
````

```text
u = [3.75, 2.5]
u1 = 3.75
u2 = 2.5
total = u1 + u2 = 3.75 + 2.5 = 6.25
```

## Plotly-style charts

`import plotly.graph_objects as go` gives a small copy of the Plotly interface. A figure shown with
`fig.show()` becomes an interactive chart in the page: hover to read values, drag to zoom, use the
toolbar to save a picture.

````sheet python
# Shear and moment with Plotly

```python
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

L_m, w_k = 6.0, 12.0
x = np.linspace(0, L_m, 61)
V = w_k * (L_m / 2 - x)
M = w_k * x * (L_m - x) / 2

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True, subplot_titles=["Shear V (kN)", "Moment M (kN.m)"])
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=V, name="V", line_color="#1f77b4"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=M, name="M", fill="tozeroy"), row=2, col=1)
fig.add_vline(x=L_m / 2, line_dash="dot")
fig.update_layout(title="Simply supported beam", height=480, xaxis2_title="x (m)")
fig.show()
```
````

This is a pass-through, not a second copy of Plotly. Every keyword argument is written into the
figure as given, and Plotly.js in the page checks it. Supported pieces:

| Supported | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `go.Figure(data=, layout=, frames=)` | `data` takes traces or dicts. |
| Traces `Scatter`, `Scattergl`, `Bar`, `Histogram`, `Box`, `Violin`, `Pie`, `Heatmap`, `Contour`, `Surface`, `Scatter3d`, `Mesh3d`, `Scatterpolar`, `Waterfall`, `Indicator`, `Table`, `Candlestick` | The class only sets the type. All other keywords are the trace's own. |
| `fig.add_trace`, `add_traces`, `add_scatter`, `add_bar` | `row` and `col` on a figure from `make_subplots`. |
| `fig.update_layout`, `update_xaxes`, `update_yaxes`, `update_traces` | Recursive merge. |
| `add_shape`, `add_annotation`, `add_vline`, `add_hline`, `add_vrect`, `add_hrect` | With `row` and `col`, the lines use that subplot's axes. |
| `make_subplots(rows, cols, shared_xaxes, shared_yaxes, subplot_titles, row_heights, column_widths, vertical_spacing, horizontal_spacing)` | |
| `updatemenus` and `sliders` with precomputed steps | Dropdowns, buttons, sliders; `frames` for animation. |

"Magic underscores" work when they are keyword arguments of a call: `line_color="red"` is
`line=dict(color="red")` and `xaxis_title="x"` is `xaxis=dict(title="x")`. Inside a dict they are
not expanded, and the shim refuses them by name rather than letting Plotly drop them silently.

Things that fail with a named error: trace types not in the table, `write_html`, `write_image`,
`fig.data`, `fig.show(renderer=...)`, `make_subplots(specs=...)`, `plotly.express`, `plotly.io`,
named templates (`template="plotly_white"`; the page applies a light or dark theme itself).

```text
NotImplementedError: go.Figure.write_html is not available in the light plotly shim
```

**Controls are Plotly's own, and they are independent.** A dropdown or slider step is a fixed
update that Plotly applies; it cannot read another control or run Python. For controls that
combine, precompute one step per combination or give each control its own traces. The "Beam
explorer" sample shows both.

### Sliders that run the Python again

For a control that runs Python again on every move, use an [interactive panel](python-panels.md):
a function decorated with `@ui.panel(ui.slider("L", 6, 2, 12, unit="m"))` that returns a Plotly
figure is called again each time the slider moves, and only its chart is redrawn.

### Plotly offline, printing and exports

Plotly.js is not bundled. It is fetched once from its CDN when the first chart is shown, and
cached. Without a connection the chart's place shows a note: "Interactive charts need a connection
to load Plotly...". The Python solve and the rest of the sheet still run. The charts follow the
page's light or dark theme.

Print, PDF, Word and Excel cannot run Plotly.js, so the chart is not carried: a paragraph
stands in its place ("Interactive chart: TITLE. It is drawn in the browser and is not carried by
print or export."). If the printout needs the picture, draw a static copy with matplotlib as well.

## 3D plots

A Plotly `Surface`, `Scatter3d`, `Mesh3d` or a 3D line figure is a 3D scene you can rotate and
zoom. The contour lines can be projected onto the floor.

````sheet python
# A 3D surface

```python
import plotly.graph_objects as go

xs = [i * 0.25 for i in range(25)]
ys = [j * 0.25 for j in range(17)]
z = [[((x - 3) ** 2 + (y - 2) ** 2) ** 0.5 for x in xs] for y in ys]

fig = go.Figure(go.Surface(x=xs, y=ys, z=z, colorscale="Viridis"))
fig.update_layout(height=420, scene=dict(zaxis=dict(title=dict(text="distance"))))
fig.show()
```
````

The samples under **3D plots** show a plate deflection surface, a column interaction surface, a
space frame drawn in 3D lines, a mode-shape explorer with a dropdown, and a 3D bar chart of
footing reactions. The walls of the 3D axes follow the light or dark theme. The buttons under a 3D scene are
Copy data and PNG.

## Plot gallery

The **Plot gallery** sample (group "Plots and diagrams") is a gallery of four plots on a grid in the style of a
plotting demo: implicit curves (f(x, y) = 0 drawn as a contour at level zero), functions,
parametric curves, noise, and polylines with markers, a legend and a second y axis. It is drawn
in a Python block with the Plotly API, so it can be zoomed and read by hovering.

## Limits

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Time per block | 10 seconds. The worker is stopped and restarted. |
| Time per calculation | 30 seconds. |
| Print output | 100,000 characters |
| Figures | 20 per sheet, 3 MB of SVG |
| Chart size | 4 MB of figure data, 20 figures and drawings together |
| Exported names | 500 |
| Interpreter memory | 32 MB |

**The longer time limit.** When a block runs out of its ten seconds, the page asks whether to run the
sheet again with a longer limit: 60 seconds per block and 180 seconds per calculation. This is for
a slow device such as a phone, which can need several times what a laptop needs. The answer is
kept for the tab.

## The sandbox

A block runs in a Web Worker: no page access, no cookies, no stored data. The worker's network
functions are removed after loading, so a script cannot send data anywhere, and the interpreter's
host-access modules are refused. A runaway loop or allocation is stopped by the time and memory
limits.

This is a practical guard and not a security boundary against a determined attacker. Calculating a
sheet executes its blocks, which is why the page asks before the first run. The **Samples** browser
never runs a sample's Python; its preview shows the source, and opening the sample asks.

## Errors

A Python exception shows as one red line naming the sheet line and the exception type, and
appears in the error list on that line. The rest of the sheet still calculates, so a failed block
leaves the names it never exported undefined, and the lines that use them report their own errors.

```text
Python error on line 5: ZeroDivisionError ...
```

Typical causes: a name that is not in the stand-in (a `NotImplementedError` naming it), a Plotly
keyword written in a dict with an underscore, an exported value that is `nan` or `inf`, or a block
that ran past its time limit.

## Calcpad `#python` blocks

In the Calcpad language the block is `#python` ... `#end python` on lines of their own, and a
sheet accepts that pair too.

---

Chapter: Interactive panels
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/python-panels

# Interactive panels

<!-- description: Sliders, drop-downs and checkboxes in a Python block that redraw a Plotly chart, a table or text in place as you move them, without recalculating the sheet. -->

An interactive panel is a set of controls drawn above a chart, a table or a line of text, all made
by one Python block. Move a slider and one Python function runs again with the new value, and its
chart or table is redrawn in place. The rest of the sheet is not recalculated, so a panel stays
quick even when the sheet is long.

The samples in the **Panels** group show three of them: a beam deflection explorer, a pump
operating point with a play button, and a column buckling player.

## Prompt-friendly summary

A complete sheet with a slider that redraws a chart:

````sheet python
# Moment explorer

```python
import ui
import plotly.graph_objects as go
L = ui.slider("L", 6, 2, 12, step=0.5, unit="m", label="Span")
@ui.panel(L)
def moment(L):
    x = [L * i / 40 for i in range(41)]
    return go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=x, y=[12 * v * (L - v) / 2 for v in x]))
```
````

The five rules:

1. Write it in a ` ```python ` fence of a sheet, `import ui`, make the widgets with `ui.slider`,
   `ui.select`, `ui.checkbox` or `ui.player`, and decorate one function with `@ui.panel(widget, ...)`.
   The function takes one argument per widget, in the same order, and receives plain values.
2. Return a Plotly figure (do not call `fig.show()`), a string, `ui.table(rows, header=[...])`, or a
   list of these. Return the chart from the very first call too: Plotly is loaded only when the
   first result holds a chart.
3. The panel cannot read the sheet's quantities, and the sheet cannot read the panel's values. Put
   every number the panel needs in the block itself.
4. The Python is a small stand-in for numpy: `reshape`, `vstack`, `hstack` and `sort` are not there
   (`meshgrid` and `math.hypot` are). Build large lists with a loop or a comprehension: a list
   literal of more than 16,000 numbers in the code is refused.
5. Do the heavy work once in the block body and keep the panel function light: it runs on every
   move of a control.

## A panel, a sheet slider or an input form

There are three ways to put a slider in front of a reader. Choose by what has to change.

| You want | Use | What a move does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A chart, table or text redrawn live while dragging | An interactive panel | Runs one Python function again. Nothing else is recalculated. |
| A sheet input with a slider, `L: ? 6 m [2 .. 12 step 0.5]` | [Templates with inputs](templates.md) | Recalculates the whole sheet with the new value, a moment after you stop. |
| A fill-in form of several inputs | Input mode, see [Templates with inputs](templates.md) | Recalculates the whole sheet; every quantity line follows. |

A sheet slider changes a quantity that the lines below use, with its unit, and the report shows the
working. A panel is for exploring: the chart follows your finger, but its numbers stay inside the
panel.

## The first run

A panel is part of a Python block, so the first calculation of the sheet in a tab asks "This
worksheet runs Python code" with **Run Python** and **Not now**. The block runs in a sandbox in the
page, see [Python blocks](python.md#the-sandbox). The first run takes several seconds while Python
starts and, for a chart, while Plotly loads from its CDN; after that a move of a control usually
redraws in a fraction of a second.

## A chart: the beam moment

````sheet python
# Beam moment explorer

```python
import ui
import plotly.graph_objects as go

L = ui.slider("L", 6, 2, 12, step=0.5, unit="m", label="Span")
w = ui.slider("w", 12, 1, 40, unit="kN/m", label="Load")

@ui.panel(L, w)
def moment(L, w):
    x = [L * i / 60 for i in range(61)]
    M = [w * v * (L - v) / 2 for v in x]
    fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=x, y=M, mode="lines", fill="tozeroy", name="M"))
    fig.update_layout(height=320, xaxis_title="x (m)", yaxis_title="M (kN.m)")
    return [fig, "Maximum moment %.1f kN.m at midspan" % (w * L * L / 8)]
```
````

The page shows two sliders, Span and Load, each with its value and unit beside it, then the chart
and the line of text. At the start it reads `Maximum moment 54.0 kN.m at midspan`. Drag Span to
10 m and the curve and the text follow: `Maximum moment 150.0 kN.m at midspan`.

What happens, in order:

1. The block runs once, top to bottom, like any Python block.
2. At `@ui.panel(L, w)` the function `moment` is called with the starting values, 6 and 12, and its
   result is drawn under the controls.
3. Each move of a control calls `moment` again with the new values, in the same Python session, and
   only the panel is redrawn. The function's name, `moment`, is the panel's name.

## A 3D surface

A 3D trace works the same way. Here one slider sets the amplitude of a surface:

````sheet python
# Surface explorer

```python
import ui
import math
import plotly.graph_objects as go

a = ui.slider("a", 1.0, 0.2, 3.0, step=0.1, label="Amplitude")
xs = [-3 + 0.2 * i for i in range(31)]

@ui.panel(a)
def surface(a):
    Z = [[a * math.sin(x) * math.cos(y) for x in xs] for y in xs]
    fig = go.Figure(go.Surface(x=xs, y=xs, z=Z))
    fig.update_layout(height=420, scene=dict(zaxis=dict(range=[-3, 3])))
    return fig
```
````

The grid `xs` is made once, in the block body. The fixed `zaxis` range keeps the box the same size
while the surface grows and shrinks; without it, Plotly rescales the axis on every move. A rotated
view is kept when the surface is redrawn.

## A table, a drop-down and a checkbox

A panel does not need a chart. This one returns only a table:

````sheet python
# Timber joist spans

```python
import ui

d = ui.select("d", [("200 mm", 0.2), ("300 mm", 0.3), ("400 mm", 0.4)], default="300 mm", label="Depth")
b = ui.slider("b", 90, 45, 200, step=5, unit="mm", label="Width")
sw = ui.checkbox("sw", True, label="Include own weight")

@ui.panel(d, b, sw)
def spans(d, b, sw):
    Z = b / 1000 * d * d / 6
    g = 5.0 * b / 1000 * d if sw else 0.0
    rows = []
    for L in [3, 4, 5, 6]:
        M = (2.0 + g) * L * L / 8
        rows.append([L, "%.2f" % M, "%.1f" % (M / Z / 1000)])
    return ui.table(rows, header=["Span (m)", "M (kN.m)", "Stress (MPa)"])
```
````

The drop-down shows the labels (`200 mm`, ...) and the function receives the value paired with the
chosen label (`0.3`). The checkbox gives `True` or `False`. A table without a chart never loads
Plotly, so it also works offline once the page has been visited.

## A player

`ui.player` is a frame number with a **Play** and **Pause** button. Each frame is one call of the
function, and the next frame is asked for only after the last one is drawn, so a slow function plays
slower rather than piling up.

````sheet python
# Travelling wave

```python
import ui
import math
import plotly.graph_objects as go

t = ui.player("t", 0, 39, fps=8, label="Frame")
xs = [i * 0.1 for i in range(101)]

@ui.panel(t)
def wave(t):
    y = [math.sin(x - t * 0.3) for x in xs]
    fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=xs, y=y, mode="lines"))
    fig.update_layout(height=260, yaxis_range=[-1.2, 1.2])
    return fig
```
````

A player never starts by itself, and it pauses when the browser tab is hidden. With `loop=False` it
stops at the last frame.

## The `ui` reference

| Call | Draws | The function receives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ui.slider(name, default, min, max, step=None, unit="", label=None)` | A slider with its value and unit beside it | A number between `min` and `max`, on a step. An `int` when `default`, `min`, `max` and `step` are all whole numbers, otherwise a `float`. |
| `ui.select(name, options, default=None, label=None)` | A drop-down | The value of the chosen option |
| `ui.checkbox(name, default=False, label=None)` | A checkbox | `True` or `False` |
| `ui.player(name, start, stop, fps=5, loop=True, label=None)` | A slider with Play and Pause | A whole frame number from `start` to `stop` |
| `@ui.panel(widget, ...)` | The controls, then the function's result | (a decorator) |
| `ui.table(rows, header=None)` | A table | (a return value) |
| `ui.text(s)` | A line of plain text | (a return value) |

Details that matter:

* **name** is the first argument of every widget. It must be unique within a panel. **label** is
  what the reader sees; it defaults to the name.
* **step**: without one, a slider of whole numbers moves by 1, and any other slider takes a round
  step that gives 100 to 200 steps across its range. A value is always kept between `min` and `max`
  and snapped to a step.
* **unit** is only shown beside the value. The function receives a plain number, so write the
  conversions yourself (`w * 1000` for kN/m to N/m).
* **options** of `ui.select` is a list of labels (`["Steel", "Timber"]`, the value is the label
  itself) or of `(label, value)` pairs. A `dict` works, but its order is not promised. `default` is
  a label or a value; without it the first option is chosen. A select needs two options or more.
* **fps** of a player is at most 30. A frame waits for the last one, so the real rate can be lower.
* **Return values**: a Plotly figure from `plotly.graph_objects`, a `str` or `ui.text(...)` (always
  shown as text, never as HTML), a number, `ui.table(...)`, or a list of these in the order they are
  drawn. `None` draws nothing. Anything else is a `TypeError` that names the type.
* Numbers in a `ui.table` are written with six significant digits. Format them yourself
  (`"%.2f" % M`) to fix the decimals.

## Several outputs, several panels

To drive two charts with the same slider, return both from one function: `return [fig1, fig2]`.

A block can hold several panels, each with its own `@ui.panel` and its own controls. A widget given
to two panels is drawn in each of them, and the two copies do not move together. Moving one control
reruns only its own panel's function.

## Errors

* An error during the first call is a normal Python error: one red line naming the sheet line.
* An error after a move (a division by zero at one end of a slider, say) is shown in the panel,
  with its type. The panel recovers at the next value that works.
* A function that runs for more than 10 seconds is stopped. The panel says so, and it stays out of
  date until the sheet is calculated again (edit any line, or press calculate).
* `print()` inside the panel function shows only on the first call. Return a string to show text
  that follows the controls.

## Printing and exports

Print, PDF, Word and Excel cannot run Python. They show the panel at the values the controls were
left at, without the controls, and a note under it, for example: "Interactive panel moment: Span =
10 m, Load = 12 kN/m. It is drawn in the browser; print and export show it at these values." Text
and tables are carried as they are. A chart is carried as a note naming it, as for any
[Plotly chart](python.md#plotly-offline-printing-and-exports).

The values the controls were left at are kept while the tab is open, so a recalculation (an edit
elsewhere in the sheet) starts the panel where you left it. They are not saved in the file: opening
the file again starts from the defaults.

## Limits

**A panel cannot read the sheet, and the sheet cannot read the panel.** Python runs before the
sheet's quantity lines and cannot see them, and a slider's value never reaches a quantity line.
A panel therefore holds its own data and inputs: write the section properties, loads and lengths
in the block. An `export()` from the block body works as in any block, but it is done once, before
any control moves; do not call `export()` in a panel function. When a value has to drive the
sheet's calculation, use a sheet input instead (`L: ? 6 m [2 .. 12 step 0.5]`).

**The numpy stand-in is small.** The block runs on MicroPython with a light stand-in for numpy,
not on full Python. The list of what works is in [Which numpy and
matplotlib](python.md#which-numpy-and-matplotlib). Things that surprise people:

* `numpy.reshape`, `vstack`, `hstack` and `sort` raise `NotImplementedError`. `numpy.meshgrid`,
  `hypot`, `arctan2`, `outer`, `interp`, `polyfit` and `polyval` work, as does `math.hypot`.
* A list literal of more than 16,000 numbers written out in the code is refused before it runs,
  with a hint to build the list in a loop or parse a text string. Shorter ones, even several
  thousand numbers, work.
* `np.linspace` and array arithmetic work, but plain lists and comprehensions are just as quick for
  the sizes a chart needs.

**It runs only in the browser.** The [MCP server](mcp.md) does not run Python blocks, so it cannot
evaluate a sheet with a panel. Word and Excel get the snapshot described above.

**Plotly comes from its CDN.** A chart needs a connection the first time (the controls, tables and
text work without one). Plotly is loaded only when the first result of a panel holds a chart, so a
panel that returns a chart only after some move shows a note instead of the chart. Return a chart
on the first call too.

**The usual Python limits apply**: 10 seconds per call, and an answer of at most 2 MB (a figure and
its data) per move. See [Python blocks](python.md#limits).

## Keeping it fast

The function runs on every move of a control, so keep in it only what depends on the controls. Work
that does not, such as a grid, a stiffness matrix or a solved model, belongs in the block body, which
runs once. The function can read the variables the block made before it.

````sheet python
# Precomputed surface

```python
import ui
import math
import plotly.graph_objects as go

xs = [-3 + 0.1 * i for i in range(61)]
base = [[math.sin(x) * math.cos(y) for x in xs] for y in xs]

k = ui.slider("k", 1.0, 0.1, 2.0, step=0.1, label="Scale")

@ui.panel(k)
def scaled(k):
    Z = [[k * v for v in row] for row in base]
    fig = go.Figure(go.Surface(x=xs, y=xs, z=Z))
    fig.update_layout(height=420, scene=dict(zaxis=dict(range=[-2, 2])))
    return fig
```
````

The sines and cosines of the 61 by 61 grid are worked out once; each move only multiplies.

* Keep charts to a few thousand points. The whole figure is sent on every move.
* Do not change globals in the function. A function that depends only on its arguments and on what
  the block computed before it gives the same picture for the same control values, whatever order
  the reader moved them in.
* Fix axis ranges (`yaxis_range`, `scene=dict(zaxis=dict(range=...))`) so the chart does not jump
  while dragging.

---

Chapter: Templates with inputs
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/templates

# Templates with inputs

<!-- description: Turn a calculation into a fill-in template: a question mark makes an input box, a drop-down, radio buttons or a checkbox, grouped as a form. -->

<p><strong>Video:</strong> Templates with inputs</p>
<video controls preload="none" poster="videos/05-templates-with-inputs.jpg" style="width:100%;max-width:960px" src="videos/05-templates-with-inputs.mp4"></video>

A template is a calculation that you fill in rather than edit. A few lines of the sheet are
**inputs**: a number with its unit, a choice from a list, a group of radio buttons, a checkbox.
Choose **Input** in the results bar and those lines become boxes, lists, buttons and ticks. Change
one and the whole sheet recalculates. The same file is still an ordinary sheet: in Preview and in
the report an input line reads like any other line.

A template is one `.sheet` file. There is nothing to install and nothing to configure: the inputs
are lines of text in the sheet.

## An input is a line with a question mark

A quantity line gives a name a value: `L: 6 m | span`. Put a `?` in front of the value and the
same line becomes an input, with that value as its default:

<!-- expect: L = 6 m | span | M = w · L ^2 8 = 12 kN ∕ m · ( 6 m ) ^2 8 = 54 kN · m -->
```sheet
# Beam moment

L: ? 6 m | span
w: ? 12 kN/m | design load
M: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum moment
```

Everything else about the line is as for a quantity: the name is a plain name (Greek spellings
work as usual), the unit is written after the number, and the text after `|` is a note. Later
lines use `L` and `w` like any other quantity. In Preview the sheet reads `L = 6 m    span`, with
the defaults. In Input mode `6` is a yellow box with `m` beside it and `span` after it. Change the
box to `8`, press Enter, and the moment follows.

The default is a number with an optional unit (`6 m`, `12 kN/m`, `0.9`, `1230000 mm³`). It is not
an expression: `2*3 m` is an error on its line, and the message says what to write. Units may be
written with the superscript signs (`mm³`) as everywhere else in a sheet. The name can be written
either way too: `phi: ? 0.9` is the input `φ`.

`name = ? 6 m` works as well as `name: ? 6 m`.

## The kinds of input

| You write | You get | The name is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `L: ? 6 m \| span` | A box with the unit after it | The number typed, with the unit |
| `E: ? [Steel = 200 GPa, *Timber = 11 GPa] \| material` | A drop-down list | The value of the chosen option |
| `k: ? (Low = 1, High = 2) \| load class` | Radio buttons | The value of the chosen option |
| `ribs: ? on \| stiffeners fitted` | A checkbox | `1` when ticked, `0` when not |
| `L: ? 6 m [2 .. 12 step 0.5] \| span` | A slider with the box beside it | The number, kept between the bounds |

### Sliders

Put bounds after the default and the box gets a slider:

```sheet
# Beam moment

L: ? 6 m [2 .. 12 step 0.5] | span
w: ? 12 kN/m [2 .. 40 step 1] | design load
M: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum moment
```

`[2 .. 12 step 0.5]` is the smallest value, the largest value and, if you give one, the step the slider moves
in. The numbers are in the unit of the default (metres for `6 m`). The default must lie between the bounds.
In Input mode the slider sits next to the box: drag it, use the arrow keys, or type a number, and the sheet
recalculates a moment after you stop moving. A number typed outside the bounds is not used; the box turns red
and says `must be from 2 to 12`. Without `step` the slider takes about a hundred steps across its range; a typed
number does not have to land on a step. Preview, Report, PDF and the Word and Excel exports show the number, as
they do for a plain input, so a sheet with sliders reads the same when it is printed. Two of the sample
templates, the beam check and the cantilever, use sliders for their span, length and loads.

### Docked inputs

A slider is most use when you can see what it moves. In Input mode the **Dock inputs** button (a pin) in the
results bar gathers every input of the sheet into one panel that stays put while the results scroll: at the left
of the results when the pane is wide, in a strip above them when it is narrow or on a phone. Scroll the results to
the plot, drag a slider in the panel, and the plot is drawn again as you drag. The panel holds the same values as
the input lines (they are hidden while it is docked), with the same checks: a number typed outside the bounds is
refused, with the message beside the box. The arrow in the panel's header folds it to one line of values.

The panel is docked when a sheet has a slider, and not otherwise; your choice is kept until the browser tab is
