closed. A sheet without inputs has no panel. Nothing printed or exported shows it.

### Drop-downs and radio buttons

A choice is a list of `label = value` entries between square brackets (a drop-down) or round
brackets (radio buttons). The label is what the reader sees. The value is a number with an
optional unit, and it is what the name becomes when that option is chosen.

* The option marked with `*` is the one selected when the sheet opens. With no `*`, the first
  option is.
* A label that contains a comma, an equals sign or a bracket goes in double quotes:
  `"Beam (A), long" = 1`.
* A choice needs at least two options, and each option needs a value.
* A drop-down, radio buttons and a checkbox show no name. Their note (the text after `|`) becomes
  the label in front of the control. With no note the name is used.

### Checkboxes

`on` or `off` (`true` and `false` also work) sets the starting state, and the name is `1` or `0`.
That makes it a multiplier (`sw * rho * A`) or a test (`if ribs == 1:`).

### A choice that picks several things at once

A choice gives one number. When a material has a modulus, a strength and a density, let the
choice give an index and look the rest up in tables written after it. The template below does this
with `E_tab.mat`, the entry of `E_tab` that `mat` points at:

<!-- expect: E = ⃗ E _tab.2 = 70 GPa | The material is aluminium. -->
```sheet
mat: ? [Structural steel = 1, *Aluminium = 2, Timber = 3] | material
E_tab: [200 GPa, 70 GPa, 11 GPa] | modulus of elasticity
E: E_tab.mat -> GPa
if mat == 2: "The material is aluminium."
```

A new material is then one more option and one more entry in each table. The report shows the
number a choice stands for (`mat = 3`), so a line such as `if mat == 3: "The material is timber."`
tells the reader what it means. Most of the sample templates do this.

## Grouping the inputs as a form

A run of input lines is drawn as one form: a block with a bar down its left edge. Put the inputs
together under a heading, so that the heading titles the form. The run ends at the first line that
is not an input (a line of prose, a calculation). A blank line inside the run does not end it.

```sheet
## Inputs
L:    ? 6 m | span
w:    ? 12 kN/m | applied uniform load
mat:  ? [Structural steel = 1, Aluminium = 2, Timber = 3] | material
sw:   ? on | include the own weight of the beam
```

Preview and the report show the same block without the bar, and **Show compiled** shows plain
Calcpad (the bar is not written). **Format Document** (Shift+Alt+F) lines the colons up.

## Using the form

In the browser a template opens as Preview. Choose **Input** in the results bar (Preview,
Unwrapped, **Input**, Report), or **Input form** on the Input/Output tab. Then:

* Each input line is a control. A box holds the number only; the unit stays beside it, so a number
  cannot be typed in the wrong unit. A box accepts digits, a decimal point and a sign.
* Type a value and press Enter, or leave the box, and the sheet recalculates. Lists, buttons and
  the checkbox act at once.
* The **Insert** panel says "Unavailable in input mode": it acts on the source, which the form does
  not edit. Choose **Preview** to edit again.
* The bar has **Report** and **Print PDF**, which use the values you entered, **Save values** (it
  appears once you have changed a value) and **Exit input mode**.
* Leaving input mode with values you did not save asks "Unsaved input values: save the values
  entered in the input form before exiting?" with Save, Don't Save and Cancel.

| View | Entered values applied | `#pre` shown | `#post` shown |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Preview | No (the defaults), unless **Apply #UI Values in Preview** is on in Settings | Yes | Yes |
| Input | Yes | Yes | No |
| Report | Yes | No | Yes |

The Word and Excel exports and **Print PDF** use the entered values. The Excel file lists the input
variables on its **Inputs** sheet. The form itself has no Word export; the report is the document. See [Exporting](exporting.md).

### Saving the values

The values you type are held in the page, so typing never changes the file. Choose **Save values**
to keep them. It writes one comment line directly under the `<!--sheet-->` line:

```text
<!--sheet-->
'<!--{"uiOverrides":{"L:1":"8"}}-->
```

The file is still a sheet. The next time it is opened and put in Input mode, or opened as a
report, the saved values are applied again. Preview still shows the defaults written in the sheet.
To change a default for good, edit the number in the sheet line.

A saved value belongs to the input's name. Rename an input and the value saved under the old name
is not used any more. Delete the comment line to go back to the defaults.

### What an input cannot do

* **Numbers only.** An input holds a number. There is no text box: a choice of names is a
  drop-down. There is no minimum or maximum either, so check a range in the sheet:
  `if L > 30 m: "Span out of range"`.
* **No expression as a default.** `2*3 m` is an error. Write the number, or compute the value in
  a line after the input.

### Known limits

Workarounds for behaviour that is to be fixed. This is the only list of them on this page.

* **No two options may have the same value.** `(Low = 1 m, High = 1 m)` is an error on its line,
  because the form could not tell which option is chosen. Give each option its own value.
* **A name cannot contain a dot.** A dot is the index operator (`E_tab.mat`), so `a.b: ? 5` is
  not an input.

## Worked template 1: a simply supported beam

Inputs: the span, the load, a section depth (drop-down), a material (drop-down), a deflection
limit (radio buttons) and whether the beam's own weight counts (checkbox). The beam is a doubly
symmetric I-beam described by one depth, so the section is a drop-down of three depths. This is
the sample **Template: simply supported beam check** in the Templates group of the Samples
browser, and the text below is the file as shipped.

The inputs, six lines:

```sheet
## Inputs
L:     ? 6 m | span
w:     ? 12 kN/m | applied uniform load
h:     ? [200 mm deep = 200 mm, *300 mm deep = 300 mm, 400 mm deep = 400 mm] | I-beam section
mat:   ? [Structural steel = 1, Aluminium = 2, Timber = 3] | material
limit: ? (L/250 = 250, L/360 = 360, L/500 = 500) | deflection limit
sw:    ? on | include the own weight of the beam
```

Note that `h` is a drop-down whose values are lengths: the choice sets the section depth directly.
The deflection limit is a number, 250, 360 or 500, and a later line divides the span by it
(`L / limit`).

<details>
<summary>The whole sheet</summary>

<!-- sample: Template simply supported beam.sheet -->
<!-- expect: M _max = w _tot · L ^2 8 = 12.5 kN ∕ m · ( 6 m ) ^2 8 = 56.26 kN · m | σ = M _max Z = 56.26 kN · m 691.76 cm 3 = 81.33 MPa | = 10.17 mm | = 0.493 | = 0.424 | Bending: OK | Deflection: OK -->
```sheet
<!--sheet-->
# Simply supported beam check

A template with inputs. Choose **Input** in the results bar to fill in the form; every change
recalculates the page. The beam is a doubly symmetric I-beam, so one depth $h$ describes it:
flange width $b = h/2$, flange thickness $t_f = h/20$ and web thickness $t_w = h/40$. The check
compares the bending stress $\sigma = M/Z$ with an allowable stress and the mid-span deflection
$\delta = 5 w L^4 / (384 E I)$ with a limit.

## Inputs
L:     ? 6 m [2 .. 12 step 0.5] | span
w:     ? 12 kN/m [2 .. 40 step 1] | applied uniform load
h:     ? [200 mm deep = 200 mm, *300 mm deep = 300 mm, 400 mm deep = 400 mm] | I-beam section
mat:   ? [Structural steel = 1, Aluminium = 2, Timber = 3] | material
limit: ? (L/250 = 250, L/360 = 360, L/500 = 500) | deflection limit
sw:    ? on | include the own weight of the beam

## Material properties
The input above picks one entry of each table, so a new material is one more entry in each.

E_tab:   [200 GPa, 70 GPa, 11 GPa] | modulus of elasticity
fa_tab:  [165 MPa, 100 MPa, 12 MPa] | allowable bending stress
rho_tab: [7850 kg/m^3, 2700 kg/m^3, 500 kg/m^3] | density
E:   E_tab.mat -> GPa
f_a: fa_tab.mat -> MPa
rho: rho_tab.mat -> kg/m^3

if mat == 1: "The material is structural steel."
if mat == 2: "The material is aluminium."
if mat == 3: "The material is timber."

## Section
b:   h / 2 | flange width
t_f: h / 20 | flange thickness
t_w: h / 40 | web thickness
A:   2 * b * t_f + (h - 2 * t_f) * t_w -> cm^2 | area
I:   (b * h^3 - (b - t_w) * (h - 2 * t_f)^3) / 12 -> cm^4 | second moment of area
Z:   2 * I / h -> cm^3 | elastic section modulus

## Load
g_acc: 9.81 m/s^2 | gravitational acceleration
w_sw:  sw * rho * A * g_acc -> kN/m | own weight, when included
w_tot: w + w_sw | total uniform load

## Results
M_max: w_tot * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum bending moment, at mid-span
V_max: w_tot * L / 2 -> kN | maximum shear force, at the supports
sigma: M_max / Z -> MPa | maximum bending stress
delta: 5 * w_tot * L^4 / (384 * E * I) -> mm | mid-span deflection
delta_lim: L / limit -> mm | deflection limit
util_b: sigma / f_a | bending utilisation
util_d: delta / delta_lim | deflection utilisation

if util_b <= 1: "Bending: OK, the stress is within the allowable stress." else: "Bending: the stress exceeds the allowable stress, choose a deeper section or a stronger material."
if util_d <= 1: "Deflection: OK, within the limit." else: "Deflection: over the limit, choose a deeper section or a stiffer material."

## Moment diagram
M(x): w_tot * x * (L - x) / 2 -> kN*m | bending moment along the span

plot M(x * 1 m) / (1 kN*m) for x in 0..L / (1 m)
```

</details>

At the defaults (6 m, 12 kN/m, 300 mm deep, steel, L/250, own weight on):

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Own weight `w_sw` and total load `w_tot` | 0.502 kN/m and 12.5 kN/m |
| Section `A`, `I`, `Z` | 65.25 cm², 10376.4 cm⁴, 691.76 cm³ |
| Moment `M_max`, shear `V_max` | 56.26 kN·m, 37.51 kN |
| Stress `σ` against `f_a` | 81.33 MPa against 165 MPa, utilisation 0.493 |
| Deflection `δ` against `δ_lim` | 10.17 mm against 24 mm, utilisation 0.424 |
| Messages | Bending: OK. Deflection: OK. |

What changing each input does (one change at a time from the defaults, unless the row says
otherwise):

| Change | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Span 8 m | Moment 100.02 kN·m, stress 144.59 MPa (0.876), deflection 32.13 mm against a 32 mm limit. Bending: OK. Deflection: over the limit. |
| Span 8 m and 400 mm deep | Total load 12.89 kN/m, moment 103.15 kN·m, stress 62.9 MPa (0.381), deflection 10.48 mm (0.328). Both OK. |
| Timber | Moment 54.14 kN·m, stress 78.27 MPa against 12 MPa (6.52), deflection 177.89 mm (7.41). Both fail. |
| Limit L/500 and own weight off | Moment 54 kN·m, stress 78.06 MPa (0.473), deflection 9.76 mm against 12 mm (0.813). Both OK. |

The first row shows a deflection utilisation of `1` next to the message "over the limit". The
value is 1.004, and two decimals show it as `1`. The message tests the full number, not the
rounded one. For a closer look, raise the decimals in Settings.

The own-weight checkbox is a multiplier: `w_sw: sw * rho * A * g_acc`. With the box ticked it is
0.502 kN/m, unticked it is 0 and the total load is the applied load alone.

## Worked template 2: a pad footing under a load and a moment

Eight inputs: the column load and moment, the footing's width, length and thickness, the depth of
its base, a soil (a drop-down of allowable bearing pressures) and a checkbox for the weight of
the footing and the soil above it. This is **Template: pad footing bearing pressure**.

<details>
<summary>The whole sheet</summary>

<!-- sample: Template pad footing bearing.sheet -->
<!-- expect: P = N + W _f + W _s = 600 kN + 57.6 kN + 43.2 kN = 700.8 kN | q _max = q _avg · ( 1 + 6 · e L ) = 146 kPa · ( 1 + 6 · 0.0856 m 2.4 m ) = 177.25 kPa | = 0.886 | OK: the largest pressure is within -->
```sheet
<!--sheet-->
# Pad footing: bearing pressure check

A template with inputs. Choose **Input** in the results bar to fill in the form. A rectangular
pad footing $B \times L$ carries a vertical column load $N$ and a moment $M$ about the axis
parallel to $B$. The total vertical load $P$ adds the weight of the footing and of the soil above
it, the eccentricity is $e = M/P$ and, while $e \le L/6$ (no uplift), the largest bearing pressure is
$q_{max} = \frac{P}{B L}\left(1 + \frac{6e}{L}\right)$. Beyond that the pressure acts on part of the
base only, $q_{max} = \frac{2P}{3B(L/2 - e)}$. It is compared with an allowable bearing pressure.

## Inputs
N:    ? 600 kN | vertical column load
M:    ? 60 kN*m | column moment, in the direction of L
B:    ? 2 m | footing width
L:    ? 2.4 m | footing length, in the direction of the moment
t:    ? 0.5 m | footing thickness
D_f:  ? 1 m | depth of the base below the ground
q_a:  ? [Soft clay = 80 kPa, Firm clay = 150 kPa, *Medium dense sand = 200 kPa, Dense gravel = 300 kPa] | soil, allowable bearing pressure
wts:  ? on | include the weight of the footing and of the soil above it

## Constants
gamma_c: 24 kN/m^3 | unit weight of concrete
gamma_s: 18 kN/m^3 | unit weight of the soil above the footing

## Vertical load
W_f: wts * gamma_c * B * L * t -> kN | weight of the footing
W_s: wts * gamma_s * B * L * (D_f - t) -> kN | weight of the soil above the footing
P:   N + W_f + W_s -> kN | total vertical load on the soil

## Bearing pressure
e:   M / P -> m | eccentricity of the load
e_lim: L / 6 | the load stays inside the middle third while e is below this
q_avg: P / (B * L) -> kPa | average pressure

if e <= e_lim:
    q_max: q_avg * (1 + 6 * e / L) -> kPa | largest pressure
    q_min: q_avg * (1 - 6 * e / L) -> kPa | smallest pressure
    The whole base stays in contact with the soil.
else:
    q_max: 2 * P / (3 * B * (L / 2 - e)) -> kPa | largest pressure, partial contact
    q_min: 0 kPa | smallest pressure
    Part of the base lifts off the soil.

util: q_max / q_a | utilisation of the allowable bearing pressure
if util <= 1: "OK: the largest pressure is within the allowable bearing pressure." else: "Fails: the largest pressure exceeds the allowable bearing pressure. Enlarge the footing."
```

</details>

Two things in this sheet are new. The soil drop-down has an option marked `*`:

```text
q_a: ? [Soft clay = 80 kPa, Firm clay = 150 kPa, *Medium dense sand = 200 kPa, Dense gravel = 300 kPa] | soil, allowable bearing pressure
```

so it opens on Medium dense sand, the third option. And the check has two branches. An `if` block
may hold quantity lines and prose, and the branch that applies is the one shown:

```text
if e <= e_lim:
    q_max: q_avg * (1 + 6 * e / L) -> kPa | largest pressure
    ...
    The whole base stays in contact with the soil.
else:
    q_max: 2 * P / (3 * B * (L / 2 - e)) -> kPa | largest pressure, partial contact
    ...
    Part of the base lifts off the soil.
```

At the defaults (600 kN, 60 kN·m, 2 m by 2.4 m, 0.5 m thick, base 1 m down, medium dense sand,
weights on):

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Footing weight `W_f`, soil weight `W_s` | 57.6 kN, 43.2 kN |
| Total vertical load `P` | 700.8 kN |
| Eccentricity `e` against `e_lim` | 0.0856 m against 0.4 m, so the whole base is in contact |
| Average, largest, smallest pressure | 146 kPa, 177.25 kPa, 114.75 kPa |
| Utilisation | 0.886. OK. |

| Change | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Soft clay | Largest pressure unchanged, 177.25 kPa against 80 kPa: utilisation 2.22. Fails. |
| Moment 200 kN·m | `e` 0.285 m, largest 250.17 kPa, smallest 41.83 kPa, utilisation 1.25. Fails. |
| Moment 400 kN·m | `e` 0.571 m is beyond 0.4 m: "Part of the base lifts off the soil." Largest 371.25 kPa, smallest 0 kPa, utilisation 1.86. Fails. |
| Weights off (checkbox) | `P` is 600 kN, `e` 0.1 m, largest 156.25 kPa, utilisation 0.781. OK. |

## Worked template 3: a rectangular column

Seven inputs: the section, the length, the end conditions (a drop-down whose values are the
effective length factors), a material (drop-down), the axial load and a factor of safety. This is
**Template: rectangular column slenderness**. The sheet picks the buckling formula by slenderness:
a short column crushes, an intermediate one uses the parabolic formula, a slender one the Euler
formula.

Here one choice is the number the sheet needs, with no table in between:

```text
k:    ? [Pinned at both ends = 1, Fixed and pinned = 0.7, Fixed at both ends = 0.5, Fixed and free = 2] | end conditions
```

<details>
<summary>The whole sheet</summary>

<!-- sample: Template column slenderness.sheet -->
<!-- expect: = 138.56 | The column is slender: it buckles elastically and the Euler formula applies. | P _allow = P _cr FS = 616.85 kN 2 = 308.43 kN | = 0.324 | OK: the applied load is within the allowed load. -->
```sheet
<!--sheet-->
# Rectangular column: slenderness and buckling

A template with inputs. Choose **Input** in the results bar to fill in the form. A solid
rectangular column of length $L$ with an effective length factor $k$ has a slenderness
$\lambda = k L / r$, where $r = b_{min}/\sqrt{12}$ is the smallest radius of gyration. Above the
transition slenderness $\lambda_c = \pi \sqrt{2E/f_y}$ the column buckles elastically (Euler),
$\sigma_{cr} = \pi^2 E / \lambda^2$. Below it the parabolic (Johnson) formula applies,
$\sigma_{cr} = f_y \left(1 - f_y \lambda^2 / (4 \pi^2 E)\right)$. The load that is allowed is
$\sigma_{cr} A$ divided by a factor of safety.

## Inputs
b:    ? 60 mm | section width
d:    ? 100 mm | section depth
L:    ? 2.4 m | column length
k:    ? [Pinned at both ends = 1, Fixed and pinned = 0.7, Fixed at both ends = 0.5, Fixed and free = 2] | end conditions
mat:  ? [Structural steel = 1, Aluminium = 2, Timber = 3] | material
N:    ? 100 kN | axial load
FS:   ? 2 | factor of safety

## Material properties
E_tab:  [200 GPa, 70 GPa, 11 GPa] | modulus of elasticity
fy_tab: [250 MPa, 160 MPa, 24 MPa] | yield strength, or crushing strength for timber
E:  E_tab.mat -> GPa
f_y: fy_tab.mat -> MPa

if mat == 1: "The material is structural steel."
if mat == 2: "The material is aluminium."
if mat == 3: "The material is timber."

## Section
A:   b * d -> cm^2 | area
b_min: min(b, d) | smaller side
I_min: max(b, d) * b_min^3 / 12 -> cm^4 | smaller second moment of area
r:   b_min / sqrt(12) -> mm | smallest radius of gyration

## Slenderness
L_e:      k * L -> m | effective length
lambda:   L_e / r | slenderness ratio
lambda_c: π * sqrt(2 * E / f_y) | transition slenderness

if lambda <= 50:
    The column is short: crushing is likely to govern rather than buckling.
else if lambda <= lambda_c:
    The column is intermediate: it buckles inelastically and the parabolic formula applies.
else:
    The column is slender: it buckles elastically and the Euler formula applies.

## Buckling resistance
sigma_E: π^2 * E / lambda^2 -> MPa | elastic (Euler) buckling stress
P_E:     π^2 * E * I_min / L_e^2 -> kN | elastic (Euler) buckling load

if lambda <= lambda_c:
    sigma_cr: f_y * (1 - f_y * lambda^2 / (4 * π^2 * E)) -> MPa | critical stress, parabolic formula
else:
    sigma_cr: sigma_E | critical stress, Euler formula

P_cr:    sigma_cr * A -> kN | critical load
P_allow: P_cr / FS -> kN | allowed load
util:    N / P_allow | utilisation

if util <= 1: "OK: the applied load is within the allowed load." else: "Fails: the applied load exceeds the allowed load. Enlarge the section, shorten the column or fix its ends."
```

</details>

At the defaults (60 mm by 100 mm, 2.4 m, pinned at both ends, steel, 100 kN, factor of safety 2):

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Area, smaller second moment, radius of gyration | 60 cm², 180 cm⁴, 17.32 mm |
| Effective length `L_e` | 2.4 m |
| Slenderness `λ` against `λ_c` | 138.56 against 125.66: "The column is slender" |
| Critical stress (Euler) and load | 102.81 MPa, 616.85 kN |
| Allowed load | 308.43 kN |
| Utilisation | 0.324. OK. |

| Change | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Fixed at both ends | `L_e` 1.2 m, `λ` 69.28: "The column is intermediate", parabolic formula, critical stress 212 MPa, allowed load 636.01 kN, utilisation 0.157. |
| Fixed at both ends and 300 kN | Utilisation 0.472. OK. |
| Timber | `λ_c` drops to 95.12, still slender, critical stress 5.65 MPa, allowed load 16.96 kN, utilisation 5.9. Fails. |

## Worked template 4: pipe flow

Eight inputs, with a flow rate in L/s, a pipe diameter and length, a rise in level, a sum of loss
coefficients, a pipe material (a drop-down of roughnesses in mm), a water temperature (radio
buttons that pick table entries) and a checkbox for the fittings. This is **Template: pipe flow,
Darcy-Weisbach**. The flow is laminar or turbulent by its Reynolds number, and the sheet uses the
matching friction factor.

<details>
<summary>The whole sheet</summary>

<!-- sample: Template pipe flow Darcy.sheet -->
<!-- expect: The water is at 5 degrees C. | V = Q A = 25 L ∕ s 176.71 cm 2 = 1.41 m ∕ s | The flow is turbulent. | h _L = h _f + h _m = 3.79 m + 0.255 m = 4.05 m | H = dz + h _L = 5 m + 4.05 m = 9.05 m | OK: the velocity is within the usual limit of 3 m/s. -->
```sheet
<!--sheet-->
# Pipe flow: friction loss and pump head

A template with inputs. Choose **Input** in the results bar to fill in the form. Water flows
through a full circular pipe of diameter $D$ and length $L_p$. The Darcy-Weisbach equation gives the
friction head loss $h_f = f \frac{L_p}{D}\frac{V^2}{2g}$. The friction factor is $f = 64/Re$ in laminar
flow and, in turbulent flow, the explicit Swamee-Jain formula
$f = 0.25 / \left[\log_{10}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{3.7 D} + \frac{5.74}{Re^{0.9}}\right)\right]^2$.
Fittings add $h_m = K V^2 / 2g$.

## Inputs
Q:    ? 25 L/s | flow rate
D:    ? 150 mm | inside diameter of the pipe
L_p:  ? 300 m | pipe length
dz:   ? 5 m | rise in level from the inlet to the outlet
K_m:  ? 2.5 | sum of the loss coefficients of the fittings
eps:  ? [Drawn plastic = 0.0015 mm, *Commercial steel = 0.045 mm, Cast iron = 0.26 mm, Concrete = 1 mm] | pipe material, roughness
temp: ? (5 degrees C = 1, 20 degrees C = 2, 40 degrees C = 3) | water temperature
minor: ? on | include the fittings

## Water properties
rho_tab: [1000 kg/m^3, 998 kg/m^3, 992 kg/m^3] | density at 5, 20 and 40 degrees C
nu_tab:  [0.00000152 m^2/s, 0.00000100 m^2/s, 0.00000066 m^2/s] | kinematic viscosity at 5, 20 and 40 degrees C
rho: rho_tab.temp -> kg/m^3
nu:  nu_tab.temp -> m^2/s
g_acc: 9.81 m/s^2 | gravitational acceleration

if temp == 1: "The water is at 5 degrees C."
if temp == 2: "The water is at 20 degrees C."
if temp == 3: "The water is at 40 degrees C."

## Flow
A:  π * D^2 / 4 -> cm^2 | flow area
V:  Q / A -> m/s | mean velocity
Re: V * D / nu | Reynolds number
rr: eps / D | relative roughness

if Re < 2300:
    The flow is laminar.
    f: 64 / Re | friction factor, laminar
else:
    The flow is turbulent.
    f: 0.25 / (log(rr / 3.7 + 5.74 / Re^0.9))^2 | friction factor, Swamee-Jain

## Head loss
h_f: f * (L_p / D) * V^2 / (2 * g_acc) -> m | friction head loss
h_m: minor * K_m * V^2 / (2 * g_acc) -> m | head loss in the fittings, when included
h_L: h_f + h_m -> m | total head loss
H:   dz + h_L -> m | head the pump must supply
dp:  rho * g_acc * h_L -> kPa | pressure drop from losses
P_h: rho * g_acc * Q * H -> kW | hydraulic power

if V <= 3 m/s: "OK: the velocity is within the usual limit of 3 m/s." else: "High velocity: more than 3 m/s, consider a larger pipe."
```

</details>

Because the first radio option is selected when none is marked, the water starts at 5 degrees C.
At the defaults (25 L/s, 150 mm, 300 m, 5 m rise, `K` 2.5, commercial steel, 5 degrees C,
fittings on):

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Velocity, Reynolds number | 1.41 m/s, 139610: "The flow is turbulent." |
| Friction factor | 0.0186 |
| Friction loss, fittings loss, total | 3.79 m, 0.255 m, 4.05 m |
| Pump head `H` | 9.05 m |
| Pressure drop, hydraulic power | 39.72 kPa, 2.22 kW |
| Message | OK: the velocity is within the usual limit |

| Change | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Water at 20 degrees C (second radio button) | Total loss 3.86 m, `H` 8.86 m, pressure drop 37.8 kPa, power 2.17 kW. |
| Fittings off | Total loss 3.79 m, `H` 8.79 m, power 2.16 kW. |
| Diameter 200 mm | Velocity 0.796 m/s, total loss 1 m, `H` 6 m, power 1.47 kW. |
| Flow 60 L/s | Velocity 3.4 m/s: "High velocity: more than 3 m/s, consider a larger pipe." |
| Flow 0.2 L/s | Reynolds number 1116.88: "The flow is laminar", friction factor 0.0573. |

## Worked template 5: a cantilever with a tip load

The fifth sample, **Template: cantilever with a tip load**, is the beam template's close relative:
length, tip load, a rectangular section, a material and a deflection limit, with the own-weight
checkbox. It ends with a moment diagram.

<details>
<summary>The whole sheet</summary>

<!-- sample: Template cantilever tip load.sheet -->
<!-- expect: M _max = P · L + w · L ^2 2 = 8 kN · 2.5 m + 1.54 kN ∕ m · ( 2.5 m ) ^2 2 = 24.81 kN · m | = 3.69 mm | Bending: OK | Deflection: OK -->
```sheet
<!--sheet-->
# Cantilever with a load at the tip

A template with inputs. Choose **Input** in the results bar to fill in the form. A cantilever of
length $L$ with a solid rectangular section $b \times d$ carries a point load $P$ at the free end
and, if wanted, its own weight $w$. At the fixed end $M = P L + w L^2 / 2$ and
$V = P + w L$, and the tip deflection is $\delta = P L^3 / (3 E I) + w L^4 / (8 E I)$.

## Inputs
L:     ? 2.5 m [0.5 .. 6 step 0.1] | length
P:     ? 8 kN [1 .. 100 step 1] | point load at the free end
b:     ? 100 mm | section width
d:     ? 200 mm | section depth
mat:   ? [Structural steel = 1, Aluminium = 2, Timber = 3] | material
limit: ? (L/90 = 90, L/180 = 180, L/360 = 360) | tip deflection limit
sw:    ? on | include the own weight of the beam

## Material properties
E_tab:   [200 GPa, 70 GPa, 11 GPa] | modulus of elasticity
fa_tab:  [165 MPa, 100 MPa, 12 MPa] | allowable bending stress
rho_tab: [7850 kg/m^3, 2700 kg/m^3, 500 kg/m^3] | density
E:   E_tab.mat -> GPa
f_a: fa_tab.mat -> MPa
rho: rho_tab.mat -> kg/m^3

if mat == 1: "The material is structural steel."
if mat == 2: "The material is aluminium."
if mat == 3: "The material is timber."

## Section
A: b * d -> cm^2 | area
I: b * d^3 / 12 -> cm^4 | second moment of area
Z: b * d^2 / 6 -> cm^3 | elastic section modulus

## Load
g_acc: 9.81 m/s^2 | gravitational acceleration
w:     sw * rho * A * g_acc -> kN/m | own weight, when included

## Results at the fixed end and at the tip
M_max: P * L + w * L^2 / 2 -> kN*m | maximum bending moment, at the fixed end
V_max: P + w * L -> kN | maximum shear force, at the fixed end
sigma: M_max / Z -> MPa | maximum bending stress
delta: P * L^3 / (3 * E * I) + w * L^4 / (8 * E * I) -> mm | tip deflection
theta: P * L^2 / (2 * E * I) + w * L^3 / (6 * E * I) | tip rotation, in radians
delta_lim: L / limit -> mm | tip deflection limit
util_b: sigma / f_a | bending utilisation
util_d: delta / delta_lim | deflection utilisation

if util_b <= 1: "Bending: OK, the stress is within the allowable stress." else: "Bending: the stress exceeds the allowable stress, enlarge the section or change the material."
if util_d <= 1: "Deflection: OK, within the limit." else: "Deflection: over the limit, enlarge the section or change the material."

## Bending moment diagram
M(x): P * (L - x) + w * (L - x)^2 / 2 -> kN*m | bending moment at a distance x from the fixed end

plot M(x * 1 m) / (1 kN*m) for x in 0..L / (1 m)
```

</details>

At the defaults (2.5 m, 8 kN, 100 mm by 200 mm, steel, L/90, own weight on) the moment at the
fixed end is 24.81 kN·m, the shear 11.85 kN, the bending stress 37.22 MPa (0.226) and the tip
deflection 3.69 mm against a 27.78 mm limit (0.133). Both checks pass. Choose timber and the stress
is 30.46 MPa against 12 MPa (2.54) and the tip deflection 57.47 mm (2.07): both fail.

## Worked template 6: a retaining wall

The sixth sample, **Template: retaining wall stability**, checks a cantilever retaining wall (a stem
on a base slab, one metre of wall) for overturning, sliding and bearing pressure under the base.
Its inputs are the geometry, a surcharge on the fill, and the backfill:

```sheet
## Inputs
H_s:   ? 3 m | height of the stem above the base slab
B:     ? 2.4 m | width of the base slab
t_b:   ? 0.4 m | thickness of the base slab
t_s:   ? 0.4 m | thickness of the stem
L_t:   ? 0.6 m | length of the toe, in front of the stem
soil:  ? (Loose sand = 28 °, *Medium sand = 32 °, Dense sand = 36 °) | backfill, friction angle
q_s:   ? 10 kPa | surcharge on the fill, when it is on
sur:   ? off | surcharge on the fill
```

Two things are new here. The radio group `soil` chooses a **friction angle** directly: its values
are angles (`28 °`), and a later line uses the chosen angle as a quantity (`phi: soil`). The
values carry the degree sign, which an input accepts like any other unit. The checkbox `sur` is
used as a multiplier, `q: sur * q_s`: ticked it is 1 and the surcharge counts, unticked it is 0.

<details>
<summary>The whole sheet</summary>

<!-- sample: Template retaining wall stability.sheet -->
<!-- expect: FS _o = M _r M _o = 179.21 kN · m 36.23 kN · m = 4.95 | Overturning: OK. | FS _s = R _h P _h = 49.77 kN 31.97 kN = 1.56 | Sliding: OK. | The resultant is inside the middle third -->
```sheet
<!--sheet-->
# Retaining wall: sliding and overturning

A template with inputs. Choose **Input** in the results bar to fill in the form. A cantilever
retaining wall of concrete (a stem on a base slab) holds back a level fill; the sheet takes a strip of wall one metre long.
The active earth pressure is $K_a = \tan^2(45^\circ - \phi/2)$, acting on the vertical plane through
the heel, so the thrust is $P_a = \tfrac12 K_a \gamma H^2$ at $H/3$ above the underside of the base. A
surcharge $q$ on the fill adds $K_a q H$ at $H/2$ and its weight on the heel. The wall slides on a
base friction of $\tan(2\phi/3)$, and overturns about the toe. The soil in front of the toe is ignored.

## Inputs
H_s:   ? 3 m | height of the stem above the base slab
B:     ? 2.4 m | width of the base slab
t_b:   ? 0.4 m | thickness of the base slab
t_s:   ? 0.4 m | thickness of the stem
L_t:   ? 0.6 m | length of the toe, in front of the stem
soil:  ? (Loose sand = 28 °, *Medium sand = 32 °, Dense sand = 36 °) | backfill, friction angle
q_s:   ? 10 kPa | surcharge on the fill, when it is on
sur:   ? off | surcharge on the fill

## Constants
gamma_c: 24 kN/m^3 | unit weight of concrete
gamma_s: 18 kN/m^3 | unit weight of the fill
b_w:     1 m | length of wall in the strip
FS_min:  1.5 | required factor of safety, for sliding and for overturning

## Geometry
phi: soil | friction angle of the fill
H:   H_s + t_b -> m | height of the thrust plane, above the underside of the base
L_h: B - L_t - t_s -> m | length of the heel, behind the stem
q:   sur * q_s -> kPa | surcharge in use

## Earth pressure
K_a: tan(45 ° - phi / 2)^2 | active pressure coefficient
P_s: K_a * gamma_s * H^2 / 2 * b_w -> kN | thrust of the fill
P_q: K_a * q * H * b_w -> kN | thrust of the surcharge
P_h: P_s + P_q -> kN | total horizontal thrust

## Weights and their lever arms about the toe
W_stem: gamma_c * t_s * H_s * b_w -> kN | stem
x_stem: L_t + t_s / 2 -> m | its lever arm
W_base: gamma_c * B * t_b * b_w -> kN | base slab
x_base: B / 2 -> m | its lever arm
W_fill: gamma_s * L_h * H_s * b_w -> kN | fill on the heel
W_sur:  q * L_h * b_w -> kN | surcharge on the heel
x_heel: B - L_h / 2 -> m | lever arm of the fill and the surcharge
W: W_stem + W_base + W_fill + W_sur -> kN | total vertical load

## Overturning
M_o: P_s * H / 3 + P_q * H / 2 -> kN*m | overturning moment about the toe
M_r: W_stem * x_stem + W_base * x_base + (W_fill + W_sur) * x_heel -> kN*m | resisting moment about the toe
FS_o: M_r / M_o | factor of safety against overturning
if FS_o >= FS_min: "Overturning: OK." else: "Overturning: the factor of safety is too low, widen the base."

## Sliding
mu:   tan(2 * phi / 3) | friction coefficient of the base on the ground
R_h:  mu * W -> kN | sliding resistance
FS_s: R_h / P_h | factor of safety against sliding
if FS_s >= FS_min: "Sliding: OK." else: "Sliding: the factor of safety is too low, widen the base or make it thicker."

## Bearing pressure under the base
x_r: (M_r - M_o) / W -> m | where the resultant crosses the base, from the toe
e:   B / 2 - x_r -> m | eccentricity from the middle of the base
q_max: W / (B * b_w) * (1 + 6 * e / B) -> kPa | pressure at the toe
q_min: W / (B * b_w) * (1 - 6 * e / B) -> kPa | pressure at the heel
if abs(e) <= B / 6: "The resultant is inside the middle third: the whole base is in compression." else: "The resultant is outside the middle third: part of the base lifts off, and the pressures above no longer apply."
```

</details>

At the defaults (medium sand, no surcharge) the horizontal thrust is 31.97 kN and the vertical
load 127.44 kN:

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Active pressure coefficient `K_a` | 0.307 |
| Overturning moment, resisting moment | 36.23 kN·m, 179.21 kN·m |
| Factor of safety against overturning `FS_o` | 4.95: "Overturning: OK." |
| Sliding resistance, friction coefficient `mu` | 49.77 kN, 0.391 |
| Factor of safety against sliding `FS_s` | 1.56: "Sliding: OK." |
| Pressure at the toe, at the heel | 63.46 kPa, 42.74 kPa |
| Message | The resultant is inside the middle third. |

| Change | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Surcharge ticked | `FS_o` 3.76, `FS_s` 1.3: "Sliding: the factor of safety is too low, widen the base or make it thicker." |
| Loose sand | `FS_o` 4.21, `FS_s` 1.15: sliding fails. |
| Dense sand | `FS_o` 5.85, `FS_s` 2.1. Both pass. |
| Base 3 m wide | `FS_o` 7.79, `FS_s` 2.02. Both pass. |

## Worked template 7: a pump and pipeline operating point

The seventh sample, **Template: pump operating point**, finds where a pump works. A pump lifts
water through a pipeline to a higher tank. The pump gives less head as the flow grows, the
pipeline needs more, and the pump runs where the two curves cross. The inputs are a choice of
three pumps (radio buttons), the pipe diameter (a drop-down whose values are lengths), the pipe
length, the static lift, and a checkbox for an aged, rougher pipe:

```sheet
## Inputs
pump: ? (Small = 1, *Medium = 2, Large = 3) | pump
D:    ? [100 mm = 100 mm, *150 mm = 150 mm, 200 mm = 200 mm] | pipe inside diameter
L_p:  ? 400 m | pipe length
H_st: ? 15 m | static lift, from the water surface to the tank
aged: ? off | aged pipe (rougher: the friction factor is 0.030, not 0.018)
```

The pump is an index into two tables (`H0_tab`, `Qmax_tab`), as in the first template. What is new
is the output. The sheet solves the crossing in closed form, tabulates both curves with a vector
of flows and `augment`, and draws them with `plot`, so the form changes the numbers, the table and
the chart together.

<details>
<summary>The whole sheet</summary>

<!-- sample: Template pump operating point.sheet -->
<!-- expect: The pump is the medium one. | Q _op = &emsp;&thinsp; max ( H _net; 0 m ) K + H _0 Q _max^2 = &emsp;&thinsp; max ( 25 m ; 0 m ) 7834.25 s 2 ∕ m 5 + 40 m ( 75 L ∕ s ) ^2 = 40.9 L ∕ s | H _op = H _0 · ( 1 − ( Q _op Q _max ) 2 ) = 40 m · ( 1 − ( 40.9 L ∕ s 75 L ∕ s ) 2 ) = 28.1 m | The velocity is within 3 m/s. -->
```sheet
<!--sheet-->
# Pump and pipeline: operating point

A template with inputs. Choose **Input** in the results bar to fill in the form. A pump lifts water
through a pipeline to a higher tank. The pump delivers the head $H_p = H_0 \left(1 - (Q/Q_{max})^2\right)$
at the flow $Q$ (a shut-off head $H_0$ and a free delivery $Q_{max}$). The pipeline needs the head
$H_s = H_{st} + f \frac{L}{D}\frac{v^2}{2g}$, the static lift plus the friction loss with a constant friction
factor $f$. The pump runs where the two curves cross. The table and the plot follow the form.

## Inputs
pump: ? (Small = 1, *Medium = 2, Large = 3) | pump
D:    ? [100 mm = 100 mm, *150 mm = 150 mm, 200 mm = 200 mm] | pipe inside diameter
L_p:  ? 400 m | pipe length
H_st: ? 15 m | static lift, from the water surface to the tank
aged: ? off | aged pipe (rougher: the friction factor is 0.030, not 0.018)

## Pump curves
The input above picks one entry of each list.

H0_tab:   [30 m, 40 m, 50 m] | shut-off head
Qmax_tab: [60 L/s, 75 L/s, 90 L/s] | free delivery
H_0:   H0_tab.pump -> m
Q_max: Qmax_tab.pump -> L/s
if pump == 1: "The pump is the small one."
if pump == 2: "The pump is the medium one."
if pump == 3: "The pump is the large one."

## Pipeline
g_acc: 9.81 m/s^2 | gravitational acceleration
f: 0.018 + aged * 0.012 | friction factor
A: pi * D^2 / 4 -> m^2 | flow area
K: f * L_p / D / (2 * g_acc * A^2) -> s^2/m^5 | friction head per flow squared

## Operating point
The two curves cross where $H_0 - H_0 Q^2/Q_{max}^2 = H_{st} + K Q^2$, so
$Q^2 = (H_0 - H_{st}) / (K + H_0/Q_{max}^2)$.

H_net: H_0 - H_st -> m | head the pump has above the static lift
if H_net <= 0 m: "The pump cannot lift the water to the tank: choose a larger pump or lower the static lift."
Q_op: sqrt(max(H_net, 0 m) / (K + H_0 / Q_max^2)) -> L/s | flow at the operating point
H_op: H_0 * (1 - (Q_op / Q_max)^2) -> m | head at the operating point
v:    Q_op / A -> m/s | velocity in the pipe
if v > 3 m/s: "The velocity is above 3 m/s: expect noise and wear, use a larger pipe." else: "The velocity is within 3 m/s."

## Table
Q_v:  [0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60] * 1 L/s | flows in the table
H_pv: H_0 * (1 - (Q_v / Q_max)^2) -> m | pump head
H_sv: H_st + K * Q_v^2 -> m | head the pipeline needs
T: augment(Q_v / (1 L/s), H_pv / (1 m), H_sv / (1 m)) | columns: flow in L/s, pump head in m, pipeline head in m

## Curves
H_p(Q): H_0 * (1 - (Q / Q_max)^2) -> m | pump head at the flow Q
H_s(Q): H_st + K * Q^2 -> m | pipeline head at the flow Q

plot H_p(x * 1 L/s) / (1 m) as "pump", H_s(x * 1 L/s) / (1 m) as "pipeline" for x in 0..60

The same crossing, found numerically from the two curves:

if H_net > 0 m:
    Q_num: solve H_p(Q) = H_s(Q) for Q in 0 L/s..Q_max -> L/s | flow where the pump head equals the pipeline head
```

</details>

At the defaults (medium pump, 150 mm, 400 m, 15 m lift, new pipe) the pump runs at 40.9 L/s and
28.1 m of head, with 2.31 m/s in the pipe. The table has seven rows, from 0 to 60 L/s: at 40 L/s
the pump gives 28.62 m and the pipeline needs 27.53 m, and at 50 L/s the pump gives 22.22 m
against 34.59 m, so the crossing lies between them.

| Change | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Small pump | 30.46 L/s at 22.27 m |
| Large pump | 49.99 L/s at 34.58 m, 2.83 m/s |
| Aged pipe | 35.21 L/s at 31.19 m |
| Diameter 100 mm | 19.37 L/s at 37.33 m, 2.47 m/s |
| Static lift 35 m | 18.29 L/s at 37.62 m |
| Small pump and static lift 35 m | "The pump cannot lift the water to the tank: choose a larger pump or lower the static lift." The flow is 0. |

## Share a template

A template is one text file. Save it (Ctrl+S) as a `.sheet` file and send that file, or paste the
text of the sheet. Whoever opens it gets the same form, in any browser, with nothing to install.
Once the app has been visited it runs offline too (see
[Saving, opening and working offline](getting-started/saving.md)). Nothing is sent to a server:
the numbers are worked out on the reader's own computer.

* The values you saved with **Save values** travel with the file, so a template can be sent already
  filled in. Send the file without that comment line to send the defaults.
* Each person who opens it and saves values keeps their own numbers in their own copy.

## Writing your own

1. Write the calculation as an ordinary sheet and check it.
2. Turn the quantities someone will want to change into inputs: put `?` in front of the value.
3. Put them together under a heading (`## Inputs`), so the form reads like a form.
4. Put the results below the inputs, with a note on every line.
5. Where a result depends on a choice, use an index and tables (worked template 1), or let the
   choice be the number itself (worked template 3).
6. Add a message for each check (`if util <= 1: "OK" else: "Fails"`), so that the report says what
   the numbers mean.
7. Test it in Input mode, then in Report with the defaults. That is what a reader without the form
   sees.

The ribbon's Input/Output tab inserts a starting line for each kind: **Entry**, **Dropdown**,
**Radio** and **Checkbox** write the `?` form in a sheet. **Data grid** and **More input forms**
(labelled, vector, matrix and formula inputs) have no sheet form and insert `#UI` lines, marked
with `>>`. See [Input forms with `#UI`](calcpad/ui-inputs.md).

## Model bindings

A `'<!--civilkit: bind L = path -->` comment before an input can tie it to a quantity in a
structural model. The specification and the in-app marker exist; no model is connected yet, so
typed values are used.

**Related calculators:** [Simply supported beam](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/simply-supported-beam-calculator/), [Cantilever beam](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/cantilever-beam-calculator/), [Column buckling](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/column-buckling-calculator/), [Retaining wall stability](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/retaining-wall-stability-calculator/), [Pad footing bearing pressure](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/pad-footing-bearing-pressure-calculator/), [Pipe flow, Darcy-Weisbach](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/pipe-flow-darcy-weisbach-calculator/), [Pump operating point](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/pump-operating-point-calculator/). More pages are in [Calculators and guides](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/).

---

Chapter: Symbolic maths
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/symbolic

# Symbolic maths

<!-- description: The Symbolic dialog works exactly: it simplifies, factors, differentiates, integrates and solves, shown on a derivation of a beam deflection. -->

<p><strong>Video:</strong> Symbolic maths for a beam deflection</p>
<video controls preload="none" poster="videos/07-symbolic-beam-deflection.jpg" style="width:100%;max-width:960px" src="videos/07-symbolic-beam-deflection.mp4"></video>

The calculation engine is numeric: it gives you numbers. The **Symbolic** dialog gives you
formulas. It rearranges an equation, differentiates, integrates, solves for the constants of
integration and substitutes values, all *exactly*, with fractions kept as fractions and symbols kept
as symbols. Then you put the result into the sheet and let the engine check it with numbers.

Open it from **Functions > Symbolic** on the ribbon. The module loads the first time you run
something, and it works offline.

## Using the dialog

1. Type an expression, or an equation with `=`. Write `*` for every product and `^` for powers.
   The functions are `sin`, `cos`, `ln`, `exp` and `sqrt`; the constants are `pi` and `e`.
   Enter runs it; Shift+Enter starts a new line.
2. Choose the operation:

| Operation | What it needs | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Simplify | the expression | like terms collected, powers combined |
| Expand | the expression | products and powers of sums multiplied out |
| Factor | the expression | common factors, and polynomials in one variable |
| Differentiate | a variable, and an order (1 by default) | the derivative |
| Integrate | a variable, and for a definite integral both limits | an antiderivative (with no constant), or the value between the limits |
| Solve for | one variable for one equation (write `=`), or several variables separated by commas for a linear system whose equations are separated by `;` or new lines | the solutions; a quadratic gives both roots |
| Substitute | values such as `x = 2, b = 3*a` | the exact result |
| Evaluate | a number for every variable | a decimal number to 12 digits |

3. The result is typeset (with KaTeX) and also shown as text, with a **Copy** button.
4. **Insert into worksheet** writes the result at the cursor:
   * in a **sheet**: a display formula block (`$$ ... $$`, typeset in the preview) or a quantity line
     `name: expression`;
   * in a **Calcpad worksheet**: a calculation line `name = expression`, or a comment line.

   A quantity line is calculated by the engine, so every symbol in it needs a value in the sheet.
   Use the formula block to keep a result in terms of symbols.

## A worked derivation: the deflection of a simply supported beam

The beam has span L, uniform load w and stiffness EI. The bending moment at x is
M(x) = w L x / 2 - w x² / 2, and the deflection y, taken in the direction of the load, satisfies
EI y'' = -M(x). These are the dialog's results for each step (the inputs are in the first column).

| Step | Operation and input | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Integrate** `-(w*L*x/2 - w*x^2/2)/(E*I)` for `x` | `-L*w*x^2/(4*E*I) + w*x^3/(6*E*I)` |
| 2 | Add a constant `C1` yourself and **Integrate** again: `-(w*L*x^2/4 - w*x^3/6)/(E*I) + C1` for `x` | `-L*w*x^3/(12*E*I) + w*x^4/(24*E*I) + C1*x` |
| 3 | Add `C2`. The supports give y(0) = 0 and y(L) = 0, so **Solve for** `C1, C2` the equations `C2 = 0; -L^4*w/(12*E*I) + L^4*w/(24*E*I) + C1*L + C2 = 0` | `C1 = L^3*w/(24*E*I); C2 = 0` |
| 4 | **Substitute** `x = L/2` into the curve `-L*w*x^3/(12*E*I) + w*x^4/(24*E*I) + L^3*w*x/(24*E*I)` | `5*L^4*w/(384*E*I)` |

The midspan deflection is 5 w L⁴ / (384 E I). That is the formula to put in the sheet. The dialog
can also **differentiate** it (`5*L^3*w/(96*E*I)` with respect to L), or **evaluate** it for given
numbers: with `w = 12`, `L = 6`, `E = 200` and `I = 250` the result is `0.00405` (in consistent
units of your choice).

## Putting the result into a sheet

In the sheet, write the derivation as prose and display formulas, then give the engine the numbers
and check the formula against the curve:

```sheet
## Step 4: midspan

Substituting $x = L/2$ into the curve and simplifying gives

$$y\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) = \frac{5 L^4 w}{384 E I}$$

## Numbers

w: 12 kN/m | design load
L: 6 m | span
E: 200 GPa | modulus of elasticity
I: 250000000 mm^4 | second moment of area
delta: 5 * w * L^4 / (384 * E * I) -> mm | midspan deflection from the formula

y(x): -L * w * x^3 / (12 * E * I) + w * x^4 / (24 * E * I) + L^3 * w * x / (24 * E * I) | the curve with its constants
y_mid: y(L / 2) -> mm | the curve at midspan
ratio: y_mid / delta | 1 when the formula and the curve agree
```

```text
w = 12 kN/m    design load
L = 6 m    span
E = 200 GPa    modulus of elasticity
I = 250000000 mm⁴    second moment of area
δ = 5·w·L⁴/(384·E·I) = 5 · 12 kN/m · (6 m)⁴ / (384 · 200 GPa · 250000000 mm⁴) = 4.05 mm
y_mid = y(L/2) = y(6 m / 2) = 4.05 mm    the curve at midspan
ratio = y_mid / δ = 4.05 mm / 4.05 mm = 1
```

The two routes agree: the exact formula from the dialog and the curve with its constants give the
same 4.05 mm. The sample **Beam deflection derived symbolically** (Samples, group Sheet syntax)
is this sheet in full, with the deflection curve plotted:

```sheet
L: 6 m
w: 12 kN/m
E: 200 GPa
I: 250000000 mm^4
y(x): -L * w * x^3 / (12 * E * I) + w * x^4 / (24 * E * I) + L^3 * w * x / (24 * E * I)
plot -y(x * 1 m) / (1 mm) for x in 0..6
```

(The plot divides by `1 mm` to give the plot a plain number, and flips the sign so the beam sags
downward on the page.)

## Limits

The algebra is exact rational arithmetic, so a result that does not fit in 128 bits is an error
rather than a rounded guess, and a refusal is shown in words with the library's own message
("Cannot integrate: power of a non-linear base."). Nothing is guessed. The limits:

* no complex numbers;
* only `sin`, `cos`, `ln`, `exp` and `sqrt`;
* integration covers a small class of integrands;
* solving covers a single equation of degree 1 or 2, and linear systems of up to four unknowns;
* symbols are treated as positive real numbers, so `sqrt(x^2)` is `x`.

For anything else, use the numeric tools: `$Root`, `$Area`, `$Slope`, `lsolve` and friends.

**Related pages:** [The beam deflection formula, derived](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/beam-deflection-formula-derivation/). More pages are in [Calculators and guides](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/).

---

Chapter: Importing worksheets
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/importing

# Importing worksheets

<!-- description: Import .xmcd and .mcdx worksheets from another calculation tool as a live Calcpad worksheet: what converts, what is frozen and what does not. -->

<p><strong>Video:</strong> Import an existing worksheet</p>
<video controls preload="none" poster="videos/06-import-a-worksheet.jpg" style="width:100%;max-width:960px" src="videos/06-import-a-worksheet.mp4"></video>

The worksheet importer converts worksheet files from a spreadsheet-like calculation format, with
text, equations, plots and pictures placed freely on a page (files ending `.xmcd` and `.mcdx`), into
a new Calcpad worksheet that this engine calculates. It evaluates nothing itself: it only translates,
and then the one engine runs the result. Every number in the output is a number that was in the
source file.

**Nothing is uploaded.** The file is read and converted in the page, by a module that loads on first use.

## How to import

Any one of:

* **File > Import worksheet...**
* the **Import worksheet** button on the Document tab
* **File > Open...** and pick the file
* drag the file onto the page (a dashed hint shows while you drag)

The converted worksheet opens as a new unsaved tab named after the file, with the extension `.cpd`.
Picture files from the source go into the library under `/imported/<file name>/`. Importing the same
file name again replaces that folder.

A dialog then says how the import went, for example:

```text
Imported tank.xmcd: 18 of 21 regions converted live, 2 shown as static pictures, 1 need attention.
```

followed by a list of what did not convert, in plain words, by the number of regions affected
(for example "calls to a function from an add-in we cannot run" or "embedded objects"). Two toggles
re-run the import in the same tab:

* **Pictures of unconverted regions** (on by default): a region that cannot be converted is shown as a
  picture of the original, so the page still reads like the source.
* **Show saved results as static values** (off by default): places the values the source file saved
  where it could not compute them.

The dialog's last line repeats that the file was read in this page and was not uploaded.

## What converts

The importer follows the author's page: it reads regions in reading order and writes Calcpad lines.

| In the source | In the result |
| --- | --- |
| Text, with heading styles, bold, italic, underline, sub and superscript, paragraph fonts, sizes and colours | Text lines. Fonts and sizes can be tidied away (see below). |
| Definitions (`x := ...`), evaluations (`x =`), functions | Calcpad definitions and equation lines, with the source's names, subscripts and Greek letters. |
| Units | The same units, converted to this engine's names. A unit the engine does not know is reported. |
| Vectors, matrices and indexing | Vectors and matrices. The array origin is shifted to 1, with a note. |
| Sums, products, integrals, derivatives (supported forms) | The engine's `$Sum`, `$Product`, `$Area` and slope commands. |
| Programs made of loops and conditions, early exits, grown arrays | Expression blocks. |
| Plots (x-y plots) | `$Plot` lines. A plot's colours, markers and axis ranges may not carry over (a note says so). |
| Solve blocks of one or two unknowns | Solved here by iteration, and kept only if the equations hold at the answer; otherwise the value the file saved. |
| Statistics functions, complex numbers, simple text values (codes) | Converted. |
| Referenced worksheets | Their definitions are read in, when the file holds a copy. |
| Pictures | Embedded in the library. |

The author's equations are shown as the author wrote them (stacked fractions, sums with bounds,
subscripts, a transpose superscript), typeset as maths, and computed out of sight. The page reads
like the source, and the Word export turns the typeset equations into Word equations.

## What is frozen

Some values cannot be computed here, so the importer takes the number the source file *saved* and
shows it as a literal marked **frozen**:

* values that came from an input component (a combo box, a list box, a text box): the stored
  selection becomes the value, and it does not follow a change of the input;
* a call into a function from an external library (an add-in) that is not available here, when the
  file saved a value;
* a table read from a data file, as the table the worksheet saved;
* a solve block whose iteration does not verify.

The dialog counts frozen values and says so.

## What does not convert

Each gap is counted under a stable code and replaced by a placeholder: a typeset, not-calculated
equation or a static picture of the original. The main ones:

* range variables that fall outside the supported uses, and programs outside the supported subset;
* solve blocks of more than two unknowns, other solvers, symbolic evaluation;
* derivative and integral forms the importer does not map, and some summation forms;
* plots that are not x-y plots, or that store binary items;
* embedded objects, components, worksheet references with no copy, add-in functions with no saved value;
* text values that are joined, measured or formatted (`concat` and similar);
* a region the source has switched off, and some page headers and footers.

A region that depends on a gap is reported as downstream of it, and the dialog ranks the missing
features by the number of regions each blocks. A calculation that depends on an unconverted region
shows that region's names as undefined; read the dialog list first.

> The importer is a work in progress. Plan on checking an imported worksheet against the source,
> line by line, before relying on it, as you would with a hand conversion.

## After the import

* **Tidy text** (Document tab) removes imported fonts, sizes and colours from paragraphs and turns
  import markers into short notes. Equations are left alone.
* **Text to Markdown** tidies and then writes runs of simple paragraphs as Markdown, which you can then
  edit as rich text by double-clicking. See [Editing](editing.md).
* **Save**. The `.cpd` refers to the pictures by library path (`imported/<name>/R12.svg`). Pictures
  stay as long as the browser's library does. A `.cpd` opened later from disk shows its pictures
  only while the library holds them; export to HTML or Word first for a self-contained file.

## Limits

Input over 64 MiB, XML nested deeper than 256, a DTD, and pictures over 16 MiB each or 192 MiB in
total are refused or skipped. Errors are messages, not crashes: "... is not a worksheet this importer
reads", "not well-formed XML", "the file is a zip package that cannot be read".

**Related pages:** [Opening .xmcd and .mcdx files](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/mathcad-worksheet-converter/). More pages are in [Calculators and guides](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/).

---

Chapter: Number format
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/number-format

# Number format

Some languages write 1,5 where others write 1.5, and group digits as 1.000,5 or 1 000,5. CivilKit Calcs lets you
choose how numbers are **shown and typed**. Your worksheets do not change: a sheet always keeps the decimal point,
so a file reads the same on every machine.

## Choosing a format

Open **Settings** (the gear at the right end of the top strip). **Number format** is on the **General** tab, under
Language.

| Choice | Looks like |
|---|---|
| Automatic | follows the language of your browser |
| Point | 1,234.5 |
| Comma | 1.234,5 |
| Space and comma | 1 234,5 |

**Group digits** adds the thousands separator; it is off by default. The choice is remembered in this browser.
Add `?numfmt=comma` to the address to try a format on one page without storing it (`point`, `comma`, `space` or
`auto`, and `&numgroup=1` for digit groups).

## What changes

Results in the preview, the report, print and PDF, and the HTML export, plus the equations and text of the Word
export and the Report sheet of the Excel export. Excel's variable sheets keep real numbers. Variable names,
subscripts, exponents and units are never touched, and neither is text you wrote: a sentence that says
"use 1.5 m" stays as typed.

```sheet
L: 6.5 m
w: 12.5 kN/m
M: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m
```

```text
L = 6.5 m
w = 12.5 kN/m
M = w·L² / 8 = 12.5 kN/m · (6.5 m)² / 8 = 66.02 kN·m
```

In the Comma format that reads `L = 6,5 m` and `M = ... = 66,02 kN·m`, while the sheet itself still says `6.5`.

## Typing numbers

In a comma format an input box shows 6,5 and accepts both 6,5 and 6.5. The value the engine and the saved
values use is always 6.5. A slider moves the box as before, and a message such as "must be from 0,5 to 2,5" uses
your format. In an input box a point is always a decimal point, so write 1234,5 or 1 234,5 rather than 1.234.

## What does not change

Pasting into the editor is not converted, because a comma in a formula separates arguments. Plot axes, 3D views,
Python output and spreadsheet-style grids keep the decimal point.

---

Chapter: Exporting
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/exporting

# Exporting

<p><strong>Video:</strong> Export a report to Word, Excel and PDF</p>
<video controls preload="none" poster="videos/08-export-word-excel-pdf.jpg" style="width:100%;max-width:960px" src="videos/08-export-word-excel-pdf.mp4"></video>

A calculated sheet leaves the page in four ways: a PDF through the print dialog, a Word document,
an Excel workbook and standalone HTML. All of them are built in the page, from the same calculated
report, so what you see is what you export. The Word and Excel writers load the first time you use
them and work offline.

The **Document** tab has buttons for **Print PDF**, **Word**, **Excel** and **Export...**. The
File menu has **Print PDF...**, **Export...** and **Export Excel...**. The **Export** dialog lists the
views you can export (Report, Preview, Input form, Unwrapped), each with its own **Save PDF**,
**Save Word** (not offered for the input form and the unwrapped listing) and **Save HTML** buttons,
and a **Plots** list that downloads each plot as an image, or all of them as a ZIP.

Which view to export: **Report** is the usual choice. It applies the values entered in an input form,
hides `#pre` text and shows `#post` text. Preview shows what the results pane shows.

## Page breaks

To start a new page at a point in the report, put a page break line there:

```sheet
# Loads

w: 12 kN/m | design load

<div style="page-break-after:always"></div>

# Bending

L: 6 m
M: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m
```

**Print PDF** and **Word** both start "Bending" on a new page. You do not need to type the line:

* In a sheet, the **+** between two blocks has **Page break** at the end of its menu.
* The ribbon has **Page break** on the **Document** tab (Page group) and the **Text Formatting** tab.
  It inserts the line at the cursor.

The preview draws the break as a dashed line labelled "Page break". The line is not printed and is
not in the Word file. A Calcpad worksheet (`.cpd`) writes the same thing as an HTML comment line,
`'<div style="page-break-after:always"></div>`, and the ribbon button inserts that form there.

Word also honours the other ways HTML forces a break on an element (`page-break-before: always`,
`break-before: page`, `break-after: page`). Excel has no pages, so the workbook ignores page breaks.

## Word

**Word** writes a `.docx` of the report:

* Equations are real Word equations (Office Math): fractions, subscripts, sums, matrices, units.
  In a test sheet with a handful of formulas the document held 21 equations.
* Headings, paragraphs, lists, links and tables keep their form. A Markdown pipe table gets rules.
* Plots and other drawings are pictures. A plot is stored as a PNG (the SVG is kept beside it, for
  versions of Word that read SVG).
* Pictures from the library are embedded.
* A formula typeset with LaTeX in a sheet appears as its TeX source in italics, not as a Word equation.
* An interactive Plotly chart cannot be carried. A paragraph stands where it was.
  A matplotlib figure from a Python block is carried as a picture.

The Word document has been checked in LibreOffice, not in Microsoft Word.

## Excel

**Excel** writes a workbook that mirrors the calculation:

| Sheet | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| Report | The report in document order. Headings and text in merged cells; every equation a row with its description, name, expression, expression with the numbers put in, value and unit. Text tables are cell ranges. |
| Variables | Every variable in the order it was first assigned, with its last value and unit. |
| One sheet for each vector or matrix | Its elements, a row per row, with the unit. A variable's row on Variables links to it. |
| Inputs | The variables set by input fields and `#UI` controls. |
| Plot data | The points of every plot, two columns per curve. |

A `plot` line or `$Plot` becomes a **native Excel XY chart** on the Report sheet at the place of the
plot, with its series pointing at the Plot data sheet, so you can edit the data and the chart redraws.
For a test sheet with one `plot` line the workbook held one chart and these sheets: Report,
Variables, K, F, u, Inputs and Plot data (K, F and u being a matrix and two vectors).

What the chart loses against the drawing: the faint fill under a curve, the exact fonts and grid
style. Colour maps and other drawings are pictures. The cells hold calculated values with the
expressions as text, not live Excel formulas.

The workbook opens in LibreOffice and a Python reader. It has not been tried in Microsoft Excel.

## PDF

**Print PDF** opens the browser's print dialog on the report. Choose "Save as PDF" as the destination.
The page size, orientation and margins come from the PDF settings (Settings, Export tab; Document > Header and footer opens it there).
The printed page carries the browser's own header and footer in place of title, date and page
numbers; turn "Headers and footers" off in the print dialog if you do not want them.

The printed page is the report: the buttons under plots are not printed, and an interactive chart is
replaced by a note.

## HTML

**Save HTML** writes a standalone page with the report, its styles, fonts and pictures. An exported
input form is static: it shows the controls, but nothing recalculates behind them.

## Files a worksheet writes

`#write` and `#append` save matrices to files. The browser keeps the file in the library and
downloads it when its content changes. By default this happens when you make a report; the Export
dialog's **Write files** choice and **Write to Disk** button change that.

## From the command line

The command-line front end of the engine converts a Calcpad worksheet to HTML, Word or Excel:
`Cli input.cpd output.xlsx`. It is built from the same code. A sheet has to be compiled first
(Convert to Calcpad, or the sheet compiler), because the command line reads Calcpad.

**Related pages:** [Export to Word, Excel and PDF](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/export-calculations-to-word-excel-pdf/), [Calculations instead of spreadsheets](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/excel-alternative-for-engineering-calculations/). More pages are in [Calculators and guides](https://civilkit.io/calcs/learn/).

---

Chapter: Editing
URL: https://civilkit.io/calcs/guide/editing

# Editing

There are two places to edit: the source on the left and, in the results, the page itself.

## What you can write

A sheet holds prose, quantity and input lines, conditions and loops, plots, Python blocks and
diagrams. [The line kinds](sheet/index.md#the-line-kinds) lists each one with its chapter. A
diagram is a fenced `mermaid` block of text that the results draw as boxes and arrows; see
[Diagrams](sheet/prose.md#diagrams) for a first example and [the Diagrams chapter](sheet/diagrams.md)
for more.

## The source editor

The editor colours a sheet by role (prose, quantity, block, raw Calcpad, plot). It underlines
mistakes and lists them in the **Errors** dialog; the status bar at the bottom shows the error,
warning and information counts.

| Action | How |
| --- | --- |
| Complete a name, function, unit or keyword | just type; Tab accepts the highlighted entry, Ctrl+Space opens the list by hand |
| Rename a name everywhere | F2, or the editor's context menu, or the Variables tab (right-click a name) |
| Find a variable or function and its value | Ctrl+; (Cmd+; on a Mac) |
| Go to a name's definition | F12, or hover to see the defining line and its Calcpad spelling |
| Find references | Shift+F12, or the editor's context menu |
| Tidy the sheet | Shift+Alt+F (Format Document) |
| Wrap long lines | Alt+Z |
| Find | Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on a Mac) |
| Insert a symbol, function, unit or snippet | the **Insert** tab in the sidebar, or the ribbon |

### Completion

The list opens as you type, in a worksheet and in a sheet alike, and offers what fits where the
cursor is:

* **Names defined above the cursor**, with their last calculated value next to them
  (`load = 12 kN`). A name defined further down is not offered, and neither is the word you are
  typing. The parameters of the function you are writing on the current line are offered too.
  Greek letters, subscripts and primes work as in any name: typing `σ` finds `σ_c`.
* **Built-in functions**, with their parameters and a one-line description. Pick one and Tab fills the
  call with a placeholder for each argument. In a sheet the arguments are separated with commas, in
  a worksheet with `;`. The same list is what the [function reference](reference/functions.md) shows.
* **Units, only units, right after a number** (`5 k` offers `kN`, `kg`, `kA`), and after a unit and
  `*` or `/` (`5kN*`). A sheet offers units after `->` as well. A worksheet's own custom units are in the list.
* **`#` directives and `$` commands** at the start of a line of a worksheet (`#fo` offers `#for`).
* **Block keywords and format markers** at the start of a line of a sheet: `if`, `else`, `for`, `while`,
  `repeat`, `plot`, `>>`, code fences for `calcpad` and `python`, `$$`, the input forms (`input`, `dropdown`,
  `slider`, `radio`, `checkbox`) and `<!--sheet-->` on the first line.

Nothing is offered where the text is not code: a text or comment line, after a quote mark, in a note
(after `|`), in a string, in a `#markdown`, `#html` or `#python` block, in sheet prose and
formulas, and after the `?` of an input. The calculated values come from one calculation of the
whole worksheet (Python blocks are not run for it), so the first list after an edit may show the
value from a moment ago; the list never waits more than a quarter of a second for it.

### Rename everywhere

Put the cursor on a variable, function or macro and press **F2** (also in the editor's context
menu, and in the Variables tab: right-click a name and choose **Rename Everywhere**). A small box
opens at the top of the editor. It says how many places and lines will change, marks every place in
the text and shows the first changed lines as they will read. Enter (or the **Rename** button) applies
it as **one undo step**; Esc cancels.

* **Scope is respected.** A function's parameters, and the name bound inside `$Sum{ ... }`, are renamed only
  on their own line; a macro's parameters only inside its `#def` block. Renaming a variable `a` leaves
  a parameter `a` alone, and the other way round. In a sheet the same holds for a function's parameters
  and the variable of a `plot` line.
* **Only code is renamed.** Comments and text lines, strings, `#markdown` and `#html` blocks, and in a sheet
  prose, notes after `|`, headings, `$...$` formulas, and the unit after a number (`3 psi` stays) are left as
  they are. A formula is typeset text, not a reference to a variable, so it is not renamed.
* **Inputs follow the name.** A `?` input (`L = ?`, `L: ? 6 m`) is an ordinary definition and is renamed with the name.
* **Python is left alone except for what it hands over.** The names a Python block passes to the worksheet with
  `export(name=...)` or `export("name", ...)` are the worksheet's variables, so they are renamed with
  the name (the box counts them). Any other Python code, which is not a reference to a worksheet variable,
  is never touched.
* **A name that would collide is refused**, with the reason, and **Rename** stays off: a name that is not valid
  (it starts with a letter and holds letters, digits, `_` and primes), a keyword or built-in function or constant,
  a name already in use in the document or in an included file, and a name a parameter on a changed line would
  capture (or that would hide a variable used inside the function). A name that is also a unit is allowed, with a note.
* A name defined in an `#include`d file cannot be renamed from here (only this document is edited).

### The variable palette

**Ctrl+;** (Cmd+; on a Mac) opens a search box over every variable, function and macro of the document, each with
its last calculated value and unit and the line it is defined on. The key is not used by the browsers or by the
editor itself. Type to filter: letters in order are enough (`sc` finds `sigma_c`), and built-in functions are included
once you type something. **Up** and **Down** choose, **Enter** inserts the name at the caret (a function goes in as
`name()` with the caret between the brackets), **Alt+Enter** (or the arrow button on the row) goes to where it is
defined, **Esc** or the same key closes it. A tap on a row inserts it, so it works on a touch screen. The Variables tab
in the sidebar has the same names, with a search box that matches the name, the definition, the parameters
and the note.

The Insert tab has a search box that filters the whole library. In a sheet, entries that have no
sheet form (the data grid and the other `#UI` forms, `$Map`, directives) carry a `>>` mark and insert Calcpad text as `>>` lines.

### The text toolbar

Select some words in a line of prose, or click into one, and a small toolbar appears above the line:
**Style** (Normal, Heading 1, 2 or 3), **B**, *I*, **</>** for code, **Link**, a bulleted list and a
numbered list. It does not appear on quantity lines, in code fences or inside a `$$` formula, where
those would only add characters that mean something else. The same toolbar appears over the text in
the in-place rich-text editor.

Each button's tooltip shows the Markdown it types (`Bold: **text**`, `Link: [text](address)`,
`Numbered list: 1. item`), so you can learn the syntax and type it yourself next time.

* A button is a toggle: Bold on text that is already bold takes the `**` off again, and a list button
  on a list takes the markers off. A button that is on is shown pressed.
* With no selection, Bold wraps the word at the caret.
* **Link** wraps the selection as `[text](url)` and selects `url`, ready for the address.
* The edit is made in the source, in one undo step, and the editor keeps the focus.
* On a phone or tablet the floating bar stays away so it does not fight the system selection menu;
  the in-place editor keeps its fixed bar there.

## In-place editing in the results

Edit a sheet *where it stands*, in the preview.

* **Click** a block (a quantity line, a plot line, a table, a formula, a paragraph) and an editor opens
  over it. Dragging to select text does not open it.
* **Click away** applies the change. **Esc** throws it away. **Enter** applies at once (Ctrl+Enter
  for prose, where Enter makes a new line).
* Input and calculation lines are one-line edits. A paragraph, a heading, a list or a table opens
  as **rich text**: a small toolbar over the text with bold, italic, heading levels, bullets, a
  table and its row and column controls. A line under the box says "Ctrl+Enter or click away to
  apply · Esc to cancel".
* Everything you apply is written back to the source in one undo step. A paragraph or table you open
  and apply without changing keeps its exact original lines.

In a Calcpad worksheet, prose written as Markdown (a `#markdown` ... `#end markdown` block) is edited
the same way, by **double-clicking** it. The worksheet importer's Tidy and Markdown options write
this form (see [Importing worksheets](importing.md)).

What the rich-text editor writes is plain Markdown: `**bold**`, `_italic_`, `~x~` subscript, `^x^`
superscript, `++x++` underline, `-` lists and pipe tables (no merged cells; a cell is one line).
It loads the first time you use it.

### Insert between blocks

Move the pointer between two rendered blocks and a dashed line appears with a **+** in the middle.
Click the **+** for a menu of blocks to insert there: Math line, Text, Heading, List, Table, Plot,
Condition, Python or Page break (see [Page breaks](exporting.md#page-breaks)). The new block goes in front of the next block's source line, indented like it,
and its first word is left selected in the editor so you can type over it. On a touch screen the
**+** stays hidden until you tap a block, and then shows only in the two gaps beside it.

### Cut, copy and paste blocks

The block menu (the **⋮** grip at the left of a block) has **Cut**, **Copy** and **Paste below**.
Copy puts the block's source text on the system clipboard, so you can also paste it into another
sheet or a chat. Cut does the same and then deletes the block, with an **Undo** toast. **Paste below**
inserts the clipboard text after the block, with one blank line between, as a single undo step. If
the browser will not let the page read the system clipboard, Paste uses the last block you copied
or cut in this window. The **+** menu between blocks also lists **Paste** whenever there is something
to paste.

**Ctrl+Shift+K** (**Cmd+Shift+K** on a Mac) deletes the block that holds the editor caret, with the
same Undo toast. In a file that is not a sheet it keeps its usual meaning, delete line.

### Turning a block off

**Disable** in the block menu comments a block out: it drops out of the preview and the calculation
but stays in the sheet. A sheet has no multi-line comment, so each line of the block is wrapped in
an HTML comment (the one comment the language has):

```sheet
a: 2 m
<!-- b: a * 3 -->
```

A disabled block is not drawn at all, so it has no grip. To get it back, put the caret in it and press
**Ctrl+Shift+/** (**Cmd+Shift+/** on a Mac), which toggles Disable and Enable, or press Undo
right after disabling. Limits: every line is wrapped on its own, a blank line inside the block
becomes an empty comment so the block stays in one piece, and a `-->` inside a line is written as
`--&gt;` while it is disabled and restored on Enable. Anything that used a disabled math line sees
an undefined name until it is enabled again.

### Collapsing sections

Hover a heading in a sheet and a small arrow shows under its grip. Click it and every block under
the heading, up to the next heading of the same or a higher level, folds away; the heading shows
how many blocks are hidden. Click the arrow again to open the section. A folded `##` section hides
only its own blocks, a folded `#` section hides its `##` sub-sections too. The grip menu of a
heading also has **Collapse all** and **Expand all**.

Folding is only a view: the sheet text and the results do not change, and printing and exporting
always include everything. Folds stay as you edit and when you switch between tabs. Headings are
matched by level, text and how many headings with the same text come before them.

### Sorting a table

Click a column heading of a table in the preview to sort its rows by that column: the first click
sorts ascending, the second descending, the third puts the rows back in the order of the source. An
arrow next to the heading shows which way it is sorted. A column of numbers sorts by value, even
with a unit after the number (`2.5 kN` comes before `10 kN`); any other column sorts as text, with
`A2` before `A10`. Empty cells stay at the bottom.

Sorting is only a view, like folding: the sheet text does not change, the sort stays as you edit,
and printing and exporting show the rows as they are written. The headings are buttons, so Tab
reaches them and Enter or Space sorts; on a phone, tap a heading. See
[Tables](sheet/prose.md#tables).

### Reordering blocks

Drag a block's grip up or down; a blue line shows where it will land, and the block goes there when
you let go. Dragging a heading takes its whole section along: the heading and the blocks up to the
next heading of the same or a higher level (folded blocks too). A section cannot be dropped inside
itself. The move is one step in the editor's history, and a toast offers **Undo**. A click on the
grip, or a movement of under 6 pixels, still opens its menu. On a touch screen, tap a block to show
its grip, then drag the grip.

### Plot chips

Under each plot in the preview there is a row of chips: Log x, Log y, 1:1 (equal axis scale),
Copy data, PNG and SVG. Copy data puts the plotted values on the clipboard as tab-separated text,
ready for a spreadsheet. The 3D plots have Copy data and PNG only.

### Sliders on inputs

Give a number input a range and Input mode shows a slider under its box:

```sheet
L: ? 6 m [2 .. 12 step 0.5] | span
w: ? 12 kN/m [0 .. 30] | design load
M: w * L^2 / 8 -> kN*m | maximum moment
```

Dragging the slider (or using the arrow keys, Home and End) fills the box and recalculates the
results while you drag; typing in the box moves the slider. The numbers are in the unit of the
default, the slider stops at the minimum and maximum, and `step` is the size of one stop (without it,
about a hundredth of the range). A line without brackets has no slider. A typed value outside the bounds is refused with a message beside the box. On a phone the track is
taller so a finger can use it. See [Templates with inputs](templates.md#sliders).

## The math keyboard

The **Keyboard** item in the status bar opens an on-screen math keyboard with tabs for numbers and
operators, functions, calculus and plots (sum, integral, root, parametric plot), matrices, capital
and lower-case letters, Greek letters and units. On a computer it is a panel you can drag by its title; on a touch screen it docks
at the bottom. A key or template inserts at the cursor of the editor, or of the in-place editor when
one is open. In a sheet, angles are degrees unless the sheet has a `#rad` line.

## Convert a selection to a formula

Select an expression you wrote in a sentence, say `w*L^2/8`, and press **Ctrl+Shift+E** (**Cmd+Shift+E** on a
Mac), or choose **Convert Selection to Formula** in the editor's right-click menu, or **= Formula** on the text
toolbar. In a sheet this

```sheet
w: 12 kN/m
L: 6 m

The moment at midspan is w*L^2/8.
```

becomes

<!-- expect: res1 = w · L ^2 8 | 54 kNm -->
```sheet
w: 12 kN/m
L: 6 m

The moment at midspan is w*L^2/8.
res1: w*L^2/8
```

The new line goes after the paragraph, and its name is selected: type a better one (`Mmid`) and it is
named. Where the selection lands:

* **In text** (prose, a note after `|`, a Calcpad text line or comment): a line of its own after the
  paragraph. In a sheet it is a named line, `res1: w*L^2/8`; in a Calcpad worksheet a plain calculation
  line, `w*L^2/8`. If the selection is the whole line, the line itself becomes the formula. A selection
  written with its name, `M = w*L^2/8`, keeps that name, and `$...$`, backticks and a full stop around it
  are dropped.
* **In a calculation**: the expression is pulled out to a named line above, and the selection becomes the
  name: `M: w*L^2/8 -> kN*m` turns into `res1: w*L^2/8` and `M: res1 -> kN*m`. Both copies of `res1` are
  selected, so typing a name renames the two at once.

The new name is the first of `res1`, `res2`, ... that the document does not use yet. The whole change is one
undo step. A selection that is not an expression on one line (plain words, a heading, a code fence, an
input's default) is left alone and the editor says so. On a phone or tablet a **= Formula** button shows
under the selection instead of the toolbar.

## The sidebar
